The report, The Invisible Toll: Rising D
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24 – The National Treasury and the State Department for Children Services are set to launch a new report proposing measures to protect government funding for children’s services amid rising public debt and declining development assistance.
The report, The Invisible Toll: Rising Debt, Shrinking Aid and Kenya’s Children, outlines practical policy options aimed at ensuring that fiscal pressures do not undermine essential services targeting children.
Prepared through the Public Debt Management Office with technical support from UNICEF Kenya, the study is expected to inform the formulation of the 2027 Budget Policy Statement and the 2027/28 national budget.
Among the proposed interventions are predictable releases of government funds, reliable social assistance programmes and protected financing for services critical to children’s welfare.
The report highlights concerns over the impact of Kenya’s tightening fiscal space on children, who account for more than two in every five people in the country.
It also estimates that approximately half of the country’s children face overlapping monetary and multidimensional poverty.
The research draws on national data and interviews conducted in eight counties, including Busia, Embu, Garissa, Homa Bay, Kilifi, Mandera, Nairobi and Turkana.
The proposed policy interventions seek to ensure that children’s needs remain a priority in public expenditure decisions despite competing demands on government resources.
The event will take place in Nairobi on Wednesday, November 25, 2026

items.text:
Yemen’s army says Houthi fighters closing in on government stronghold of Aden
Yemen's military on Tuesday said that Houthi fighters were closing in on the internationally recognised government's stronghold of Aden from about 60km (40 miles) away and vowed to repel any assault. A military spokesman said defences were prepared following Houthi advances and government pullbacks near the Red Sea.
Yemen's armed forces said Tuesday that Houthi fighters were ready to attack the internationally recognised government's stronghold of Aden, vowing to head off any potential assault.
"Yes, Houthi forces are about 60 kilometres (40 miles) from the city. We take that seriously, and we are ready for it," said military spokesman Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili during a briefing.
Read moreYemen: Why the Houthis may besiege Aden rather than storm it
"They are now ready to attack. We have made our preparations to defend Aden."
The comments come on the heels of recent advances by the Houthis this month, as the Yemeni government pulled back its forces from areas near the Red Sea to reinforce troops "where current circumstances require", with securing Aden and nearby provinces taking priority.
On November 15, six Yemeni sources told AFP the Houthis had seized control of the Al-Maqatirah and Al-Madaribah districts and positioned themselves 60 kilometres from the southern city.
"The situation is not where we want it to be. But it's not as dire as reported," Nuzaili insisted.
"Taking Aden is a hypothetical situation. It will not happen," he said. "Our forces and our government will make sure that Aden is not at risk."
On Tuesday, Yemen's leader Rashad al-Alimi – the head of the country's presidential council – struck a defiant tone in the face of the Houthi threat.
"We trust in the ability of the Yemeni people and their armed forces to end the Houthi threat, no matter how the front lines shift," he wrote in a post on X.
Read moreYemen's Houthis target Riyadh after Saudi coalition's 'special operation'
The Houthis have repeatedly struck the city of Aden in recent weeks, including an assault on October 15 that targeted the presidential palace and left four people dead, according to government military sources.
The Iran-backed group previously launched an unsuccessful bid to seize Aden early in the war in 2015.
Yemen's internationally recognised government has been based in Aden since it was driven from the capital Sanaa by the Houthis in 2014.
Yemen, embroiled in more than a decade of civil war, was sucked into the wider US-Iran conflict in July when a truce between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed government unravelled.
Since then, the fighting has left more than 1,600 people dead and over 300,000 displaced in the country, the poorest on the Arabian Peninsula, according to the latest UN toll.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

French ex-President Sarkozy and wife Carla Bruni to face trial
- Published
Nicolas Sarkozy and his wife Carla Bruni-Sarkozy are to face trial next year over charges stemming from the former French president's conviction for conspiring to fund his election campaign with money from late Libyan dictato
items.text:
French ex-President Sarkozy and wife Carla Bruni to face trial
- Published
Nicolas Sarkozy and his wife Carla Bruni-Sarkozy are to face trial next year over charges stemming from the former French president's conviction for conspiring to fund his election campaign with money from late Libyan dictator Muammar Gaddafi.
The charges centre on the retraction of the testimony of a key witness who had initially said he had evidence that could incriminate Sarkozy.
The pair deny any wrongdoing.
Sarkozy was given a five-year sentence in the case last September and became the first French ex-president to go to jail, even though he only spent 20 days behind bars. He has always denied doing anything wrong in the case and the appeals verdict is expected next Monday.
Since losing his re-election bid in 2012, Sarkozy has faced several criminal investigations.
In 2024, he was handed a one-year sentence – of which six months were suspended – over the illegal financing of his 2012 re-election campaign.
In 2021, he was found guilty of trying to bribe a judge and sentenced to three years in jail – two of them suspended – and thus became the first former French president to get a custodial sentence. He was allowed to serve his time at home wearing a tag instead of going to jail.
The new case centres on a Libyan businessman, Ziad Takieddine, who had said he had written proof that Sarkozy's 2007 campaign bid was "abundantly" financed by Tripoli, and that the €50m (£43m) in payments continued after he became president.
Takieddine, who died last year, withdrew his accusations in an interview in 2020.
At the time, Sarkozy was said to have stated: the "truth is finally coming out", but officials found the retraction to be "insincere" and a new investigation was launched into the "Save Sarko" file – the nickname the alleged perpetrators had used for the operation, according to French media.
So the former head of state and his wife, an Italian-born former supermodel and singer, will now face the charge of "criminal conspiracy to commit fraud as part of an organised group and receiving stolen goods related to witness tampering". They deny any wrongdoing.

items.title: Tidal to ban and remove millions of AI-generated tracks as AI slop inundates music streaming
items.summary: Music streaming service Tidal said on Tuesday that it will start banning and removing songs generated fully with AI in a bid to stem the flood of submissions to its platform. The company said that over the past 90 days, more than 43% of tracks uploaded to its platform were generated by AI, and that
items.text:
Music streaming service Tidal said on Tuesday that it will start banning and removing songs generated fully with AI in a bid to stem the flood of submissions to its platform. The company said that over the past 90 days, more than 43% of tracks uploaded to its platform were generated by AI, and that was a major reason driving this decision.
Tidal said it will start removing fully AI-generated music on December 9, and the process will result in more than 29 million songs being deleted from the platform by the end of the year. With the new rules in place, the platform said it will be rejecting roughly 80,000-85,000 tracks per day.
Tidal is also banning distribution services from delivering 100% AI-generated tracks, and will reject submissions if songs’ metadata says they are made fully using AI.
The company said it will still accept songs that were made with AI assistance, but not fully generated.
The move comes as AI-generated music inundates streaming services across the board. Tidal is one of the first major platforms after Bandcamp to ban AI music outright. Deezer, which also provides detection tools to other streaming services, said that it will introduce a toggle to let users filter out AI music. Larger platforms like Spotify and YouTube Music have adopted a milder approach to this issue, choosing to label AI-generated music instead of offering filters or taking stronger measures.
Tidal started de-monetizing songs made using AI in June, but that did not prove enough of a deterrent, Tidal Music’s lead, Robert Anderson, said on X.
The company said that 27 million, or 6.3% of tracks on the platform, are fully AI-generated, but 96% of those have no streams.
“It’s true that not all songs catch on immediately, and artists should have time to build their fanbases. But this situation is different – at this scale, the authentic music and artists that Tidal subscribers are looking to listen to and discover get buried,” the company said in a post.
Meanwhile, music labels are trying to make money by partnering with platforms and AI model makers to sell their catalog for training or remixing features. Goldman Sachs estimates that by 2035, AI-related licensing tools and new monetization opportunities have the potential to improve record labels’ revenue by 10%.

Saurav Das said he was meant to b
items.text:
Indian government has 'lost the plot', says 'cockroach' leader barred from UK flight
- Published
One of the leaders of India's "cockroach" movement has said the Delhi government has "completely lost the plot" after he was stopped from leaving the country for the UK.
Saurav Das said he was meant to board a flight on Tuesday morning but was told by immigration officers his passport had been "flagged" because of discrepancies involving his date of birth.
In an interview with the BBC, Das said there were no discrepancies in his documents, accusing the Indian government of using cheap tactics to stop activists from travelling and speaking on issues that matter to young people.
The BBC has reached out to the federal home ministry, Delhi police and airport officials for comment.
Saurav told the BBC World Service's Newshour programme the incident showed the government was "scared".
"They are scared of the cockroach movement. They're scared of young people asking them questions because they have never had to deal with a generation that wants to ask questions so head on. So that jitters them."
By not allowing him to travel, he said the government had lowered India's stature in the world.
"It's international news that I am unable to travel to the UK," he said. "And this shows Prime Minister Modi in such poor light.
"It's a way to harass, to target activists, young voices in India by the Modi government."
Das said he had been invited by the Oxford Union, as well as universities including Cambridge and Edinburgh, to speak about the movement.
Ratna Singh, another leader of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), wrote: "The manner in which Saurav was not allowed to board today raises deeply troubling questions about the state of freedom of expression and the space being allowed for young voices in this country."
On Tuesday, the London School of Economics Student Union's Amnesty International Unit, a student-led charity group, shared a post on Instagram saying that an event featuring Das had been "indefinitely postponed".
Das, a former journalist, became one of the faces of the CJP - a Gen Z-led movement that began as satire but has since emerged as a youth-led pressure group.
In July, protests spearheaded by the CJP over exam paper leaks led to the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan .
In October, CJP leaders including Das were among thousands detained by the police for trying to hold protests demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Kumar and the Election Commission have denied wrongdoing.
The same month, Das and Ashutosh Ranka, another CJP leader, were jailed for seven days after being arrested for trespassing at a banned protest site in Delhi.
Das insisted the CJP would continue protesting, but it did not want to be a political party "as of today".
"It's a long haul. We are not here for a short time. We are looking at India in the next 10 to 20 years. How do we develop India into a better country? That is the vision that we want to carry forward."
Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of CJP, wrote on X that if Das "had looted a bank or committed financial fraud", he may have been allowed to fly to London, referring to billionaire bank-loan defaulters who have left India.
There have been other instances in recent years of people being prevented from boarding flights.
In September 2025, Bhanu Tatak, an environmental and anti-dam activist from India's north-eastern Arunachal Pradesh state, was stopped from boarding a flight to Dublin.
In March 2022, Rana Ayyub, an investigative journalist and outspoken critic of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government, was also stopped from boarding a flight to London at the Mumbai airport. She was due to speak at different events on media freedom and the targeting of journalists.
Additional reporting by Cherylann Mollan.

Hewitt was granted access to the i
items.text:
FA chief signs NDA to view Fifa sell-off plot documents
- Published
Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt has signed a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) as a condition of viewing documents related to Fifa president Gianni Infantino's failed World Cup sell-off plot.
Hewitt was granted access to the information at the world governing body's headquarters in Zurich.
Earlier this month, Fifa said "key documents" on the abandoned plan to sell stakes in its tournaments to private investors would be made available to members of its council, but only in person and under "strict review protocols to preserve confidentiality".
Uefa had demanded Fifa release details about the controversial Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, and answer questions relating to its decision-making.
Hewitt was among a group of council members who wrote to Fifa to say they were "concerned that any review would seemingly be limited to certain 'key documents'… which in turn would only be available for review under unknown 'strict review protocols'".
They also asked for clarity on what the protocols were, and "an explanation as to why Fifa considers such restrictions necessary since it is not clear why our rights are being limited in such a way".
The NDA means Hewitt cannot reveal what she has read, or comment about it publicly.
Fair Square, which campaigns for greater accountability in sport, told BBC Sport: "Debbie Hewitt and the FA didn't need to see the details of FFE to know that it was a gross abuse of presidential power.
"As a member association, the FA is entitled to hold the Fifa president accountable for his actions, and as a Fifa Council vice-president, Hewitt should have seen these plans as soon as they were hatched.
"They had the right to demand to see these documents, and should have exercised that right forcefully and publicly, rather than signing a gagging clause that puts Fifa and Infantino back in control."
- 115 days, 39 private-jet flights, one election - Infantino's globetrotting 
  - Published11 hours ago
- Senegal reinstated as Afcon 2025 winners by court ruling 
  - Published40 minutes ago
Hewitt has previously criticised Infantino for a lack of transparency.
However, she embraced the Fifa president at a ceremony in Zurich on Monday when the UK bid to host the 2035 Women's World Cup was ratified at a special ceremony.
It is unclear whether she viewed the files on the same day, and which documents have been made available.
Last week, BBC Sport revealed the FA had considered challenging Infantino's eligibility to run for a fourth term as Fifa president, and that it is backing French candidate Philippe Diallo in next year's presidential election.
Fifa has been approached for comment. Sources have previously indicated Fifa's ability to answer some questions is limited by legal action that Uefa launched in October in the US, requesting disclosure of evidence and documents, warning it could lodge a criminal complaint in Switzerland.

items.title: France's ex-president Nicolas Sarkozy, wife Carla Bruni to stand trial for alleged witness tampering
items.summary:
France's ex-president Nicolas Sarkozy, wife Carla Bruni to stand trial for alleged witness tampering
France's former president Nicolas Sarkozy and his wife, singer Carla Bruni-Sarkozy, are set to be tried in 2027 on charges of "criminal conspiracy with intent to commit fraud" as well as benefitting
items.text:
France's ex-president Nicolas Sarkozy, wife Carla Bruni to stand trial for alleged witness tampering
France's former president Nicolas Sarkozy and his wife, singer Carla Bruni-Sarkozy, are set to be tried in 2027 on charges of "criminal conspiracy with intent to commit fraud" as well as benefitting from witness tampering. The new charges are related to the Sarkozy couple's actions during the case examining illegal campaign funding from Libyan strongman Muammar Gaddafi over which Sarkozy was imprisoned last year.
France's ex-president Nicolas Sarkozy, his wife, singer Carla Bruni-Sarkozy, and a paparazzi boss will stand trial next year over alleged witness tampering in a case over funding for his 2007 election, a source close to the case said Tuesday.
France's right-wing leader from 2007 to 2012 has been embroiled in legal woes since leaving office.
Last year he became modern France's first former president to go to jail over seeking illegal campaign funding from late Libyan dictator Muammar Gaddafi in exchange for help restoring his international image.
Read moreEx-president Sarkozy’s 20-day prison diary: ‘Like the Count of Monte Cristo’?
The former head of state was freed from jail after 20 days pending his appeal, and an appeals court is to issue its ruling on Monday.
One of the main accusers in the case was French-Lebanese businessman Ziad Takieddine, who died in Lebanon last year.
In 2016 he claimed he helped deliver up to €5 million ($6 million) in cash from Gaddafi to Sarkozy and the former president's chief of staff in 2006 and 2007.
But in November 2020, Takieddine suddenly retracted his incriminating statement in an interview with French media.
He later returned to his initial claims.
Read moreKey Lebanese-French accuser in Sarkozy Libya funding probe dies on eve of verdict
This prompted accusations that Sarkozy and his wife enlisted the help of paparazzi queen Mimi Marchand to pay the witness to change his mind, something they have always denied.
Bruni is suspected of having requested a clandestine phone line in late 2019 to communicate with Marchand about the Takieddine operation.
A court will in November next year try Sarkozy and Bruni on charges of "criminal conspiracy with intent to commit fraud" as well as benefitting from witness tampering, the source told AFP.
Marchand stands accused of "criminal conspiracy with intent to commit fraud" as well as witness tampering.
Their lawyers did not immediately respond to an AFP request for comment.
The defendants face a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison and a fine of €150,000.
Sarkozy has received two definitive convictions in other cases – linked to overspending in his failed 2012 re-election bid, and later trying to extract favours from a judge.
Marchand was last year handed an 18-month suspended prison sentence for blackmailing a television host, who feared the paparazzi boss would publish images of her daughter leaving police custody.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

items.summary:
African rivals fret over Morocco’s growing football dominance
As Morocco enjoys success on and off the pitch, is it benefitting from preferential treatment, or setting an example?
Morocco’s growing influence in African football is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.

items.text:
African rivals fret over Morocco’s growing football dominance
As Morocco enjoys success on and off the pitch, is it benefitting from preferential treatment, or setting an example?
Morocco’s growing influence in African football is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.
From reaching the semifinals of the 2022 FIFA World Cup to hosting major continental competitions and preparing to cohost the 2030 World Cup, it has arguably become Africa’s dominant footballing nation.
Morocco is also preparing to welcome FIFA’s 77th Congress in Rabat on March 18, 2027, and the country hosted the last two editions of the Confederation of African Football (CAF) Awards. Three of its players – Achraf Hakimi, Brahim Diaz and Ismael Saibari – feature on the 10-person shortlist for the 2026 men’s CAF Player of the Year award.
For some, Morocco represents what sustained investment, strategic planning and football diplomacy can achieve. Others, however, question whether its growing concentration of hosting opportunities and institutional influence is creating an imbalance within African football.
Kamilla Swart, an associate professor and Director of the Master of Science in Sport and Entertainment Management programme at Hamad Bin Khalifa University in Doha, Qatar, says Morocco’s current position is the product of a strategy developed over several years.
“I think it’s a case of Morocco building its expertise over a long period of time,” she said.
“So if you even think of, you know, everybody talks about the Mohammed VI Football Academy that was inaugurated in 2010. So it’s not something that’s just happened now.”
Morocco bid unsuccessfully to host the World Cup several times before finally winning a joint bid for 2030. Swart said those bids enabled the country to assess its weaknesses and establish the infrastructure needed to compete for major international events.
However, Swart said that Morocco’s repeated hosting of CAF events has raised questions about whether other African countries are getting sufficient hosting opportunities.
“On the one hand, I can understand why all these events are going to Morocco,” Swart said.
“And on the other hand, I can see the point of view where there may be some scepticism or mixed feelings about that – potentially the rest of the continent is not benefitting from that.”
Some have also accused CAF of giving Morocco preferential treatment. These concerns intensified following the controversial 2025 Africa Cup of Nations final between Senegal and Morocco. Senegal initially won the game 1-0 after extra time, but the match was overshadowed by a late penalty awarded to Morocco, prompting Senegal’s players to temporarily leave the pitch in protest.
On March 17, 2026, CAF’s Appeal Board overturned an earlier disciplinary ruling, declared Senegal to have forfeited the final by leaving the pitch under Articles 82 and 84 of the Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) regulations and awarded Morocco a 3-0 victory.
The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled in favour of an appeal by Senegal and reinstated them as champions on Tuesday.
Speaking before that ruling, Kenyan sport lawyer and arbitrator Khayran Noor told Al Jazeera, “I think we need to distinguish between two issues: Morocco’s genuine institutional and infrastructural progress, and the responsibility of CAF to ensure that its decision-making processes are transparent and beyond reasonable suspicion.”
When it comes to awarding hosting rights, a CAF Executive Committee assesses the facilities and documentation submitted by bidding countries before making the final hosting decision.
However, Noor believes the process would benefit from greater transparency, including published evaluation criteria, independent technical assessments, disclosure of potential conflicts of interest and explanations of final decisions.
She also warned against allowing financial strength to translate into disproportionate political influence. Article 17 of the CAF Statutes provides each member association with one vote at the General Assembly, irrespective of its financial capacity.
“Morocco should be entitled to benefit from its investments, but every other African federation should have a meaningful opportunity to demonstrate its own capacity,” Noor said.
“Ultimately, institutional confidence is built not only by making the right decisions, but also by demonstrating that those decisions were reached fairly.”
Morocco’s hosting profile also has an important commercial dimension, some experts say. CAF depends heavily on broadcasting and sponsorship revenues, making the quality of its competitions and broadcasting standards central to its financial sustainability.
Gerard Akindes, a Beninese-born sports management scholar, international consultant and former professional athlete, believes the concentration of major competitions in Morocco is partly down to the uneven quality of football infrastructure and broadcasting production elsewhere on the continent.
“AFCON is what makes CAF’s revenue,” Akindes told Al Jazeera. “And they want the best product possible that they can sell to broadcasters to generate revenue that is going to sustain the organisation.”
Akindes also suggested that Morocco’s willingness to host competitions when other countries were unable or unwilling to do so had strengthened its relationship with CAF.
“Morocco managed to get a lot of influence because they saved the organisation several times by hosting events that nobody wanted to host,” he said. “When you do that, they probably get some return.”
‘It’s a conspiracy theory’
Morocco’s growing presence on the CAF Awards shortlist has also generated debate over preferential treatment.
The 2026 ceremony returns to Lagos on December 2, marking Nigeria’s first time hosting the event since 2014. items.text:
Jensen Huang is partying it up in Ibiza. In a video with nearly 6 million views on Instagram, the former CEO of Nvidia is dancing in a crowded club, champagne glass in hand, still wearing his signature black leather jacket. Suddenly, from behind him, Alice Huang — the Chinese technology executive and suspected spy he had an affair with, sparking congressional investigations and his resignation from the chipmaking company he cofounded — appears. She puts her hand on his shoulder and he wraps his arm around her waist as they begin dancing together. The video’s caption reads “Honey Trap Final Boss. #inthemoodforlove.”
Jensen Huang deepfakes are the hot new AI slop
Influencers are chasing viral success with the saga — and tech stack — of Nvidia’s CEO.
Jensen Huang deepfakes are the hot new AI slop
Influencers are chasing viral success with the saga — and tech stack — of Nvidia’s CEO.
Of course, it’s AI-generated. This Instagram Reel is one of hundreds of AI deepfakes featuring Huang, his wife Lori, Alice, and sometimes Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, Kimberly Powell (the second of three reported affair partners). In this case, Huang is being swapped into an existing meme called “Ibiza Final Boss.” The original video featured a British construction worker with a bowl cut dancing in exactly the same way, minus a woman sidling up to him. Other viral AI hits include Huang in a scene from The Office, Huang in the music video for George Michael’s “Careless Whisper,” and Huang as the former Astronomer CEO who got caught in an affair with one of his employees by the jumbotron at a Coldplay concert last summer. Even the rapper 50 Cent posted an AI edit of his “P.I.M.P.” music video, now featuring Huang with some flashy silver accessories.
Unlike deepfake pornography or election disinformation, these AI videos aren’t necessarily intended to harm or mislead people. They’re memes making fun of Huang’s cheating scandal and its global implications, created with AI technology that in many cases relies heavily on Nvidia’s tech stack: video diffusion models running on the Nvidia GPUs that power much of the modern generative AI industry. “It’s ironic that without Nvidia generating millions of these AI memes ... would not be possible,” reads one of the top comments on the Ibiza deepfake. “In some sense, Jensen is making Nvidia richer by his own scandal.” The comment was punctuated by multiple cry-laughing emoji.
As it turns out, Huang may benefit, too. On Monday, the Nvidia board announced he was reinstated as president, CEO, and board director following “a series of discussions and meetings” and “input from senior levels of the United States government.” Nvidia’s stock has since surged, and new AI Huang memes cast him in a victorious light. One variation swaps him into a scene from The Wolf of Wall Street, announcing “I’m not leaving” to a crowd of cheering men that has been edited to include AI versions of Donald Trump, Elon Musk, and Mark Zuckerberg.
While the saga continues, many social media users are finding the humor in these Huang deepfakes, and their creators are churning out variations to meet the sudden demand. The Instagram account behind the Ibiza one has made three Huang deepfakes so far, all remakes of the same scene. Another version features Powell dancing with him, and the third one shows a sea of young women in bikini tops and shorts surrounding Huang, who lifts his champagne up in celebration. Each has accrued millions of views.
“His story has just come at the best time for ai creators and a terrible time for him,” wrote the account behind the Ibiza videos in a direct message to The Verge. “Everyone was doing him. Most I’ve seen anyone AI-ed.”
This deepfake creator identified himself as a 40-year-old man from Melbourne, Australia, but wouldn’t share his real name. He says he has spent “thousands” on AI video generation, using models like TikTok developer ByteDance’s Seedance 2.5 and Alibaba’s Wan 3. These, along with other AI tools like Google’s Nano Banana, help power the ecosystem of deepfakes.
He said his Instagram page has been going “super viral” in the past two weeks, thanks to the Ibiza meme format. He has nearly 100 million views on various iterations of it featuring different celebrities. The Huang ones are among the most popular, alongside versions featuring Elizabeth Holmes and Amanda Seyfried playing her in the hit Nathan Fielder documentary You Can See Everything.
“I wanted to elevate the content and know that putting what is happening in the news ... would get traction,” he wrote. “Always wanted to be a filmmaker but this technology is beyond whatever I imagined was possible.”
As generative AI has taken hold of the internet in recent years, a lot of the resulting viral content has been disparaged as “AI slop.” Hollywood productions, mainstream artists, and even local businesses have been maligned for using (or appearing to use) AI in their advertisements and final cuts. Video trends like putting sexy AI fruit characters in Love Island parodies racked up millions of views online but failed to deliver any real cultural momentum. The ubiquity of the Huang deepfakes and the relative lack of blowback from AI critics may indicate that the future of AI-generated content is similar to the rest of meme culture: If the topic’s trending, people will engage with something, even if it’s following the same formula as the slop. That an AI tech titan’s own indiscretions are inspiring this latest evolution in deepfakes is just the sardonic cherry on top.
“It’s not that we’re inundated in deepfakes of Trump being like ‘Nuclear war tomorrow,’ like the way it was framed as the big problem,” says misinformation researcher Abbie Richards. “Instead, it just feels like there is so much slop to push through to have any grounding in reality.”

items.text:
Ukraine: Zelenskyy and Hungary's Magyar meet amid thaw in ties
November 24, 2026
Hungary's new Prime Minister Peter Magyar arrived in Ukraine on Tuesday afternoon for meetings with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as well as with ethnic Hungarians living in the west of the country.
The meeting comes as both say they want better relations after a change of leadership in Budapest — no doubt a welcome change for Kyiv after years of Viktor Orban obstructing funding for its self-defense against full-scaler Russian invasion.
Ukraine's Zelenskyy posted his thanks for the meeting with a photo on X, writing: "A visit that is sure to bring positive results. We already have agreements in the areas of politics, energy, and infrastructure. Thank you!"
Despite his softer approach, Magyar has said Hungary will not be sending arms to Kyiv while at the same time vowing, "we stand with Ukraine against the Russian aggressor."
Rights of ethnic Hungarians tied to war support and EU accession talks
Magyar has insisted that the rights of tens of thousands of ethnic Hungarians in the Transcarpathia — a region that was part of Austria-Hungary until the end of World War I and situated at the borders of Ukraine, Hungary, Poland, Romania and Slovakia — be resolved before Budapest can wholeheartedly back Ukraine and its possible accession to the European Union.
Relations deteriorated significantly over the issue in 2017, when Kyiv passed a law making Ukrainian the official language of all secondary education in Ukraine, something Budapest viewed as discriminatory toward ethnic Hungarians.
Last month, Ukrainian lawmakers passed legislation allowing ethnic minorities in the country expanded rights regarding the teaching and use of their native languages. The move was welcomed by Budapest and Hungary dropped its opposition to Brussels opening accession talks with Ukraine.
Magyar pitched this week's trip — the first to Transcarpathia by a Hungarian prime minister since 2015 — in April, after defeating Orban.
Before departing for Ukraine, the Hungarian leader said: "I hope these talks will be successful. I think this is a historic day and a good opportunity to put Ukrainian-Hungarian relations on a new footing and to rebuild trust as we did with our other neighbors."

items.title: Disease Surveillance, Healthcare Staffing Top Public Health Budget Priorities
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 24 – Strengthening disease surveillance systems, addressing healthcare staffing shortages and improving sanitation are among the key priorities identified by the State Department for Public Health and Professional Standards ahead of the 2027/28 financial year.
Principal Secretary
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 24 – Strengthening disease surveillance systems, addressing healthcare staffing shortages and improving sanitation are among the key priorities identified by the State Department for Public Health and Professional Standards ahead of the 2027/28 financial year.
Principal Secretary Mary Muthoni outlined the priorities on Tuesday when she appeared before the National Assembly Departmental Committee on Health to present the department’s proposals for the 2027 Budget Policy Statement.
The presentation, chaired by Committee Chairperson James Nyikal, focused on critical areas requiring additional investment to strengthen public health service delivery.
Muthoni highlighted the need to enhance disease surveillance and response capacity to ensure the country is better equipped to detect, monitor and respond to public health threats.
She also called for investment in Primary Health Care, improved sanitation and expanded access to essential public health services.
Human Resources for Health was another key area highlighted during the engagement, with the PS pointing to the need for adequate staffing to support service delivery across the health system.
The department also identified health coordination and relations as a priority, emphasising the importance of collaboration with stakeholders in planning and implementing public health programmes.
Muthoni urged the committee to consider interventions to address the funding deficit facing the State Department, warning that adequate financial support was necessary to implement its proposed programmes.
The submissions will inform budgetary considerations for the 2027/28 financial year.

It took a while for the video call to connect. When Volodymyr Zelenskyy finally greeted the delegates in Berlin, applause broke out. The Ukrainian president appealed to the gathered parliamentarians from 32 NATO member states to keep supporting his country, especially against the massive aerial bombardment from Russia.
"Dear friends, winter is now ahead of us. And of course, our number one priority is air defense," Zelenskyy told the delegates. His country urgently needs more Patriot and other comprehensive anti-air attack systems. "And your countries have them. Missiles that can stop Russian ballistic missiles should not be sitting in warehouses collecting dust. And we say this openly. Please help us with this."
Ukraine seeks to join NATO
Zelenskyy renewed his call for his country to join the NATO military alliance. That issue is not for the NATO Parliamentary Assembly, which was gathered for its 72nd annual meeting in Berlin, to decide. But it was important to the Ukrainian president to reiterate his request.
After the war ends, Ukraine needs strong security guarantees and NATO could ensure those. "Wouldn't it be more effective to simply bring Ukraine into NATO?" Zelenskyy asked, arguing: "Wouldn't that be better for all of us, for everyone? Cheaper to put in place? And more reliable when it comes to actually protecting security?"
There is conflict among NATO members about the possibility of admitting Ukraine. The alliance has affirmed multiple times that the path to membership stands open to Ukraine — however, in the long term rather than the near future. This is primarily because of the ongoing war and the possible assistance obligations of other NATO countries for Ukraine, which was attacked by Russia.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte rejected the Ukrainian demands at the summit, which for the first time in 26 years was held in Berlin. Ukraine had entry prospects; however, NATO members currently lack unanimity on this issue. NATO alone decides who becomes a member. "There is total clarity on that within the alliance," Rutte said.
Merz: Denying Ukraine NATO membership in 2008 'was a mistake'
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz advocated for Ukraine to receive security guarantees similar to what NATO members have, in the instance of a possible ceasefire. In retrospect, it was clear "what a mistake it was not to follow the American suggestion back in 2008 at the NATO summit in Bucharest to admit Ukraine as a member," Merz said at a joint press conference following a meeting with Rutte.
Whether or not a NATO entry for Ukraine could be part of negotiations with Russia is another question, according to Rutte. He approved of current US efforts to bring about peace talks, and how Europe was closely consulting with Ukraine and the US for a unified position. "But it is also to test now whether Putin is willing to play ball, and then these issues might come up again."
The Russian invasion of Ukraine has led to NATO arming itself on a massive scale. Members have committed to raising their countries' defense spending to 5% of their gross domestic product (GDP) by 2035.
Rutte warned that all the allies needed a credible path to get there, "and ideally, they get there sooner than 2035." In addition, he said weapons production among member states needed to further increase because "right now, demand still far exceeds the supply."
Germany's military budget has had a massive increase
The contribution by Germany's Bundeswehr armed forces to NATO was explained by Carsten Breuer, Germany's highest-ranking soldier. For example, the massive increase in military spending: "Our defense budget has tripled since 2021. The goal is to achieve the 5% target, which was set at the summit in The Hague, well before 2035." In the coming year, Germany's defense budget has risen to more than €139 billion ($151 billion).
The Bundeswehr was further developing into a "constantly modernized, effective and innovative army, Breuer said. Also, a much larger one than before: "To reach our current capability goals we are expanding the Bundeswehr to a total of 460,000 soldiers by the mid-2030s," the German chief of defense said. Of those, 200,000 are to be reservists. "This is like walking a tightrope because we must find the right balance between growth and operational readiness."
Following his speech, Breuer answered questions from the delegates who showed keen interest in the developments. The discussion was a preview of Breuer's new post: He has been voted in as the new chair of the NATO Military Committee and will move to the alliance's headquarters in Brussels mid-next year. Then he will become the principal military advisor to NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. "I take this election as a sign of recognition that Germany has now accepted its responsibility as well as its role in security policy," Breuer commented.
This article was originally written in German.

items.text:
Man Utd's Yoro has Anfield red card overturned
- Published
Manchester United defender Leny Yoro has had the red card he was shown during Sunday's Premier League match at Liverpool overturned.
The Football Association has confirmed Yoro will now be clear to face Brentford at Old Trafford on Saturday.
"Leny Yoro's one-match suspension has been removed following a successful claim of wrongful dismissal," said the FA in a statement.
New United head coach Mauricio Pochettino was furious at the decision, which came just eight minutes in and, he felt, changed the course of the game, which Liverpool won 4-0.
Liverpool striker Alexander Isak ran on to a ball that bounced over Matthijs de Ligt but took a heavy touch that meant the ball was likely to run through to United goalkeeper Senne Lammens even if Yoro had not brought the Swede down.
Nevertheless, referee Sam Barrott sent Yoro off, drawing criticism from Pochettino.
"The ball wasn't in his control," he said. "Isak, when he saw the control wasn't good, it's normal to delay, and stop to the run. In that moment that Yoro came from the back, and you go down.
"But all that we play football; you know that wasn't intentional. That is never a foul."
- 'No-one's coming to save us' - but how can Man Utd save themselves? 
  - Published23 hours ago
Sporting boss Fonseca dismisses Man Utd fragile talk
United have travelled to Lisbon for their next Champions League match on Wednesday (20:00 GMT).
The early dismissal of Yoro at Anfield meant Sporting had no chance to assess any changes Pochettino might have made after he replaced Michael Carrick during the international break.
But despite United sitting 19th in the Premier League, Sporting boss refuses to accept United are "fragile".
"I don't following the reasoning," said Fonseca, who was only appointed on 4 November after the Portuguese club bought him out of his contract at Lyon.
"Manchester is a great team," he said. "I don't believe a lot that great teams are fragile. The last game they played in the Champions League, they were trailing 2-0, then won 3-2 against a very difficult opponent in Roma.
"Moreover, when they have a new head coach, with such world-class players, it's extremely unpredictable to see if they will have a good day or bad day."
United have not won in the Premier League since August and have conceded 19 goals in their past six games in all competitions.
Yet, such was the nature of the Liverpool game, Fonseca has had to watch analysis of Pochettino's time in charge of the United States to get an idea of what to expect.
"Eight minutes, red card. It's impossible to make an analysis," he said.
"I tried to see Pochettino with the United States and what kind of solutions he used. There is some information but it is very difficult to predict."

items.title: Football Daily | The game’s gone: has fantasy football been ruined by AI gafferbots?
items.summary:
FAN-TASTIC
Sometimes, the beautiful game can make Football Daily feel old. Even Monday’s ostensibly old-school fixture between Brentford and Everton felt like the future destroying the past. The analytics-coded hosts prevailed 4-0 and James Tarkowski was dismissed by the VAR overlords for a challeng
items.text:
FAN-TASTIC
Sometimes, the beautiful game can make Football Daily feel old. Even Monday’s ostensibly old-school fixture between Brentford and Everton felt like the future destroying the past. The analytics-coded hosts prevailed 4-0 and James Tarkowski was dismissed by the VAR overlords for a challenge that would have been considered “firm but fair” on the muddy pitches of our youth. “I don’t think you can tackle like that in this day and age,” a misty-eyed David Moyes sighed after the game, before heading to the team bus to rewatch the Battle of Santiago.
Tarkowski’s red card was also a blow for Fantasy Premier League contenders who had misguidedly added the centre-back to their team, and now need the world to know about it. Listen, back in our day, Fantasy Football was a cosy Friday TV show with guests, low-budget goal recreations and some gags that haven’t dated so well. Now, it’s an entire industry, and like all good industries, it’s under threat from AI. A slow-news-day report from Reuters reveals that AI programs (we’re calling them ‘gafferbots’) are catching up to humans in the world of FPL. Will Thomas, a fantasy football veteran who created an AI platform for players, was defeated by his own gafferbot last season. “I thought, ‘oh my God, I’m being beaten by my own creation’,” Thomas sobbed. That might be how Moyes felt watching Tarkowski lunge in, boot in the air, on Monday night.
The rise of the gafferbots, and the fact almost every entrant will have access to an AI model – a sort of synthetic Sammy Lee that can fine-tune your dubious decisions – will only serve to make fantasy football even more pointless. Still, it might help end our unbroken 1,057-week run of picking the wrong captain, so it’s worth a shot. We asked our own advanced AI model, fd.ai.ly, for advice on our current FPL team and after 20 minutes of whirs and bleeps, it suggested handing the armband to Dominic Calvert-Lewin for Leeds’ home game against Coventry this weekend. So alongside misinformation, excessive water consumption and opening up a new avenue towards extinction, we can also denounce AI for underestimating promoted sides on the road.
But that’s enough of this old man yelling at the cloud. Football still throws up scenarios so complicated that the bots are just as baffled as we are. We asked fd.ai.ly whether Senegal or Morocco were the true winners of the 2025 Afcon final and it started to overheat, the chat window repeating “game’s gone” 1,057 times before imploding. In the human courts, Senegal have now been re-awarded the trophy they won on the pitch, which was previously handed to hosts Morocco after a court of arbitration for sport appeal. This debate will never end unless we sort it the old-fashioned way. Send Brahim Díaz and Édouard Mendy to a suburban park with Baddiel and Skinner, and make them replay that penalty. Fd.ai.ly advises there’s a 110% chance of putting this nonsense to bed if Brahim simply puts his foot through it this time.
LIVE ON BIG WEBSITE
Bigger Cup is back, baby! Join Scott Murray for piping hot coverage of Arsenal 3-2 Borussia Dortmund, while Simon Burnton is on deck for our clockwatch of the other 8pm GMT kick-offs including Manchester City 2-1 Napoli and Real Madrid 4-1 PSV Eindhoven.
QUOTE OF THE DAY
“Villarreal CF, in response to reports published in various media outlets recently, clarifies that it is completely false that Nicolas Pépé’s eye surgery has any connection to viewing the solar eclipse. The surgery had been scheduled in advance for reasons entirely unrelated to this event” – not on our 2026 bingo card, but now Football Daily really wants to know the reasons why Pépé had eye surgery, causing him to miss five Villarreal matches this season.
FOOTBALL DAILY LETTERS
 If Sunday was Gary Neville’s Sistine Chapel [Monday’s Football Daily], then his commentary on the Fernando Torres goal for Chelsea against Barcelona must be his David” – Ronnie McMahon.
 Regarding Declan Hackett’s assertion [Monday’s letters] that Donald Trump will be helping his mate Mauricio Pochettino by ringing the FA to overturn Lenny Yoro’s red card, perhaps Poch should be careful what he wishes for: Trump may equally decide to get Michael Carrick reinstated, as he also has a bit of previous for that sort of thing” – Dexter O Riordan.
 In all the time that I have been watching football, I don’t think I have ever seen a player dismiss himself and be away down the tunnel before given a red card. Thanks James Tarkowski” – Nigel Sanders.
 Brighton had only failed to win twice in the league since 5 September. A 1-1 draw with Leeds and a 2-0 defeat at Liverpool - their only opponents with double letters in their name. That bizarre hoodoo struck again at Hull on Sunday. Good good news for Seagulls fans is the only double-lettered encounters they have before hosting Hull in February are trips to Forest and Spurs. Even better news is that since that 1-1 draw with Leeds on 5 September, they have a 100% win record against sides without double letters and have not conceded a goal” – Dan Ashley (and no others).
If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day goes to … Dexter O Riordan. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.
MOVING THE GOALPOSTS
The latest edition of our sister email is Jeff Rueter’s take on the 2026 NWSL goals, players and (quadruple) nutmegs we won’t forget.
RECOMMENDED LOOKING
David Squires + Manchester United x topical video game release = this cartoon.
RECOMMENDED LISTENING
Women’s Football Weekly will see you now. Faye Carruthers is joined by Suzanne Wrack, Ayisha Gulati and Freddie Cardy to discuss the latest WSL action.

items.title: 83pc of maternal deaths reviewed linked to delays in hospital care
items.summary:
NAIROBI,Kenya Nov 24 – Delays in receiving medical attention at health facilities were identified in 83 per cent of maternal deaths reviewed in a Ministry of Health surveillance dataset, exposing persistent gaps in staffing, essential medicines and emergency response in Kenya’s healthcare system.
Th
items.text:
NAIROBI,Kenya Nov 24 – Delays in receiving medical attention at health facilities were identified in 83 per cent of maternal deaths reviewed in a Ministry of Health surveillance dataset, exposing persistent gaps in staffing, essential medicines and emergency response in Kenya’s healthcare system.
The findings, presented by University of Nairobi researcher Dr Njoki Kimani during a Kenya Editors Guild forum in Nairobi on November 19, point to weaknesses in the quality and timeliness of care even as more women deliver in health facilities.
The analysis also found that 71 per cent of the maternal deaths involved delays in deciding to seek medical attention, highlighting challenges that begin before women reach hospitals.
“We know that 71 per cent of deaths were due to the first delay and 83 per cent were due to delay within the facility,” Kimani said.
The findings examined three categories of delays: deciding to seek medical care, reaching a health facility and receiving appropriate treatment after arrival. Some deaths involved more than one category of delay.
Kimani said postpartum haemorrhage, or excessive bleeding after childbirth, remained the leading cause of maternal deaths in the records examined.
She further revealed that health facilities reporting staff shortages had more than four times the risk of maternal mortality, while shortages of medicines, blood and blood products were also associated with increased risks.
Garissa and Nairobi were among the counties facing significant challenges linked to delays in maternal healthcare. Kimani noted that Nairobi’s facilities also serve patients from neighbouring counties, placing additional pressure on available services.
The findings point to a gap between access to healthcare and the ability of facilities to provide timely, quality emergency treatment.
Medical Services Principal Secretary Dr Ouma Oluga said only 37 per cent of health facilities offering delivery services could provide all seven basic emergency obstetric care functions, raising concerns about their preparedness to manage complications during childbirth.
He urged journalists to investigate weaknesses in maternal healthcare and increase public awareness of preventable deaths.
“Every morning, one minute awareness. It will speak louder than the headlines,” Oluga said, calling on radio and television stations to dedicate daily airtime to maternal and newborn health education.
The Principal Secretary said the government was implementing interventions under the Every Woman Every Newborn Everywhere (EWENE) Acceleration Plan to strengthen maternal and newborn healthcare services.
The measures include providing essential medical supplies and obstetric and neonatal equipment to 635 health facilities, establishing training and simulation centres and recruiting an additional 5,000 midwives to address workforce shortages.
Oluga also highlighted the expansion of healthcare coverage under the Social Health Authority (SHA), saying 33.7 million Kenyans had registered under the scheme.
He said the registration data would help improve healthcare planning and resource allocation, while urging expectant mothers to begin antenatal care early, complete the recommended eight visits and attend postnatal appointments.
Kenya Editors Guild President Zubeidah Kananu challenged journalists to sustain coverage of maternal and newborn health beyond individual tragedies, calling for closer scrutiny of government commitments and their implementation.
“We must follow up on promises made, investigate systemic gaps, examine whether interventions are working, and establish whether lessons from previous tragedies are informing better healthcare decisions,” Kananu said.
She cited the September case of Mercy Kanini, a mother from Juja who lost all five of her babies after giving birth prematurely, saying the tragedy raised questions about the management of high-risk pregnancies, access to specialised newborn care and the effectiveness of referral systems.
Kananu said journalists should examine whether lessons from maternal and newborn deaths were being translated into measures that prevent similar tragedies.
She also urged the media to monitor healthcare funding, staffing and the implementation of government programmes to establish whether services promised to expectant mothers were actually available in hospitals.
Dr Wangui Muthigani, Director and Programme Lead for Women’s Health at Savannah Global Health Institute, said maternal mortality statistics should be examined beyond the numbers to understand the circumstances surrounding individual deaths.
She observed that although many pregnant women make initial contact with healthcare facilities, some fail to complete the recommended antenatal visits, resulting in missed opportunities for early diagnosis and intervention.
Muthigani said examining where women drop out of the healthcare system could help identify communities requiring additional support.
“So once we see a mother has died, do we sit and cry? I mean, we should. We should sit and cry, but we should act so that we don’t have a situation like this arising tomorrow,” she said.
Dr Hellen Barsosio, Assistant Principal Clinical Research Scientist at the Kenya Medical Research Institute’s Centre for Global Health Research, said Kenya had generated substantial evidence on interventions capable of preventing maternal and newborn deaths, but translating that knowledge into practice remained a challenge.
She said preventive services, including malaria protection, vaccinations, anaemia prevention and antenatal screening, could significantly reduce pregnancy-related risks.
“The truest gap is delivery, meaning that the proven tools, the proven interventions are not reaching all the women, and if they are, they’re reaching women a bit too late,” Barsosio said.

items.title: Why a Crusoe investor is betting on solar and batteries to power future AI data centers
items.summary:
The problem of supplying power to AI data centers has become one of the central debates of the AI era. In just a few years, the U.S. grid has gone from basically zero growth to adding several gigawatts a year.
“Demand is growing faster than people appreciate,” Brook Porter, partner at G2 Venture Par
items.text:
The problem of supplying power to AI data centers has become one of the central debates of the AI era. In just a few years, the U.S. grid has gone from basically zero growth to adding several gigawatts a year.
“Demand is growing faster than people appreciate,” Brook Porter, partner at G2 Venture Partners (G2VP), told TechCrunch. “It’s atoms, not bits, and the world is in the process of recognizing the realities of those challenges.”
It’s been a bumpy road. Because it takes a while to scale supply chains, companies have been securing power in any form they can. In many cases, that has meant buying, renting and deploying natural gas power plants, but Porter thinks that hyperscalers and data center developers should look at the bigger picture if they want to move faster.
That picture involves solar paired with energy storage, based on an analysis Porter and his colleagues at G2VP recently conducted on the state of the data center power market.
“Global capacity of natural gas is only about 60 or 70 gigawatts per year, where solar is already at well over a terawatt,” he said. “Probably the most important lesson that we’ve learned over the last 20 years of backing companies is that Wright’s Law is the thing you want to leverage — making the same thing over and over again.”
Both solar and most forms of long-duration energy storage are built on small, modular technologies that can be manufactured at massive scale. “This is about speed and scale and economics, and we can win across all those dimensions,” Porter said.
G2VP had an early window into AI data center development, having led Crusoe’s Series C. “We’ve had a front-row seat at what’s been happening at that company, how they’ve evolved, how the different waves of data centers have evolved,” Porter said.
The venture firm estimates that data center investment will top $4 trillion until the end of the decade. As the next wave takes shape, the firm sees two different paths for data centers: small, on-grid facilities with their own generating capacity, and larger data centers powered by solar and long-duration energy storage.
“The big idea is to go off-grid,” Porter said. “What that would enable you to do is build with renewables in a way that’s independent of the grid. You can determine your own fate, go around some of the constraints of permitting, whether that’s access to the grid or air permits. You can accelerate your time to market dramatically.”
In recent years, energy storage has been synonymous with lithium-ion batteries, which are too expensive to compete with fossil fuels for round-the-clock power. But a new generation of long-duration energy storage products from the likes of Form Energy and G2VP portfolio company Antora Energy have brought the cost per megawatt-hour down significantly.
Even though the technologies might be a few years away from broad acceptance among data center developers, Porter said they should start thinking about them now.
“It’s analogous to surfing the biggest waves off of Mavericks here in Northern California. The wave is so big that you really have to be paddling and moving and be incredibly nimble to catch it. If you’re at a standstill, it’s just gonna blow you by,” he said.

items.summary: The New York Times is asking freelance photographers not to use the newest version of Adobe Photoshop because features in the 2027 update use AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users.” In an email seen by The Verge and posted on Threads, two of the Times’ photography leaders, Meaghan Looram and
items.text:
The New York Times is asking freelance photographers not to use the newest version of Adobe Photoshop because features in the 2027 update use AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users.” In an email seen by The Verge and posted on Threads, two of the Times’ photography leaders, Meaghan Looram and Josh Haner, write that the use of these features “can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated.”
The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features
An email sent to freelance photographers says Photoshop’s latest update uses AI ‘in ways that may not be apparent.’
Adobe has spent the past few years filling Photoshop and other apps in its creative suite with a trove of AI-powered tools. The November update cited by the NYT’s email adds several new AI features, including Adobe’s new “AI Assisted Editor” view, which lets users access all of Photoshop’s AI features from a single toolbar. It also adds an AI assistant for step-by-step editing instructions, prompt-based image transformation and editing, new AI upscaling options, and an AI-powered tool that recomposes images for different canvas sizes.
It’s not always clear which tools in Adobe’s apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production. For a newsroom like the Times, where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers’ trust. Last year, the Times said that it does not “retouch or digitally manipulate” photos but may “make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image.”
In August, Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps, which indicates whether an image is AI-generated or edited using AI features. The NYT is issuing its restriction to keep these tags from inadvertently appearing in its photos. “At this time, we are requiring that all contributing photographers avoid using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (release 28.0.0 and subsequent updates) when working on assignment for The Times,” the email reads.
It’s not clear which specific Photoshop features the NYT is referring to. Neither Adobe nor the NYT immediately responded to The Verge’s request for more information.

items.text:
HIV infections could rise after historic lows amid aid cuts, UN warns
November 24, 2026
New HIV infections could rise next year for the first time in years, reversing a historic decline amid funding cuts and anti-rights campaigns, the United Nations (UN) warned on Tuesday.
"The world has moved closer towards controlling the HIV pandemic, but changes in funding and resulting service disruptions jeopardize this progress," the UNAIDS agency said in its annual global update.
AIDS-related death numbers has fallen to its lowest in more than two decades. According to the organization, this was made possible by broader access to treatment and improvements in the quality of care programs.
The virus claimed roughly 570,000 lives globally in 2025. This means almost 1,600 people died everyday. In comparison, this figure was 600,000 in 2024 and 1.3 million in 2010.
Based on data from 172 countries, the agency estimated that 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV in 2025, of whom 32.1 million were receiving antiretroviral treatment.
The wider use of antiretroviral medication also reduces the risk of HIV transmission, the organization said. It estimates that 1.2 million people contracted HIV in 2025, down from 1.3 million the year before. The peak in 1994 saw 3.5 million.
"HIV, which was once a death sentence, has become a manageable health condition for millions of people thanks to life-saving HIV medicines," said UNAIDS.
'Dramatic impacts' of US aid cuts
Despite the encouraging data so far, cuts to international funding have hampered efforts to fight HIV, the agency warned.
HIV programs faced an 18-percent decrease in international financing over the past year, said UNAIDS.
"Funding losses have destabilized HIV programs worldwide, coinciding with a wider contraction in official development assistance over the years," it said.
Although the United States remains the largest international donor for HIV programs, its contributions dropped by 26% between 2024 and 2025.
After dismantling USAID, the world's largest foreign aid agency, last year, the Donald Trump administration has sought to replace decades of aid with new bilateral deals.
"The impact of the United States government funding cuts has been especially dramatic given the reliance of many countries on its support for core HIV programs," said UNAIDS.
Meanwhile disbursements from the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria dropped by 13% in 2025.
Next year's data may show rising infections
"We are on the cusp of ending AIDS – this has been the greatest story of global health – and just when we should finish it, cuts and the rolling back of human rights is threatening to take away our gains," Winnie Byanyima, executive director of UNAIDS, told Reuters.
"We haven't ‌got the data yet, but we see the signs. We see all the signs of reversals," she added.
Byanyima predicted that data released in 2027 would begin to reflect a rise in new HIV infections.
In 2015, the UN set a goal to end AIDS by 2030.

items.summary:
The 2028 Copa América will be played in the United States and expanded to include teams from the Concacaf region, bringing the landmark South American international competition to the US for a third time in five editions.
Conmebol, the South American confederation that runs the tournament, and Conca
items.text:
The 2028 Copa América will be played in the United States and expanded to include teams from the Concacaf region, bringing the landmark South American international competition to the US for a third time in five editions.
Conmebol, the South American confederation that runs the tournament, and Concacaf, the confederation governing soccer in North and Central America and the Caribbean, jointly announced the long-rumored arrangement on Tuesday, framing it as an extension of a “strategic partnership” between the organizations.
The tournament will be played from 9 June to 9 July 2028 – notably the same dates as Uefa’s European Championship, to be co-hosted by England, Scotland, Wales, and the Republic of Ireland. The 2028 summer Olympics will then follow in venues across the US, with the opening match of the men’s soccer tournament kicking off on 10 July, and the women’s tournament following the next day. The Olympic finals will land on the 28th (men’s) and 29th (women’s) of July.
The 2028 Copa América will involve 16 teams – all of Conmebol’s 10 member nations, along with six from Concacaf. The confederations announced that the Concacaf participants will be determined based on results at the 2027 Gold Cup, set to be played in the US in June and July next year. The exact qualification criteria have yet to be announced.
While the US’s large and growing appetite for soccer is part of the reason it has become a common landing spot for the Copa América over the last decade-plus, commercial considerations will also have been a major factor. The 2024 Copa América, which was also held in the US and involved six Concacaf teams, generated approximately $319m in revenue for Conmebol, the confederation said – a significant rise over the $118m generated by the 2019 edition in Brazil.
Argentina won the 2024 edition of the Copa América, with the final in Miami marred by ugly scenes of ticketless fans rushing the gates, causing injuries and damage to the stadium, delaying the start time by nearly 90 minutes. The previous edition hosted in the US, 2016’s Copa América Centenario, was won by Chile on penalties over Argentina at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.
As with that tournament, the 2024 Copa América and the 2026 World Cup, the 2028 tournament can be expected to be played largely in American football stadiums, most with capacities exceeding 60,000 people. But unlike those previous editions, the tournament will not overlap with Major League Soccer, thanks to the US league’s recent calendar flip.

items.title: Pinterest will now let parents limit the AI-generated content their teens see
items.summary: Pinterest announced this week that it’s expanding its parental controls, but one new feature stands out: parents can now control how much AI-generated content their children are exposed to. This additional setting arrives alongside more standard options, like tools to adjust notifications or whether
items.text:
Pinterest announced this week that it’s expanding its parental controls, but one new feature stands out: parents can now control how much AI-generated content their children are exposed to. This additional setting arrives alongside more standard options, like tools to adjust notifications or whether or not videos autoplay.
The change makes Pinterest one of the first major social platforms to allow parents to control how much AI-generated content is shown to their children as part of the overall user experience.
Aside from Pinterest, social media platforms have focused more on limiting minors’ access to specific AI-powered features, as when Snap added a parental control setting that prevented its AI chatbot from responding to teens or when Meta did when it announced a global pause on teens’ access to existing AI characters after retooling the product based on parents’ feedback.
WhatsApp currently allows parents to adjust the level of access teens have to Meta AI, in terms of using AI to create content or having the AI respond to their teen’s questions.
But when it comes to AI-generated content filling users’ feeds and recommendations, there are few controls available on social media platforms in general, much less those provided as part of the parental controls.
This problem, parents say, is harming children’s well-being in favor of profits. For instance, in April, the children’s advocacy group Fairplay sent a letter to YouTube CEO Neal Mohan and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, signed by over 200 organizations and experts, calling on YouTube to remove AI-generated content from YouTube Kids and bar AI-generated videos from being recommended to users under 18.
Pinterest has fought its own battle against AI content, which still finds its way into users’ feeds even when the settings that restrict AI-modified content, which the company introduced in 2025, are enabled.
Putting a similar set of tools into parents’ hands is at least a good first step in allowing the users themselves to dictate the type of experience they want to have on the app.
The new feature arrived alongside other parental controls, including one to stop auto-playing videos and another that lets parents adjust the volume of push, browser, in-app, and email notifications. The Parental Controls Page was also redesigned to make it easier to find and configure certain controls and to allow parents to configure settings related to personalized ads.

items.title: More than 300 Russians killed as Moscow props up Mali’s junta, leaked data reveals
items.summary: When the attack on Kidal began before dawn on 25 April this year, the Russian fighters were caught off guard. Within the first hour, checkpoints on the outskirts of the remote desert city nestled among the rocky hills of northern Mali had fallen to the insurgents, who pushed towards the police stati
items.text:
When the attack on Kidal began before dawn on 25 April this year, the Russian fighters were caught off guard. Within the first hour, checkpoints on the outskirts of the remote desert city nestled among the rocky hills of northern Mali had fallen to the insurgents, who pushed towards the police station where fierce fighting erupted.
“Everything was happening at once. Explosions were going off all around us, people were shouting,” recalled a former member of Russia’s Africa Corps who was stationed in Mali at the time and spoke on condition of anonymity. “Nobody knew where the enemy was coming from.”
The Kremlin-controlled forces and their Malian allies were facing a coordinated surprise assault by the al-Qaida-linked JNIM and the Tuareg-led Azawad Liberation Front (FLA), whose fighters used suicide car bombs and drones to break through the city’s defences.
Leaked Russian state records suggest the losses were heavy that day. Death certificates of Russian fighters killed in Mali, held by Rosstat, Russia’s state statistics agency, were obtained by the hacker groups Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow and analysed by the Guardian.
The records show that 43 Russians died in Mali on 25 April, including six in Kidal and one in nearby Aguelhok. Others were recorded as dying in the capital, Bamako, and in Gao, where rebels shot down a Russian military helicopter that day.
By the following morning, the Russians had abandoned Kidal, which Russian mercenaries had helped capture in November 2023 and which Moscow had since held up as a showcase of its growing influence in Africa.
In all, the records list 349 Russian deaths in Mali between September 2023 and September 2026, most of which the Guardian was able to link to known battles with rebel groups.
The figures offer a previously unseen glimpse into the human cost of Moscow’s efforts to prop up Mali’s military junta, in what has become Russia’s largest military deployment in Africa.
Two western officials who have travelled to Mali and were shown the data said the death toll was higher than previously estimated.
“That’s over 10% of Russia’s forces killed in action,” said one of the officials, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to comment publicly.
Moscow does not publish its losses in Africa, and its foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment.
The Wagner private military group, led by the warlord Yevgeny Prigozhin, first arrived in Mali in late 2021, a year after a military coup had toppled President Ibrahim Boubacar Keïta. French forces were ordered to leave the country as relations with the junta deteriorated, bringing an end to France’s decade-long counter-terrorism operation and leaving Russia as the regime’s main foreign protector.
Wagner handed over its operations in Mali to the Africa Corps in June 2025, two years after Prigozhin led a failed mutiny on Moscow that discredited the group in the eyes of the Kremlin. By that summer, British intelligence estimated that about 2,000 Africa Corps personnel were deployed in the country.
The Africa Corps, closely overseen by Russian military intelligence, currently provides backing to several African governments in return for payment or lucrative contracts granting access to natural resources.
Despite the Russian presence, Mali’s security situation has continued to deteriorate. In late July 2024, Russian and Malian forces fought Tuareg separatists for several days near Tinzaouaten, on the Algerian border.
Wagner at the time issued a rare statement admitting losses, including the death of a commander, but gave no figure. Estimates from Russian sources ranged from about 20 to more than 80 dead.
The Rosstat records list 70 Russians who died on 27 July 2024, all but one of them in the Kidal region. The figures make the battle of Tinzaouaten the deadliest single day for Russian forces in Africa since Wagner mercenaries first deployed to the continent in 2017.
The toll in Mali may have been driven up by Ukraine, which has extended its war against Russia to the Sahel. Kyiv has been assisting Tuareg rebels there, according to two people with knowledge of the operations. CNN has reported that about 15 Ukrainian specialists were deployed to Mali to help local rebel forces fighting Russian troops.
The records are probably an undercount. Registration often lags, and no Russian deaths in Mali are recorded for March 2026 although at least three Africa Corps fighters were reported killed in an ambush near Nampala that month.
The leaked data also sheds light on Russia’s military activity elsewhere in Africa. Central African Republic, where Wagner fighters guard the president, Faustin-Archange Touadéra, accounts for 30 deaths. While not all could be linked to known incidents, three men died on the night drones struck Wagner camps in Kaga-Bandoro in December 2023.
In Libya, where Russian forces back the eastern commander Khalifa Haftar and use his airbases as a supply route to their deployments in the Sahel, some of the recorded deaths were probably linked to a helicopter crash at the Maaten al-Sarra base in February 2026. On Sunday, Ukrainian drones sunk a Russian warship off the coast of Libya; it is unclear whether there were any casualties.
In Niger, where Russia’s Africa Corps moved in after the military junta expelled French and US troops, a Russian fighter died two days after Islamic State militants attacked Niamey airport in January, a previously unreported casualty.
Moscow has in recent months stepped up its effort to show it is back in control in Mali. On 6 October, Malian troops and the Africa Corps recaptured Kidal after what the army called an air and ground campaign.
A report this month by the US-based Conflict Insights Group (CIG) found that the Africa Corps had sharply increased its use of drones in Mali, including Lancet suicide drones, amid an intensifying air campaign.
