items.text:
Palestine Weekly: A night of arson sees Israel ‘Jewish terrorism’ reckoning
Israeli settler pogroms have continued in the occupied West Bank.
Israeli settlers set fire to at least a dozen vehicles and several homes in five Palestinian villages across the occupied West Bank over the weekend, spray-painting “Revenge” and “Greetings from Susya”, apparently referring to the recent evacuation of an outpost near that village.
Police said they had opened investigations, according to local media, but no arrests have been reported.
In chat groups, settlers made light of the organised attacks, with one joking about the coming Jewish festival of lights: “Hanukkah is only in two weeks. We are in suspense.”
The attacks, part of a surge in settler violence against Palestinian villages, drew unusually sharp condemnation from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s political rivals. Former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, seeking to form a new government, called them “Jewish terrorism in every sense of the word” and blamed far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.
Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett accused the government of enabling the attacks, with Yair Lapid calling them “pogroms”. The criticism came as Britain froze the assets of eight Israeli settlement firms and Australia imposed sanctions on settlers and their organisations.
Occupied West Bank: Arson and demolitions
Arson attacks restricted the olive harvest; according to the United Nations Humanitarian Country Team’s latest report, more than 400 attacks causing casualties or damage have occurred since September, including attacks against activists, journalists and diplomats.
- Shootings and beatings: Settlers shot Asmat Tamimi in the abdomen while attacking olive pickers in Nabi Saleh on November 20, and beat farmer Mahmoud al-Harimi on his land in Abu Njeim on November 23, the Wafa news agency reported. During an olive harvest in Beitillu on November 20, settlers slashed the tyres of four cars of journalists. After soldiers forced pickers to leave the groves in Area B, settlers invaded the village, with troops using tear gas in the streets, according to witnesses and videos shared with Al Jazeera. Also on November 20, the Beit El illegal settlement’s civilian security coordinator shot dead Hamza Abdo, 42, near its perimeter wall.
- Roads and sieges: Settlers attacked Palestinian vehicles on a near-daily basis on al-Mughayyir’s only access road, according to village council member Marzouq Abu Naim. On the night of November 22, settlers cut the village’s main power line and blocked its entrances under army protection. They also blocked roads in Burqa and Qabalan and pelted cars with stones near Efrat and on Route 60. On November 23, soldiers closed roads around Hebron with iron gates, concrete blocks and earth mounds. Hizma, northeast of Jerusalem, was sealed overnight on November 22 after soldiers fired live rounds at workers crossing the separation wall into Jerusalem, arresting 18, according to Israeli field monitor Jonathan Pollack.
- Land, crops and water: Wafa and locals reported that settlers bulldozed dozens of olive trees in al-Mughayyir despite a court ruling allowing the owners back, destroyed about 70 trees in Aghziwa, burned groves in Burqa, ploughed 50 dunams in al-Farisiya and cut a water line in al-Masoudiya, where residents say they have been without electricity for two months. The UN’s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs says more than 4,000 trees and saplings have been damaged this harvest season and over 25,000kg of produce vandalised or stolen.
- Demolitions: Over the weekend, Israeli forces and Civil Administration officials demolished every structure at Khirbet Samra in the northern Jordan Valley, including water tanks that supplied its drinking water, according to Wafa and Pollack, who said more than 20 structures had no demolition orders and residents were given none. In Hebron, the army posted demolition notices on two Area A buildings containing 25 and 40 apartments, citing their proximity to a settler road. The Office of the State Attorney told Haaretz that the November 17 demolition of a home housing 32 people in Kafr ad-Dik, despite a High Court freeze, was “human error”.
- Outposts: Haaretz reported that settlers built a yeshiva, a traditional Jewish educational institution, in Area A, meant to be under full Palestinian Authority (PA) control, in the village of Yasid, as a “satellite campus” to the Homesh outpost. Near Hebron, bulldozers began levelling land in Kharas for an industrial zone serving the Gush Etzion bloc after more than 500 dunams were declared a closed military zone.
- Prisoners: A military judge upheld the administrative detention of Burin olive harvest and community organiser Ghassan Najjar, though the prosecutor acknowledged it was unrelated to armed activity. An Israeli court also extended the detention without charge of Gaza doctor Hussam Abu Safia by six months.
- In Israel: On November 18, a Jewish driver rammed pedestrians at several locations in Kafr Qasim, wounding eight Palestinian citizens; police said there was no nationalist motive and the driver tested positive for drugs. On November 19, masked men set fire to a mosque in Ed-Dahi and left graffiti about revenge for a settler killed in March, according to The Times of Israel.
Gaza: Killings continue as health crisis deepens
The Gaza Ministry of Health’s death toll since the October 2025 “ceasefire” rose from 1,650 on November 16 to 1,679 on November 23, bringing the number of deaths in the genocidal war since October 2023 to 74,746. On November 18, Israeli tanks and bulldozers crossed the “Yellow Line” in central Gaza in the first publicly announced ground push since the “ceasefire”.

Five women killed every hour globally by partner, relative last year: UN

About 47,000 women and girls were killed intentionally by an intimate partner or family member last year, a
items.text:
Five women killed every hour globally by partner, relative last year: UN
Home remains the most dangerous place for a woman or girl, ‘a pattern that has barely shifted in years’, UN Women says.
About 47,000 women and girls were killed intentionally by an intimate partner or family member last year, according to new data from the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) and UN Women.
The 2026 Femicide Brief, published on Tuesday, marked the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women.
The report found that home remains the most dangerous place for a woman or girl, “a pattern that has barely shifted in years”, UN Women said in a statement.
About 60 percent of last year’s 78,000 femicides were committed by an intimate partner or family member. That amounts to five women being killed every hour, or 129 per day, on average.
While the 47,000 figure is lower than the 2024 estimate of 50,000 victims, this change is largely due to improvements and not indicative of an actual decrease, the UN statement said.
The femicides took place across the globe, with no region safe from such violence.
“Africa remains the continent with the highest rate of victims of intimate partner/family member femicide (2.9 victims per 100,000 female population), followed by the Americas (1.4 victims), Oceania (1.1 victims), Asia (0.6 victims), and Europe (0.5 victims),” UN Women said.
“For far too long, we have seen alarming statistics,” Executive Director of UNODC Monica Juma said in the statement. “Frightening attitudes, social norms, and the failure of institutional safeguards create an environment in which killing a wife, daughter, mother, or sister becomes ‘tolerable’.”
Juma called for action across all levels of society, including strategies targeted at changing societal behaviour and harmful attitudes, and investing in specialised programmes and interventions to “deal with perpetrators of domestic violence, protect women, and secure their human rights and dignity”.
Femicide is rarely an isolated act, but rather the final one in a long pattern of violence, threats, and abuse, said UN Women. Yet, most women and girls never seek help or are left without protection, while “perpetrators escape justice their entire lives”.
“We must ensure women can report violence safely, access protection, and receive support before it is too late,” said UN Women Executive Director Sima Bahous. “When warning signs go unreported, cases are not properly investigated, women and girls are not protected and perpetrators are not brought to justice, the consequences can be fatal.”
The UN has found that while homicide rates globally have declined, femicide rates have done so at a slower pace.
In fact, between 2010 and last year, homicide rates declined nearly twice as fast as femicide rates in the Americas, and about 1.5 times as fast in Europe.

items.title: Amazon’s Decart acquisition is a bet on using software to narrow the gap with Nvidia in the AI chip race
items.summary: Jensen Huang’s comeback as Nvidia’s CEO is understandably making waves, leaving people wondering about the longer-term implications of his quick reinstatement and the U.S. government’s active role in his return. But there was another development yesterday that could also matter for Nvidia down the r
items.text:
Jensen Huang’s comeback as Nvidia’s CEO is understandably making waves, leaving people wondering about the longer-term implications of his quick reinstatement and the U.S. government’s active role in his return. But there was another development yesterday that could also matter for Nvidia down the road: Amazon’s decision to acquire Decart‘s tech and its team for a reported $7.5 billion.
The broader industry seems to agree that Decart’s tech for optimizing AI models to run on non-Nvidia chips is worth several billion dollars. Anthropic reportedly tried to acquire the startup in the same ballpark, and Nvidia, which invested in the startup’s $300 million funding round at a $4 billion valuation, was also rumored as a prospective buyer.
Amazon was ultimately the one to pull the trigger and bring on board Decart’s co-founders Dean Leitersdorf, Orian Leitersdorf and Moshe Shalev and their team, but the company is not interested in the world models they had been working on. At the heart of the deal is the startup’s tech that helps AI models run better on all kinds of chips.
By incorporating the startup’s Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), Amazon is now hoping to extract more performance out of its Trainium chips, as the company tries to turn AWS into a $1 trillion revenue business.
In its announcement, Amazon said it has worked with Decart since 2025 to optimize the Trainium chips. This deal is ostensibly aimed at accelerating that work, which could eventually result in the company offering its Trainium-based data centers, which Anthropic already uses, to more customers. Amazon has already been working to make Trainium easier to switch to.
One way Nvidia managed to leapfrog its competitors was by spending $6.9 billion to acquire Israeli chipmaker Mellanox, which eventually grew to become a core piece of its international manufacturing strategy. Amazon could well be following a similar path.
Annapurna Labs makes for a more interesting parallel than Mellanox, however, as the latter formed the basis of Amazon’s custom chip-designing unit following its 2015 acquisition. Add Intel into the mix, and this becomes a broader story. “Most of the hardware powering the AI wave was built in Israel. Annapurna; Mellanox; Habana Labs; etc…,” VC Eric Reiner observed on X a few months ago.
In an email to TechCrunch, Eze Vidra, co-founder and managing partner at Remagine Ventures, said the deal is “a strong signal for the Israeli deep-tech ecosystem, showing that specialized local talent continues to attract major global players.”
Amazon still has a ways to go before it can make a dent in Nvidia’s near-monopoly on AI chips, but the deal could help the e-commerce giant speed up its efforts. Dean Meyer, a partner at Sequoia who co-led the firm’s seed investment into Decart, said on X that the deal “will be looked back on as one of the most strategically important acquisitions in many, many years.”

The Frenchman will no longer be required to ser
items.text:
Manchester United have successfully appealed against the decision to send off Leny Yoro in their 4-0 defeat to Liverpool. The defender was dismissed for denying an obvious goal scoring opportunity after eight minutes but this was found to be incorrect.
The Frenchman will no longer be required to serve a one-match suspicion. He fouled Liverpool’s Alexander Isak when through on goal in the early stages at Anfield but Mauricio Pochettino insisted the striker would not have reached the ball, and therefore is was not a sending off offence. The referee Sam Barrott made a different assessment, which the video assistant did not disagree with.
United’s head coach said: “I don’t agree because the ball wasn’t in Isak’s control. Leny was running with him and when Isak saw the control wasn’t good and the ball was going to the keeper it is normal you delay, you stop running, and you wait to feel the touch and you go down. It is never a foul.”
Dominik Szoboszlai scored the resulting free-kick, setting Liverpool on their way to victory to make it a difficult first match in charge for Pochettino. Yoro will now be available to face Brentford on Saturday in the Premier League.

items.text:
Nvidia stock cools after Huang’s return-driven surge
Nvidia regains $952bn in market value after Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO following scandalous resignation less than two weeks ago.
Nvidia lost $1.16 trillion in market value when CEO Jensen Huang resigned less than two weeks ago amid reports of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
By Monday, Nvidia had recovered $952bn of that loss, according to an analysis by the Financial Times, after the company’s board unanimously voted to reinstate Huang, who cofounded the company, amid unprecedented pressure from United States President Donald Trump.
“At the end of the day, the Board knew it had no choice but to bring him back and for the US technology sector this was the move it had to make,” Dan Ives, managing director of Yorkville Ives, said in a note on Tuesday.
Shares of the Santa Clara, California-based chip giant jumped 31 percent on Monday as Huang returned to the company’s offices to cheers and fanfare from employees.
“Founders are rare, and there is most often no second similar person at a founder-led company,” Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of Founders 100 ETF, told Al Jazeera.
However, Nvidia’s stock reversed course as trading began on Tuesday, falling more than 5 percent.
Investor sentiment began to sour over reports that new tariffs on China could be on the horizon. Other semiconductor stocks also pulled back. Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) slumped more than 10 percent as markets opened on Tuesday. Broadcom fell 4.2 percent while Micron Technology was down more than 8 percent.
Data centre companies also suffered losses with CoreWeave falling 7.6 percent in early trading.
Monday’s surge offered a brief reprieve for the artificial intelligence sector, which has struggled after this month’s US midterm elections. Democrats, who largely ran on platforms more sceptical of AI than those of their Republican rivals, will take control of both the House of Representatives and Senate in the next Congress, which convenes in January. Meanwhile, ballot measures seeking to restrict data centre construction were successful in all but one jurisdiction.
Tuesday’s drops also hit Anthropic, which, following a blockbuster initial public offering last week, began trading at $111.50 per share, up from its initial offering price of $83. However, the surge was short-lived. The stock has fallen 22 percent since its trading debut, including a 7.3 percent drop in early trading on Tuesday.
Overall, US markets were mixed in early trading. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite index was down 1.3 percent while the S&P 500 fell 0.6 percent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, meanwhile, was in positive territory, up 0.4 percent.

items.summary:

items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24 – The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) has admitted it has no legal powers to punish politicians conducting premature campaigns ahead of the 2027 General Election, following the failure to enact legislation governing political campaigns.
The commission says it cannot impose sanctions on politicians mobilising support and soliciting votes outside the official campaign period because there is no specific law empowering it to take action against early campaigns.
IEBC officials said the gap persisted despite a High Court directive issued in June 2025 requiring the Attorney General to take steps towards enacting legislation to regulate political campaigns within 12 months.
Speaking during an engagement with journalists, IEBC officials said the court had recognised the dangers posed by premature campaigns but acknowledged that the commission lacked a legal framework through which it could enforce restrictions.
The commission said the absence of legislation left it unable to take punitive action against aspirants already traversing the country, holding political rallies and mobilising supporters ahead of the August 10, 2027 elections.
Mukhwana said the court had ruled that premature political campaigns undermined constitutional principles and fundamental rights, including equality before the law, freedom from violence, impartiality and the right to free and fair elections.
“The court noted that there was no law upon which the IEBC would act,” he said, explaining why the commission could not sanction politicians engaging in early campaigns.
Mukhwana said the June 9, 2025 judgment in Legal Advice Centre t/a Kituo Cha Sheria v IEBC and Others arose from a petition challenging political campaigns conducted before the officially designated election period.
A three-judge bench comprising Justices Hedwig Ong’udi, Patricia Gichohi and Heston Nyaga declared that conducting political campaigns outside the election period violated constitutional principles, including equality, equal protection of the law, freedom from violence, impartiality, the rule of law and the right to free and fair elections.
The judges directed the Attorney General to take the necessary steps within 12 months to enact legislation governing political campaigns conducted outside the official election period.
The deadline expired on June 9, 2026, but IEBC officials said the commission was still without the legislation needed to enforce restrictions on premature campaigns.
Mukhwana said the commission would therefore rely on the existing electoral framework, which provides for the formal campaign period ahead of the 2027 elections.
According to the IEBC’s operational plan, the General Election will be held on August 10, 2027, with the formal campaign period expected to commence after the candidate registration process, which is scheduled to conclude by May 29, 2027.
Campaign financing
IEBC said the commission was also working to enforce the Election Campaign Financing Act, which requires political parties and candidates to comply with prescribed contribution and expenditure limits.
The commission had published campaign financing regulations, contribution limits and spending ceilings, alongside timelines for enforcing the framework.
However, two court cases had complicated implementation, with one filed at the Milimani High Court and another at the Kiambu High Court.
The official said the Kiambu court had issued conservatory orders restraining the commission from enforcing the campaign financing framework.
IEBC subsequently challenged the orders and succeeded in having them vacated last week, with the Kiambu case also transferred to Milimani for consolidation with the existing petition.
The official said the cases were scheduled for mention in February 2027, adding that the absence of restraining orders meant the commission could proceed with enforcement in accordance with its published timelines.
The Election Campaign Financing Act is intended to regulate contributions and expenditure by candidates and political parties, preventing wealthy individuals and organisations from exerting disproportionate influence over electoral competition.
The commission’s attempts to operationalise the framework have previously faced legal and procedural challenges ahead of the 2017 and 2022 elections.
The official also gave an update on procurement disputes involving election technology and ballot papers, saying the commission had faced about eight cases before the Public Procurement Administrative Review Board and the High Court in the past three months.
He said a High Court judgment delivered on Tuesday had dismissed the latest case challenging the election technology procurement process, allowing the evaluation of the tender to proceed.
However, a fresh constitutional petition had been filed immediately after the judgment. The court declined to issue conservatory orders, with the matter scheduled for mention on November 30.
On ballot papers, the official said the remaining case was scheduled for judgment on November 26, expressing hope that its determination would allow the commission to proceed with the procurement process.

China’s probes Shanghai party chief Chen Jining over corruption
Chen is the fourth Politburo member to be probed since last year in a campaign that has targeted top Chinese leaders.
China’s anticorruption watchdog has launched an investigation into the top Chinese Communist Party leader in Shanghai
items.text:
China’s probes Shanghai party chief Chen Jining over corruption
Chen is the fourth Politburo member to be probed since last year in a campaign that has targeted top Chinese leaders.
China’s anticorruption watchdog has launched an investigation into the top Chinese Communist Party leader in Shanghai and member of the elite Politburo, Chen Jining, according to state media.
The 62-year-old, who is the fourth member of the top leadership body to be probed since last year, is suspected of “severe violations of discipline and laws”, the Xinhua news agency reported. The phrase is a common euphemism for corruption.
As part of President Xi Jinping’s widening anticorruption campaign, three Politburo members from the 24-member body have already been removed in its current term, which began in 2022, including General Zhang Youxia and He Weidong, both senior members of the Central Military Commission that oversees the armed forces, and Ma Xingrui, a provincial party secretary.
Mingda Qiu, a senior analyst at the Eurasia Group, said Chen’s investigation was part of an “unprecedented pattern”.
“The takedown again shows that Xi Jinping’s anticorruption campaign has no limits,” he said.
Chen earned a doctorate in environmental engineering at Imperial College London and rose through the ranks at China’s elite Tsinghua University to become its president.
He entered government as China’s environmental protection minister before becoming the mayor of Beijing. In 2022, he joined the Politburo as the party boss of Shanghai, China’s financial hub.
The post is one of China’s most prestigious provincial-level positions, often serving as a springboard to top leadership roles. Xi briefly served in the role in 2007 before joining the Politburo’s Standing Committee, the country’s highest decision-making body.
China’s second-ranking official, Prime Minister Li Qiang, as well as Vice President Han Zheng, also held the Shanghai post before moving into central leadership roles.
In a separate development, Liu Min, a senior official at the Ministry of Science and Technology, has also been placed under investigation for suspected “serious violations of party discipline and national laws”.

items.text:
Pope Francis diaries recount spiritual crisis, him seeing the 'Devil'
November 24, 2026
The late Pope Francis suffered a spiritual crisis during his papacy when he struggled with how to lead the Catholic Church and believed he saw and heard the devil on several occasions, according to an annotated collection of his private diaries published on Tuesday.
Francis was pope for 12 years until his death last April.
Cardinal Victor Fernandez, a compatriot and close collaborator of Francis', collated the diary entries and provides accompanying commentary, in the first set of papal diaries to be published posthumously since those of John XXIII, who died in 1963.
What does the book say about Francis' difficulties as pope?
The diary entries speak of the Argentine-born pontiff not wanting to be someone "who uses others like puppets," according to the accompanying commentary.
"It was all mixed with governance issues, pressure regarding decisions to make, and aridity and desolation," a December 2022 entry from Francis said.
Although the book does not make clear exactly who Francis worried he was using like puppets or the nature of the internal pressures, Francis encountered stern resistance from more conservative forces within the Church as he urged the staid institution to modernize.
Cardinal Fernandez wrote that Francis "ultimately recognized it was the worst trial that had toremented him ... and that he felt that he was in a continual battle not to fall into this demonic seduction."
What does the book say about Francis' religious visions and dreams?
The 160-page selection of excerpts — starting in 1992 when he was still known as Jorge Mario Bergoglio and running until a few months before his death — are arranged by theme and pay closer attention to Francis' internal spiritual experiences than Vatican politics.
But one of the three occasions listed where the late pope believed he had seen the Devil was during a meeting with Vatican officials in January 2021 early in what he termed a spiritual crisis. In that instance he even believed to have heard the figure speak.
"I can't forget the powerful raspiness of his voice," Francis wrote in an entry. "The Lord granted me an opportunity to leave that meeting, and thus he freed me."
Other entries detail how Francis believed that God spoke to him in his dreams, and one from 2018 stated: "Last night I saw the entrance to Hell. I peeked in to look a little, and it terrified me."
What else features in the diary excerpts?
The papers show Francis to be self-critical at times, chastizing himself for "feelings of disdain, envy, pride" or for ignoring a drunken man who approached him "because I wanted to have a serene walk."
At one point in a 2022 entry he refers to himself as the "proud, self-sufficient, cynical, self-deceptive Jorge."
They also show how in later years he felt anxious to make the most of his remaining years, and regretful about some of his deicsions earlier in his life.
"I want to do good during the little time I have left, desiring to be good," he wrote in 1996 on turning 60. "How much time I've used badly! How much badly done!"
The accounts also list his regret after a visit to Chile in 2018 when he faced stern criticism for initially dismissing allegations of sexual abuse and cover-up against a bishop there before later apologizing.
"It was hard for me to admit what happened in Chile; I didn't think it was so serious," a "devastated" pontiff wrote three years later.
Fernandez also recounts comments from Francis on some senior officials in the Vatican including his successor, US Cardinal Robert Prevost, now Pope Leo XIV. According to Fernandez, Francis called him "a great pastor, a generous missionary, and an irreproachable man."

items.text:
UK police arrest two after break-in at Prince William’s country residence
The arrests were made at a property on the royal family’s Sandringham estate in Norfolk, eastern England.
Two men have been arrested on suspicion of burglary and trespass after a break-in at the country residence of Britain’s Prince William and Princess Catherine in eastern England, according to police.
The suspects were arrested on Tuesday after officers were called on Monday night in response to a report of suspicious activity at a property on the royal family’s Sandringham estate in Norfolk. The property was unoccupied at the time, police added.
The Sun newspaper first reported that police were investigating a break-in at Anmer Hall, a 10-bedroom house, which the late Queen Elizabeth gave William and Catherine as a wedding present in 2011.
The men were arrested after a search involving police dogs, drones and a helicopter.
Although William and Catherine use the country retreat for holidays and short breaks, their main home is on the Windsor Castle estate, west of London.
The news came as William visited Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the British leader’s office in the capital.
Intruders have breached royal properties several times over the years.
In October 2024, burglars broke into the Windsor Castle estate west of London and stole a pick-up truck and a quad bike from a farm building.
King Charles III and Queen Camilla were not in the castle at the time, but it was reported that William and Catherine were in their nearby house.
Three years earlier, a man armed with a crossbow was detained on the castle grounds. Jaswant Singh Chail was later sentenced to nine years in prison after admitting he had been encouraged by a chatbot to kill Queen Elizabeth.
In 1982, intruder Michael Fagan managed to sneak into the monarch’s private chambers while she was in bed. The queen spent 10 minutes chatting with the burglar before raising the alarm when he asked for a cigarette.
Fagan was sent to a psychiatric hospital, then released and later jailed for unrelated criminal offences.

items.text:
Land mine casualties soar in Syria, two years after war
- Published
Eleven-year-old Alaa was tending her family's goats with her siblings in a field behind their home in Umm Khuzaym, north-west Syria, on Sunday when there was a flash and a deafening bang.
"Then we heard people screaming," Alaa's father, Walid Mohammed Al-Ghafar, told the BBC.
Walid ran outside to find his daughter lying face down, killed, and her 10-year-old brother, Mahmoud, seriously injured.
Unwittingly, the children had triggered a landmine.
The incident and others this week bring to nearly 1,000 the number of children killed or injured by explosive ordnance in Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, according to the UN Mine Action Service (Unmas).
The village is one of many where families have returned to homes and farmland that were once on the front lines of Syria's 13-year civil war.
Alaa's father said demining teams had visited several times to clear the fields. He and other residents believed it was safe for farmers and children to move around.
But mines and other explosives can lie far beyond former battle lines, making it difficult to establish which areas are safe.
"Remnants of war from today's conflicts are often very widely and broadly scattered, often without patterns, which makes it extremely difficult to do clearance," Katrin Atkins, research lead at Landmine Monitor, a global mine monitoring initiative, told the BBC.
The dangers are reflected in a sharp rise in casualties across Syria.
A total of 1,602 people were killed or injured by landmines and explosive remnants of war in 2025 alone, an increase of more than 50% on the previous year, according to the Landmine Monitor report, published by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines on Tuesday.
Only Myanmar, with 1,891 casualties, recorded more.
The report attributes the rise in Syria partly to the large-scale return of refugees and internally displaced people following Assad's overthrow.
"When you look at population movement, a couple of months later you see an increase of incidents in these areas, because that's exactly where people go and start to use the fields again," Atkins said.
More than 60% of casualties recorded by the world's largest landmine clearance charity, the Halo Trust, involve farming, agriculture or shepherding, according to its Syria programme manager, Simon Jackson.
"They're not going to wait for the government or for organisations like us to come and tell them that everything is safe and clear," he told the BBC. "People are taking risks out of desperation."
Since Assad's fall on 8 December 2024, Unmas has recorded at least 1,556 incidents in Syria involving explosive ordnance.
They have caused 2,701 casualties: 935 people killed and 1,766 injured. Children account for 995 of those victims, or about 37%.
But the toll is likely to be higher, with experts estimating that overall casualties could be under-reported by 25-50%.
For many of those who survive, the consequences are devastating and permanent.
Majid Abdul Rahman, 27, was travelling in a car in the Ghouta region on the outskirts of Damascus in March 2025 when it struck an explosive device. The vehicle filled with smoke and he felt a pain in his leg.
More than a year later, Majid has difficulty walking and has been unable to return to work, leaving him struggling to provide for his family.
The danger has continued into this month, with at least 20 people killed and more than 40 injured by explosive ordnance in November.
In one of the worst recorded incidents, an explosion in a school courtyard in Hasakah on 4 November killed a 12-year-old and injured 19 others. And on Monday, a 13-year-old boy was killed when an unexploded cluster munition detonated in southern Daraa province.
The threat is also holding back Syria's economic recovery. Contaminated farmland cannot be safely cultivated, while people collecting scrap metal or trying to salvage materials from abandoned areas also risk triggering explosions.
The Syrian Ministry of Defence says since the end of 2024 its teams have found and dealt with more than 315,000 mines and unexploded munitions.
But no nationwide survey has established how much land remains contaminated, making it difficult to assess the full scale of the problem.
"We're in a bit of a black hole," Atkins said.
And with the extent of contamination still largely unknown, the war continues to claim victims two years after it ended.
Additional reporting by Lana Antaki in Damascus

items.text:
Players Championship Finals 2026: Schedule and order of play as Gerwyn Price eyes another major title in Minehead
Gerwyn Price looks to back up his Grand Slam of Darts win by claiming a second straight major title; former champions Luke Humphries and Michael van Gerwen also among the 64-player field in Minehead, but world No 1 and defending champion Luke Littler did not qualify
Tuesday 24 November 2026 16:05, UK
The 2026 Ladbrokes Players Championship Finals sees 64 players competing to win the PDC's last major event before the World Darts Championship gets under way in December.
The tournament - which has a newly increased prize fund of £750,000 - features the top 64 ranked players following the conclusion of the 34-event Players Championship season, and takes place at Butlin's Minehead Resort from November 27-29.
Gerwyn Price, recently crowned Grand Slam of Darts champion for a fourth time, opens his bid for back-to-back major titles against Sebastian Bialecki on Friday, with record seven-time winner Michael van Gerwen in action against Connor Scutt and Luke Humphries - triumphant in 2023 and 2024 - going up against Darryl Pilgrim.
Top seed Wessel Nijman has been handed a tough opener against exciting youngster Henry Coates, while Beau Greaves makes her Players Championship Finals debut against Christian Kist.
World No 1 and defending champion Luke Littler did not qualify for the Finals.
Friday's first round winners advance to Saturday's double session, with the second round scheduled for the afternoon and round three in the evening.
The tournament concludes on Sunday November 29, with the afternoon's quarter-finals followed by the semi-finals and final in a decisive evening session that also includes the Winmau World Youth Championship final between Cam Crabtree and Jan Schmidt.

NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 24 – Improved rural roads, cheaper farm inputs, faster-maturing sugarcane varieties and increased financial support are among the priorities Samuel Ongou, one of the aspirants for the Kenya Sugar Board Director position says he will pursue as he seeks to represent the Central Catchment Area in the Board.
Ongou, who is contesting for the director’s position covering Kisumu, Kericho and Nandi counties, says addressing production challenges and improving farmers’ earnings will be central to his agenda as the sugar industry enters a new phase of reforms.
Speaking as the Kenya Sugar Board elections entered their final stages, Ongou said significant progress had been made in addressing some of the challenges that have troubled sugarcane farmers for years, but maintained that more needed to be done to make the sector sustainable.
He cited the introduction of weekly payments to farmers, clearance of historical arrears and reduction of fertiliser prices as some of the gains achieved under the current administration.
“In the past, there used to be a lot of arrears, particularly from the State-owned mills. Nowadays, all the sugar millers in Kenya are paying weekly,” he said.
Ongou noted that the cost of fertiliser had also been reduced from Sh7,000 to Sh2,000 per 50-kilogramme bag, easing the financial burden on farmers and creating room for increased production.
He further pointed to the ongoing distribution of bonuses as an important intervention in improving farmers’ earnings, noting that President William Ruto had launched the payments in the Nzoia region, with a similar exercise expected in the Central Catchment Area.
However, Ongou said poor road infrastructure remained one of the major obstacles affecting sugarcane production, particularly in areas where farmers struggle to transport mature cane to milling factories.
He pledged to prioritise road rehabilitation and ensure funds allocated for infrastructure development were utilised to improve access to farms and facilitate timely cane delivery.
“We will make sure that the roads are fixed. We will also make sure that we roll out money for cane development to farmers, which will be at three per cent,” he said.
Another key area he wants addressed is the development of early-maturing sugarcane varieties, which he believes could transform productivity and profitability in the region.
Ongou said the Kenya Sugar Research and Training Institute (KESRETI) had received funding to prepare planting materials for improved varieties expected to mature within nine to 12 months.
He contrasted the proposed varieties with existing ones, including Company 617, which takes at least 18 months to mature, saying shorter maturity periods would enable farmers to harvest more frequently.
The development, he said, would help farmers improve their annual production cycles, increase income and reduce the time and resources spent maintaining their crops before harvesting.
“We want to make sure that farmers in the coming future will be harvesting yearly, compared to the current varieties which take at least 18 months and above. The new varieties will be between nine and 12 months,” he said.
Ongou expressed confidence that continued investment in research, infrastructure and farmer support would help restore the competitiveness of the sugar industry and make cane farming a commercially viable enterprise.
He also called for unity among farmers and candidates, urging them to maintain peace as the election process concludes.
He said leadership should be viewed as an opportunity to serve all farmers regardless of their political or regional affiliations, adding that divisions would only undermine efforts to address challenges in the sector.
“We are one Kenya. Once elected, I will serve everybody. I don’t see why we need to fight,” he said.
Ongou said his focus would be on consolidating the gains already made while pushing for practical interventions that directly improve the livelihoods of sugarcane farmers across the Central Catchment Area.

items.text:
How the Iran war is reshaping the US military presence in the Middle East
Experts say fallout from the Iran war and domestic opposition could force a smaller permanent presence in the Middle East.
The United States military presence across the Middle East is sprawling.
There are as many as 50,000 US troops and about 19 major military installations in the region, as well as assets spread across countries such as Bahrain, Jordan and Saudi Arabia.
But experts warn that the US-Israel war on Iran has exposed vulnerabilities in protecting Washington’s military assets in the region, leading some to speculate that a downsizing may occur once the war is over.
Michael O’Hanlon, senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, a Washington-based think tank, is among those who expect the US to eventually scale back its military presence in the Middle East.
“I think we will go smaller, more dispersed, more hardened, and generally further away from Iran — but not in each and every case,” O’Hanlon said.
As the war enters its 10th month on Saturday, the damage inflicted on US installations in the Middle East could one day translate into a strategic shift — not just for the US but for other countries that have been shaped by its military presence as well.
Billions of dollars in damage
One of the long-term obstacles to maintaining the US military presence will be the cost of repairs.
Repairing damaged infrastructure on US bases in the region could cost $9.4b, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a Washington, DC-based think tank.
Hundreds of structures on US bases have been damaged by Iranian attacks since February 28, when the war began.
One of those bases was in Bahrain, home to the US Naval Forces Central Command and its Fifth Naval Fleet. The US has established a naval command presence in the country as far back as 1948.
But according to a report from the Congressional Research Service, the base — called Naval Support Activity (NSA) Bahrain — “sustained serious damage” in the early days of the Iran war. It estimated the cost of repairing the base at more than $400m.
Other US military assets in the region have also been impacted by the war.
In September, a Department of Defense inspector general report found the US had lost dozens of aircraft during the war, among them attack helicopters and sophisticated fighter jets like the F-35A and the F-15E.
By October, the total cost of the Iran war reached more than $47bn, according to Pentagon figures.
Rethinking the need for large bases
Rebuilding the US bases is unlikely until the Iran war is over, according to Mark Cancian, a senior adviser with the Defense and Security Department at CSIS.
“If the war ends with some sort of ceasefire or we get to a place where it’s somewhat stable,” Cancian said, “then you will see some reduction in US forces and reduction of the surge forces certainly and some rebuilding of the bases.”
But Cancian expects that the US will not rebuild all the military sites struck by Iran.
He pointed to the Bahrain headquarters of the Fifth Naval Fleet and the Combined Air Operations Center at Al Udeid airbase in Qatar as examples.
Some military facilities, he explained, will likely be moved underground to protect against aerial attack. Others may be relocated further from the Gulf, to places such as Israel or Jordan.
Major bases like those in Bahrain or Qatar were a liability because “they are right within the range of Iranian missiles and drones”, according to Kelly Grieco, a defence policy expert and senior fellow at the Stimson Center, a global security think tank.
But simply moving bases further away will not protect them in the long term. Grieco pointed out that Iran keeps improving its ability to reach longer-distance targets with drones and missiles.
One alternative to rebuilding bases, she said, would be instead to cultivate access to a network of airstrips and temporary bases in the Middle East that could be used if another conflict erupts.
In the Iran war, for instance, the US has relied extensively on facilities like Israel’s Ben Gurion airport for refuelling combat aircraft.
“What mattered more was access to places and the ability to move around those places, more than having a permanent operating facility,” Grieco said.
What the region wants
Experts say downsizing the US military presence in the Middle East has been a goal across several administrations.
President Donald Trump, for instance, has completed troop withdrawals from Syria and Iraq since the start of his second term in 2025. His predecessor, Joe Biden, also oversaw the US military pullout from Afghanistan in 2021.
But practical realities — including the emergence of new conflicts involving the US — have put that aspiration of a large-scale drawdown out of reach.
“The Biden administration wanted to reduce the force posture. The Trump administration wanted to reduce the force posture,” Cancian said. “They haven’t been able to, and it’s not clear they will be able to.”
Allies and adversaries alike also help to determine the heft of the US military presence, he added.
“The world gets a vote, and even if the administration wants to reduce the force posture, it may not be possible, because of continuing tensions,” Cancian said.
New alliances, however, have emerged that might make certain regional allies less reliant on US military resources.
In August, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, a pact that theoretically commits the countries to come to each other’s aid in case of an attack.
Experts say the deal could trigger a regional realignment away from the US and its military might.
Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan could potentially wield formidable force: Together, they have more than 1.4 million active military personnel, own thousands of tanks and military aircraft and spend more than $124bn on their combined defence budget.

France's femicide orphans: The invisible victims of violence against women
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

Issued on: Modified:
In France, 111 women were killed by their current or ex-partners in 2025 alone, leaving behind dozens of children. How can they rebuild their lives without their mother? How can they seek help? In this episode of France in Focus, we meet Cloé and Eva-Louise, whose world collapsed when their father brutally murdered their mother. FRANCE 24's Natacha Vesnitch, Olivia Bizot, Clément Di Roma and Aurore Cloé Dupuis report.
Eva-Louise remembers every detail of March 28, 2023. That day, she received a phone call from the man she now refuses to call her father. "He told me my mother had left him, that she'd sent him a message saying she was tired of living together. It didn't sound like her at all," recalls the young woman, now 23.
A month and a half later, on June 14, 2023, Michel Pialle was taken into police custody. Karine Esquivillon's husband confessed to killing her, although he claimed it was accidental. Following his confession, her body was found in a wooded area around 15 kilometres from her home. The autopsy showed she took a bullet to the chest. Pialle was formally charged with murdering his wife and is due to stand trial in February 2027.
'At 20, you're not ready to organise your mother's funeral'
Eva-Louise hoped her mother might still be alive, but when her corpse was found, the young woman's world was turned upside down. Her younger brother and sister, both under 18, were initially placed in the care of child protection services before their older brother took over guardianship.
At just 20, Eva-Louise also had to organise her mother's funeral, find a lawyer and deal with media requests. "You stop sleeping, you cry, but you don't have time to grieve," she says, adding that she was never offered any support to cope with the trauma.
The family home remained sealed off as part of the investigation for almost three years. When Eva-Louise was finally allowed back inside in December 2025, she retrieved a few personal belongings, including photographs and documents bearing her mother's handwriting – precious reminders of a life brutally cut short.
Charities step in to support victims' families
After a femicide, children often lose both parents: their father either takes his own life, flees or ends up in prison after killing their mother. To support these children and their families, Sandrine Bouchait and Isabelle Seva-Boismoreau founded the National Union of Families Affected by Femicide (UNFF) in 2019.
Throughout the year, the two women travel across France to support victims' relatives, particularly during court proceedings. The organisation has also produced a leaflet to help children identify and understand the emotions they may experience after losing their mother: sadness, anxiety but also happiness. The aim is to reassure them that all these feelings are legitimate and that they have no reason to feel guilty about them.
Another crucial challenge is helping children navigate conflicting loyalties. "A child can continue to love their father while condemning what he has done," Bouchait explains.
Burned alive in front of her seven-year-old daughter
Bouchait's own sister, Ghylaine, was killed by her partner on September 22, 2017. She was 34 and wanted to leave him. He doused her in petrol and set her on fire. Her seven-year-old daughter Cloé witnessed the attack.
Sandrine promised her sister on her deathbed that she would take care of Cloé. She eventually adopted her after navigating all the necessary procedures alone. Fortunately, she realised how important psychological support would be for the little girl.
"We received no support," Bouchait says. "But we knew that Cloé had lived through a war zone, and that she would need help to overcome it and have a safe space of her own where she could process everything she had seen that night."
Femicide support protocol still not widely implemented in France
Now 16, Cloé is in high school and dreams of becoming a forensic doctor "to help ensure that the perpetrators of the most heinous crimes are convicted". Eva-Louise, meanwhile, has moved in with her boyfriend and returned to university.
In France, a dedicated femicide response protocol provides free medical and psychological support for children whose mothers were murdered. First introduced in the Paris suburb of Seine-Saint-Denis 11 years ago, it was extended nationwide in 2022. Yet implementation remains patchy. According to a July 2024 report by the National Committee on Domestic Violence, only one in five French departments have set it up.
As for young adults like Eva-Louise, there is no support system for them, following the murder of their mother by their father.

items.text:
Senegal reinstated as Afcon 2025 winners by court ruling
- Published
Senegal have been reinstated as winners of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) after a ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas).
The court's award overturns a previous decision which had stripped the West Africans of the title they won on the pitch during a chaotic final against host nation Morocco in January.
The result of that match in Rabat, which saw the Teranga Lions triumph 1-0 after extra time, was overturned almost two months later when a Confederation of African Football (Caf) appeals board decreed Senegal had breached competition regulations by leaving the field of play in second-half stoppage time in protest at a penalty awarded against them.
Senegal's football federation (FSF) subsequently appealed to Cas, sport's highest legal authority, with a three-man panel hearing its case behind closed doors in Lausanne on 8 October.
In a unanimous verdict, the Cas panel has effectively backed the decision by referee Jean-Jacques Ndala to restart the game after Senegal returned to the field and the match was played to a conclusion. The result of the final stands and Senegal are now confirmed as Afcon 2025 winners.
The court said it considered that "the referee's decision to resume the match or to stop it fell definitively within his sole authority".
"By blowing his whistle to restart play, the referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met - both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume."
The FSF immediately reacted with a social media post featuring a picture of the side lifting the trophy in January captioned with the phrase "again and always".
Caf is yet to comment on the decision but its president Patrice Motsepe has repeatedly said that his organisation will respect and adhere to the Cas ruling.
Morocco's football federation (FRMF) is also yet to comment on the verdict.
- 'Shameful' and 'terrible look' - the chaos that marred Afcon 2025 final 
  - Published19 January
Morocco and Senegal have both changed coach since the final and earlier this month secured their places at the 2027 edition of the tournament with two rounds of qualification remaining.
This ruling should now settle any debate about who the history books will recognise as continental champions - although plenty in Morocco may not agree with the outcome of the case at Cas.
What happened in the Afcon final?
A tightly-contested match between the continent's top-ranked sides produced two moments of controversy in second-half stoppage time, with referee Jean-Jacques Ndala at the centre of the drama.
First the Congolese official denied Senegal a near-certain goal, blowing his whistle for a challenge by Abdoulaye Seck on Morocco right-back Achraf Hakimi moments before Ismaila Sarr nodded in.
The free-kick looked soft, but the video assistant referee (VAR) was unable to get involved because Ndala had awarded the foul before the ball crossed the line.
Three minutes later came a flashpoint in the Senegal box, when El Hadji Malick Diouf tugged Morocco playmaker Brahim Diaz back before heading a corner clear.
Diaz vehemently claimed a penalty and Ndala eventually awarded a spot kick after being sent to consult his pitchside monitor by VAR.
Senegal coach Pape Thiaw called his players over to the touchline, and Thiaw subsequently headed down the tunnel to the changing room in protest against the decision - accompanied by several players.
They eventually returned, but over 15 minutes had elapsed since the award of the penalty by the time Real Madrid's Diaz failed to convert, with his Panenka-style attempt easily saved by goalkeeper Edouard Mendy.
Meanwhile, there was unrest inside the Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium as a small contingent of Senegal supporters clashed with security staff.
The game went into extra time, with midfielder Pape Gueye scoring the goal which settled the contest in Senegal's favour.
But, off the pitch, another match involving disciplinary boards and lawyers would soon begin.
What was the fallout?
Senegal celebrated their second continental title but the FRMF quickly lodged an appeal with Caf, arguing their opponents had breached Article 82 of Afcon regulations, which covers withdrawals.
It states that if a team "refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee" it shall be "considered [the loser] and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition".
A disciplinary board from the continental game's governing body rejected the FRMF's protest days after the final as it sanctioned and fined those found guilty of unsporting conduct during the match.
Yet in March, almost two months on from the final, a Caf appeals board ruled that Senegal had forfeited the match and awarded Morocco a 3-0 victory.
The FSF described the ruling as "unfair, unprecedented and unacceptable" and swiftly lodged its case with Cas.
The director general of the Switzerland-based court said arbitration proceedings would be conducted "as swiftly as possible", but it was over five months until all parties descended on Lausanne for a one-day hearing.
The Cas panel was led by Frenchman Gerald Simon, founder of the Sports Law Laboratory at the University of Burgundy and a Cas member for 23 years.
Both the FRMF and FSF were able to nominate an arbitrator to exercise an independent judicial function once their appointment was confirmed.
The FRMF nominated Italian international law professor Luigi Fumagalli, while the FSF nominated Hamburg-based attorney and professor of law at the University of Zurich Ulrich Haas. Those two men completed the Cas panel.
Over six weeks on from that hearing - and 10 months since the Afcon 2025 final - Senegal have been proclaimed champions once again.
But the debate and damage done to the reputation of African football is likely to linger for some time yet.

items.text:
The photos from Gaza resonating with the people of Sarajevo
From a photography exhibition to a weekly vigil reading out the names of killed children, solidarity grows in Sarajevo.
Sarajevo, Bosnia and Herzegovina – A mother holds her daughter, trying to shield and comfort her at the same time. It is the eyes you notice first. And something aches deep inside you, especially if you come from Sarajevo, a city that survived a siege by Serb forces from 1992 to 1995.
Then you remember that you are still in Sarajevo, where there is peace now.
The image is the work of Salah Ostaz, who is still in Gaza, where rockets are falling and food and water are scarce, and where the silence of most world leaders may ring louder than the explosions, even as people in the streets around the world are raising their voices.
I have been a journalist for a long time. I took my first steps as a reporter in wartime Sarajevo: front lines, massacres, morgues, mass graves, hospitals, empty markets, cultural events that people risked their lives to attend for some semblance of normality. I wrote about all of it and thought nothing could get to me any more.
Until Gaza.
Another photograph. A girl’s eyes, wide open, as though she were looking back over the past three years at everything she has seen, which I do not even want to imagine.
In the next photograph, people line up for a spoonful of food.
And then something altogether different – children smiling and swimming at dusk off a crowded beach, as if this were the happiest time of their lives. There is hope in that picture.
That is what the people who organised Ostaz’s exhibition in Sarajevo believe. I went over to ask them how it came about.
Valida Hadzimuratovic, a radio journalist and DJ known in Los Angeles as Valida Carroll, was in Sarajevo when Ostaz video-called her in October last year. Alongside other activists, she had been organising weekly TikTok livestreams in which Palestinian journalists spoke about what they had witnessed. That call was the beginning of a friendship. Over the following months, she shared his photographs and learned more about his life, including why he had not been able to collect his diploma.
“I remember thinking how frustrating it must be to finish your studies, put in all that work, and then not be able to get hold of something as basic as your own diploma,” Valida told me.
She and her friend Nasiha, a Bosnian who also lives in Los Angeles, began raising money to cover his tuition fees. In September, they decided to show Ostaz’s work in Sarajevo. He sent them more than 150 photographs. Milomir Kovacevic, who documented life in his own city during the siege of Sarajevo, helped curate the show to include about 60.
A silent auction was held alongside the exhibition, with about two dozen artisans and small businesses donating work and prizes. Volunteers and activists from the Ka Gazi (Towards Gaza) movement helped organise the event.
Every Tuesday evening, Ka Gazi volunteers gather in central Sarajevo at the Eternal Flame, an antifascist memorial commemorating those who died resisting fascism during the Second World War. They read aloud the names of Palestinian children who have been killed. If you pass by, you hear the name of one child, then another.
Last year, the names were also read at Sarajevo’s MESS International Theatre Festival. The year before, the festival opened with Metro Gaza, a production featuring the Palestinian Freedom Theatre from Jenin, in the occupied West Bank. That year’s motto was “Unstoppable Life”.
“No one who lived through the siege of Sarajevo should be indifferent to the suffering of others,” said MESS director Nihad Kresevljakovic, while visiting the photography exhibition.
At the end of the evening, people walked out of the Bosnian Cultural Centre carrying photographs and items they had won at the auction. All the proceeds went towards covering the costs of getting Ostaz his diploma.
“We can’t help everyone in Gaza. The needs are enormous and the destruction is immeasurable. But we can help one person,” Hadzimuratovic said.

items.text:
EU enlargement: Who's blocking whom — and why?
November 24, 2026
It's been quite a while since the EU's last enlargement: Croatia was the last country to join the bloc back in 2013.
If everything goes according to plan, another enlargement might soon be on the cards: Montenegro, with a population of just 620,000, could complete accession negotiations in the coming months and join the European Union in early 2028.
But no sooner had EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos made this announcement in October than news emerged that Croatia might veto Montenegro's accession unless the country meets a series of Croatian demands.
EU politicians and MEPs were dismayed.
This is not the first time that something like this has happened: The veto rights that member states have on many EU matters have increasingly been used by individual countries in recent years as a means of blackmail and a political weapon, paralyzing the EU in the process.
DW takes a look at some of the most significant cases, the background to them and what are — in some instances — the serious political consequences of them.
Montenegro: Croatia's eight demands
Montenegro is the most advanced EU candidate country, with a potential accession date of 2028. It has already provisionally closed several of the EU's 33 negotiating chapters.
As of November 23, however, Croatia is blocking the closure of three chapters that have already been negotiated.
Zagreb is demanding, among other things, compensation for former prisoners held in Montenegrin camps during the Yugoslav wars of the 1990s, clarification of the fate of Croatians who have been missing since that time, and more rigorous prosecution of war crimes.
There are also disputes over the precise maritime boundary between the two countries. In addition, Croatia is demanding payment of about €2.4 billion (about $2.6 billion) for assets that belonged to the Yugoslav People's Army, the army of the former Yugoslavia to which both countries belonged before its breakup in the early 1990s.
Montenegro has already responded to some of Croatia's demands, including those concerning compensation for former prisoners. Others, such as the one relating to the assets of the Yugoslav People's Army, are disputed.
It is clear that Croatia's list of demands is also driven by domestic politics. No government in Zagreb can afford to appear compliant on issues relating to the Croatian War of Independence (1991–95).
Moreover, moderate conservative Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic, who is regularly accused in Croatia of being too pro-EU, can use the dispute to portray himself as a staunch defender of national interests.
Ukraine: Hungarian domestic politics in the name of a minority
After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the EU in June 2022 granted Ukraine and the Republic of Moldova EU candidate status through an accelerated procedure as a gesture of solidarity.
Many EU member states have reservations about Ukraine joining the bloc quickly. Nevertheless, only Hungary, under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, adopted an obstructive stance.
Ostensibly, Hungary's obstruction was about getting Ukraine to improve the rights of the Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia in western Ukraine. Ultimately, however, Orban used the matter for domestic political purposes and as an election campaign issue, portraying Ukraine as a "mafia state."
In an effort to appeal to widespread anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Hungary, the country's new prime minister, Peter Magyar, has also adopted a tough stance on Ukraine.
Nevertheless, Magyar's government lifted several temporary blocks on the opening of new negotiating chapters, among other things after the Ukrainian parliament passed a law in early October strengthening the educational rights of national minorities.
North Macedonia: The never-ending blockade
No EU candidate country has suffered as much or as long from veto politics as North Macedonia: It was granted EU candidate status in 2005 but only began accession negotiations in July 2022.
Greece blocked the start of negotiations for 13 years because it objected to the name "Republic of Macedonia," as the country was previously known, and accused its neighbor of laying territorial claims to the region of Macedonia in northern Greece.
The dispute was settled in 2018 through a compromise that saw the country change its name to the Republic of North Macedonia the following year.
But just as the path to accession negotiations seemed clear, Bulgaria blocked the opening of talks in November 2020.
Bulgaria regards the Macedonian language as a dialect of Bulgarian and disputes the existence of a distinct Macedonian nation.
Here, too, domestic Bulgarian politics is ultimately a factor.
Former Bulgarian President and current Prime Minister Rumen Radev, for example, fueled the escalation with North Macedonia to enhance his political profile.
Serbia: Croatia is not the only country obstructing progress
Although Serbia has been negotiating EU accession since 2014, little progress has been made.
In July, when the country was still led by President Aleksandar Vucic, no less than eight EU member states — including Croatia — opposed opening further negotiating chapters with Serbia.
While the main reservations relate to democratic shortcomings, deficiencies in the rule of law and corruption in Serbia, Croatia also has its own disputes with its eastern neighbor.
These concern the 1991–95 war, including missing persons, war crimes, minority rights and differing interpretations of history. Relations are also strained by nationalist rhetoric on both sides.
Whether the election victory of the Student List in Belgrade in late October after almost two years of anti-government, anti-corruption protests will change this situation is impossible to say.
Albania: Greece threatens to use minority rights as leverage
The EU opened accession negotiations with Albania, which has been an EU candidate since 2014, in July 2022.

items.summary:
CAS reinstates Senegal as 2025 AFCON champions
November 24, 2026
Just over eight months after Senegal were stripped of their 2025 African Cup of Nations (AFCON) title, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has announced that Senegal's appeal has been upheld, reinstating them as 2025 AFCON winners
items.text:
CAS reinstates Senegal as 2025 AFCON champions
November 24, 2026
Just over eight months after Senegal were stripped of their 2025 African Cup of Nations (AFCON) title, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has announced that Senegal's appeal has been upheld, reinstating them as 2025 AFCON winners. Morocco, who had been declared champions after a Confederation of African Football (CAF) review, has now been confirmed as runners-up.
"The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has upheld the appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) against the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and the the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF, in French)," the CAS statement read.
"The decision rendered by the CAF Appeal Board is set aside and the decision by the CAF Disciplinary Board is reinstated. Consequently, the result obtained at the end of the AFCON 2025 final is confirmed."
The statement continued that it felt "the Referee's decision to resume the match or to stop it fell definitively within his sole authority" and that his "decision was covered by the ‘field of play’ doctrine."
The decision comes after a closed-doors hearing at CAS' headquarters in Lausanne in early October.
Before the verdict was delivered, Morocco captain Achraf Hakimi posted a message on Instagram saying he would disagree with Senegal being stripped of the title because "its players fought so hard to win."
"I respect the authorities responsible for football, but I firmly believe that what happens on the pitch should be the most important thing of all. Senegal won that Africa Cup of Nations final through their performance, their determination, and the effort of every player, just as every player represents his country. They fought for that title, and no one can erase what those players achieved on the pitch," Hakimi wrote.
"African football needs unity, fairness, and credibility. We cannot keep building our game if decisions like these leave players and fans questioning everything."
An infamous AFCON final
The final was played on January 18, with Senegal winning 1-0 after extra-time. However, the game was thrown into confusion when many Senegal players walked off the pitch following the referee's decision to award Morocco a penalty in the final minutes. Around 15 minutes later, and after furious Senegalese fans had attempted a pitch invasion, the players did return. Morocco's Brahim Diaz inexplicably missed the penalty, sending the game into extra time, which is when Senegal scored the eventual winner.
Just 10 days afterwards, the CAF issued fines worth more than $1 million (€835,000) and banned players from both teams.
Two months later, and after the Senegal team had paraded the trophy to their fans, CAF declared that Senegal had "forfeited" the final by leaving the pitch. CAF then overturned the result, awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory and the title. The Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) denounced the CAF decision and took the case to CAS.
The aftermath had rumbled on for months, with many believing it damaging for African football as a whole.
"If you look at it critically, the value of African football will definitely go down with this," Collins Okinyo, a former CAF media consultant, told DW after the result had been overturned in March.
Impact on future World Cup host
The ruling brings an end to a saga that had cast a cloud over a well-organized tournament in Morocco.
The country is emerging as a major football hub in Africa. Already confirmed as a co-host for the World Cup in 2030, Morocco also hosted the 2026 Women's AFCON and has been hosting the U17 Women's World Cup annually since 2025 and is set to do so until 2029. It is further rumored that the Morocco, along with fellow 2030 World Cup hosts Spain and Portugal, is keen to host the next Club World Cup in 2029 as a form of preparation ahead of the big event in 2030.
Although it has made significant advances in sports infrastructure, not everyone is happy about Morocco's push into the football world. In 2025, there were major protests by Gen Z questioning the country's priorities in light of struggling health and education systems.

items.text:
Why Iran's medicine supply chain is seizing up
November 24, 2026
Ahmad,* 67, visited nearly 20 Tehran pharmacies for the antipsychotic drug chlorpromazine, but left empty-handed.
"When a patient has to go to this many pharmacies just to find an essential drug, you really have to ask who is responsible for supplying medicine," he told DW.
Mitra,* a 37-year-old Tehran resident with diabetes , spent days hunting for insulin. "These are not drugs I can postpone taking or simply give up," she said. "My life depends on regular access to this insulin."
Their ordeal reflects a wider crisis across Iran's health care system.
Along with Tehran residents, DW spoke with an official at Iran's Food and Drug Administration (IFDA) and pharmacy workers in Tehran, Rasht and Mahabad. The interviews were conducted anonymously or using pseudonyms as speaking with foreign media remains dangerous in Iran.
Iran's broken drug supply chain
The official said that Iran's falling currency, along with price controls, have drained domestic drugmaker profits, while unpaid hospital debts have delayed deliveries.
"Add our own hospitals' heavy unpaid debts to distributors, and you can see why distribution has ground to a halt and companies are no longer supplying hospitals," the official said.
"Unless the Plan and Budget Organization makes our currency allocation realistic, banks step in with loans for drugmakers and insurers settle their debts, the Health Ministry's hands will remain tied and this disaster cannot be stopped," the official warned.
IFDA spokesman Mohammad Hashemi told Iran's semi-official ILNA news agency on November 9 that fewer than 40 of roughly 700 essential drugs faced supply difficulties. However, pharmacists told DW about how difficult it can be to get drugs on shelves.
A pharmacy manager in Tehran said insurance payments are often delayed by months, while drug prices continue to climb. Another pharmacist in the northwestern Mahabad region said distributors demand cash upfront for scarce items.
The insurance delays and shifting rules have pushed some pharmacies to drop contracts or refuse costly insured drugs.
The pharmacist in Mahabad, who prefers to be called Leili,* said that general pharmacies can lack about 40 items, and larger specialty pharmacies stocking chemotherapy and complex treatments can lack over 100, including psychiatric and Parkinson's drugs, and insulin vials.
"Many drugs can no longer be found in the official supply chain at all, such as nimodipine tablets [used to treat certain strokes] or hospital injectable antibiotics that have no substitutes," she said.
Turning to low-quality, black market medicine
As common items like cold medication become scarcer or more expensive, some people are turning to home remedies, she said. She added that for essential medicines like insulin, chronic patients are using smaller doses to preserve supply.
Many of those unable to pay are middle-class customers whom pharmacists cannot easily refer to charities, she said, with elderly and psychiatric patients among the hardest hit.
Leili warned that lower quality seen in some reverse-engineered domestic drugs presents a high risk for cancer, transplant and autoimmune patients.
She added that some families are forced to turn to street markets usually located outside of clinics, which lack cold-chain controls and sell counterfeit medicines or drugs with altered expiration dates.
Another pharmacy manager who asked to be called Khadiv* said scarce medicines fetch up to 10 times official prices.
Sanctions and blockades
Amid the current conflict with the US, Khadiv said US sanctions, along with border disruptions and the US maritime blockade in the Strait of Hormuz inflate import costs.
In a statement, the US State Department told DW its sanctions follow international law to deny Tehran funds for "destabilizing behavior," stressing the measures allow "broad authorizations and exceptions" for food, medicine and medical devices. It pointed to what it called Iran's "corrupt ruling elite" for not properly allocating resources.
Iranian officials, however, reject that claim. In late summer, Health Minister Mohammad Reza Zafarghandi called US exemption claims "a big lie," saying banking, insurance, flight and shipping sanctions block imports.
Earlier this fall, the IFDA's raw materials chief cited currency, banking, customs and shipping hurdles as the main bottleneck.
DW emailed the Iranian Embassy's media office in Berlin for comment but received no reply.
"Seeing so many people unable to afford their medicine or reach medical centers leaves me with a sense of guilt and helplessness," Khadiv said, adding that lack of access can even lead to patient deaths.
For patients like Ahmad and Mitra, the standoff offers no relief, and every day, the gap between official assurances and what is actually on pharmacy shelves grows harder to ignore.
*Names changed for safety reasons.

items.summary:
Senegal reinstated as 2025 Africa Cup of Nations winners over Morocco
Court of Arbitration for Sport rules in Senegal’s favour over the controversial final in January.
Senegal have been reinstated as 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) winners after the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) upheld ‌‌t
items.text:
Senegal reinstated as 2025 Africa Cup of Nations winners over Morocco
Court of Arbitration for Sport rules in Senegal’s favour over the controversial final in January.
Senegal have been reinstated as 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) winners after the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) upheld ‌‌their appeal against being stripped of the title.
The Moroccans will lose the title that was controversially awarded to them by the Confederation of African Football (CAF) two months after the chaotic final on January 18 in Rabat, where Senegal emerged 1-0 winners.
CAS’s ruling follows an appeal by Senegal after they were stripped of the title in March by African football’s governing body.
CAF had declared that Senegal forfeited the match when players walked off the pitch in protest at a penalty awarded to Morocco. The Senegal team returned after 14 minutes and scored in extra time.
The CAS panel, presided over by French sports law expert Gerald Simon with assistance from Italian international law professor Luigi ‌‌Fumagalli and Ulrich Haas, a Hamburg-based lawyer and professor of law at the University of Zurich, found that “the ‌‌referee ‌‌did not commit any error of law”, said CAS secretary general Matthieu Reeb.
Senegal, who celebrated the trophy win with fanfare on their return home in January, were incensed by the penalty decision and lodged an appeal at CAS, the highest court for sports-related disputes.
Announcing its “crusade” against CAF’s ruling, Senegal’s football governing body then claimed the move could “reshape the world of football” and undermine the principle that refereeing decisions are final.
“This decision cannot even be considered a true sporting justice ruling – it is so crude, so absurd, so irrational,” lawyer Juan de Dios Crespo Perez, representing Senegal’s governing body, had said.
What was the Senegal-Morocco AFCON final controversy?
Senegal were enraged after a late penalty was awarded to Morocco in the second half. The players left the pitch in protest as Congolese referee Jean-Jacques Ndala awarded the spot kick, following a VAR review of a challenge on Morocco forward Brahim Diaz by El Hadji Malick Diouf.
The Senegalese had already protested to the referee in the second minute of stoppage time about an Ibrahim Sarr goal which was ruled out for a foul.
Before Diaz could take the penalty, the Senegalese players and coaching staff left the field, with many believing the game might well end there.
Senegal eventually returned and Diaz missed the spot kick before the match headed to extra time, when Pape Gueye’s stunning strike settled the game 1-0 in favour of the Teranga Lions.
How did Morocco win the final?
Senegal were ruled to have forfeited the final after walking off the pitch, led by coach Pape Thiaw, in protest at the potentially decisive penalty awarded to Morocco.
When play resumed after a delay of about 15 minutes, Morocco forward Brahim Diaz’s penalty was saved. In extra time, Pape Gueye scored the decisive goal that saw Senegal become champions of Africa for the second time.
Less than two months later, CAF ruled Senegal to have forfeited the match by walking off and officially recorded the result as a 3-0 win for Morocco.

items.summary:
