President William Ruto announced the changes on Tuesday, alongsid
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 24 – Some 4.5 million regular borrowers under the Hustler Fund are set to benefit from enhanced credit limits, with eligible individuals now able to access loans of up to KSh150,000 through the bridge loan facility.
President William Ruto announced the changes on Tuesday, alongside an additional KSh5 billion allocation to the Government-backed credit programme.
Ruto said the increased funding is intended to address the inadequacy of resources available to borrowers and ensure more Kenyans can access affordable financing.
The enhanced borrowing limits will target regular borrowers through the bridge loan facility, allowing them to access higher amounts to support their financial needs and economic activities.
The President also directed the Hustler Fund management to develop a group financing product that will enable organised groups to borrow and determine how to lend the money to individual members.
The proposed arrangement is expected to give groups greater flexibility in accessing credit and distributing funds according to members’ needs.
Ruto made the announcements during the 17th anniversary celebrations of the Joyful Women Organisation at State House, Nairobi.
The event was attended by First Lady Rachel Ruto, the organisation’s patron, and Deputy President Kithure Kindiki.
The latest interventions are part of the Government’s efforts to widen access to affordable credit, particularly among individuals and groups seeking financing outside conventional lending arrangements.

A tower in Riyadh’s financial district has been struck by an unspecified projectile amid attacks on Saudi infrastructure by Yemen’s
items.text:
Saudi-led coalition condemns ‘terrorist attack’ on tower in Riyadh
The Saudi-led coalition says building in financial district targeted, marking second time in a week.
A tower in Riyadh’s financial district has been struck by an unspecified projectile amid attacks on Saudi infrastructure by Yemen’s Houthi group, also known as Ansar Allah.
In a post on the social media platform X, the spokesman of the Saudi-led coalition called the Tuesday strike targeting the King Abdullah Financial District a “cowardly terrorist attack”, adding that authorities are conducting an on-site investigation.
The strike marks the second attack on Riyadh’s financial district in less than a week. An earlier attack on Riyadh damaged the Public Investment Fund (PIF) tower, the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund and the country’s tallest skyscraper. The strike caused “material damage”.
The Saudi-led coalition has not named the building that was struck on Tuesday. However, three separate witnesses said a strike targeted the PIF skyscraper.
A fourth witness told the news agency AFP that a vehicle fitted with a speaker had warned pedestrians in the area to take cover.
No warning was sent to phones about any threats to the capital, as has been the case during recent strikes.

items.summary:
Who really owns the land in Albania that Jared Kushner wants to develop?

items.text:
Who really owns the land in Albania that Jared Kushner wants to develop?
ZVERNEC, Albania — In the summer of 2021, Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump boarded a yacht owned by Nat Rothschild, an heir to the European banking family. On the way from Montenegro to Greece, the yacht anchored off the coast of Albania.
And, as Kushner told an investment conference last year, that's when Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama arrived at the boat to tell them about his plan for the country.
"I was very impressed by what he wanted to do with the country," said Kushner. "I really didn't know anything about the country and I didn't understand the history, and the darkness of the history with the communism and terrible leadership led to it being fully undeveloped as a nation."
A year later, Kushner was looking for development opportunities in the Balkans. He returned to the Albanian coast — to the city of Vlore, which was finishing the construction of an airport atop a wetland near an undeveloped coastline. "And obviously, a country's going to build an airport by the coast in a place they think is most beautiful," Kushner told the conference, "so we went there and we were looking for opportunities, and we found some incredible opportunities."
Kushner found those opportunities at Hidrovor Beach, an expanse of caramel-colored sand along the southern Albanian coast, with the gentle waves of the Adriatic lapping its perimeter and a view of an uninhabited island. A company working for Kushner purchased this land and 300 acres surrounding it for more than $130 million in April. But several people here tell NPR this is not Kushner's land.
They say it's theirs.
Land grabs and falsified documents
"This land here belonged to my family for centuries," says Gentian Mocka, who claims his family has owned this strip of beach and wetland since the time of the Ottoman Empire. He provided NPR land titles that appear to prove this.
After World War II, Albania's Communist government seized it — along with all private land.
When communism fell in 1991, families like Mocka's embarked on a years-long process to get their land back. "But then our problems started with the guys that were much more powerful than we were — had a lot of political support, were very rich and very well connected with the politics of that time," says Mocka.
In 2005, Mocka learned that someone else was laying claim to his family's land — a fellow Albanian named Artur Shehu. It was a familiar name for those who lived here in the 1990s, when the regional capital of Vlore was outside the control of the country's government. It was instead run by mafia-style gangs. At the time, Shehu was well-known to police in Vlore for his alleged involvement in a crime syndicate that, according to Albanian prosecutors, smuggled drugs and migrants into Europe. He fled Albania in 1999, after what police say was a shootout with a rival gang.
He ended up in the United States, where he received asylum in 2001 and, later, became a U.S. citizen. The 60-year-old Shehu now lives in a villa in Miami Beach. But he's continued to manage a growing real estate portfolio back in Albania through an associate in Vlore named Pellumb Petritaj.
The pair has claimed plots of land — including Mocka's family plot — up and down the southern Albanian coast, and prosecutors have taken notice. In 2018, Petritaj served three years in prison for forging land titles on behalf of Shehu. And on Nov. 18, Petritaj was sentenced to another seven years in prison for falsifying documents to $17 million worth of oceanfront property in the city of Vlore on behalf of Shehu. The court ordered the land — which does not include Mocka's family plot — confiscated from Shehu last week. The pair has also claimed oceanfront farmland in the village of Zvernec, adjacent to Mocka's land.
Albanian prosecutors say land linked to Kushner may have been "illegally acquired"
The pair has also claimed oceanfront farmland in the village of Zvernec, adjacent to Mocka's land.
The quiet village has only a couple hundred residents. Most of them, like Minella Konomi and Natasha Kota, are past the age of 70. On a recent warm and sunny afternoon, the two are resting on benches in the courtyard of the village church after a day of harvesting olives. They nod their heads when asked about Artur Shehu.
"He is from the village of Kanina, far from here and up in the mountains," says Konomi, motioning inland, "but his family has never lived here. He's involved in shady dealings."
Then Kota speaks up. "There wasn't a single soul of that family living here, going back to the Ottoman times," she says. "But we've heard stories about him, and we're very scared of him."
Twenty years ago, Kota, Konomi and dozens of others in this village learned that Artur Shehu had somehow acquired their farmland. They filed suit in Albanian court to reclaim their land, a fight that escalated this past April when Shehu sold the 300-acre parcel that includes what they say is their farmland to a company developing a luxury resort project for Kushner.
That transaction, however, is under review.
In court documents obtained by NPR, Albanian prosecutors argue that the land involved in Kushner's development is "suspected of having been illegally acquired through forgery."
A spokesman for Kushner did not respond to NPR's request for comment by the time this article was published. Kushner had previously issued a statement on his website saying his partnership purchased the land from a private party in a private transaction. "Title was reviewed by counsel and verified," the statement says.
Shehu did not respond to NPR's request for comment. He has previously denied any wrongdoing. However, in Tirana, a former lawyer for Shehu was willing to talk.
Oceanfront properties are now claimed by several parties

items.text:
Millwall face partial stadium closure over chants
- Published
Millwall have been ordered to play a future Championship match in front of a partially-closed stadium as punishment for fans' discriminatory chants.
The club has also been fined £70,000 by an independent regulatory commission, and been told another offence this season will lead to a further partial stadium closure.
The sanctions were imposed for ableist and homophobic chants, heard at a game against Charlton Athletic in January.
"These chants are discriminatory, unacceptable, and will not be tolerated at The Den or anywhere Millwall play," Millwall's managing director Mark Fairbrother said in an open letter to supporters., external
"The club condemns them without reservation. They do not represent this club, and the vast majority of supporters who follow Millwall home and away with passion and pride.
"Incidents like this hurt all of us, but none more so than people who are directly discriminated against by ableist, homophobic or other unacceptable chanting, and we apologise to anybody that was affected, offended or impacted by the chants."
Blocks 19, 20, 47 and 48 of the Dockers Stand - the two-tiered east stand at The Den - will have to be closed for the Championship fixture against Sheffield United on 8 December.
It is the first time a club has been given this level of sanction for discriminatory chanting, with the commission saying "the club's previous disciplinary record was a significant aggravating feature".
'This is a serious outcome'
The commission pointed to chants relating to race in a 2019 fixture against Everton, religion in a 2023 fixture away at Wigan Athletic, and sexual orientation and disability in a 2025 visit to Crystal Palace, all of which resulted in fines for the club.
"History has shown that combinations of action plans and fines have been wholly ineffective to prevent the club - through its supporters - committing breaches" of Football Association (FA) rules around discriminatory behaviour, the commission added.
The FA had charged Millwall in March for the chanting against Charlton.
The club admitted the charge, and in its submissions suggested the chants were limited to 80 to 100 individuals in the north-eastern corner of the Dockers Stand, in the blocks that will be closed as part of the punishment.
However, based on other evidence, the commission concluded the actual figure involved in the chants was "likely to have been in the hundreds, quite possibly more".
It also found that the club did not make any announcement over the stadium PA system ordering for the discriminatory chanting to stop, nor did it deploy any additional stewards or police to the areas from where the chanting was originating.
"I won't dress this up. This is a serious outcome," Fairbrother said.
"This significant sanction was given because, although this is the first charge relating to a match at The Den for many years, the commission took into account a number of incidents of discriminatory chanting involving our supporters over the past few seasons at away games.
"This is the cumulative cost of that pattern. Most importantly, the current and any future sanctions mean the next incident won't just cost the club money. It will cost supporters their seats.
"Innocent fans will be shut out of their own stadium because of someone else's behaviour, and with future sanctions likely to be tougher, that threat is very real."

items.title: Senegal restored as Africa Cup of Nations champions after court ruling
items.summary:
Senegal have been restored as the Africa Cup of Nations champions after a ruling by the court of arbitration for sport (Cas).
Senegal beat Morocco 1-0 in a chaotic Afcon final in January but the result was overturned two months later as a 3-0 default win for Morocco by an appeals panel appointed by
items.text:
Senegal have been restored as the Africa Cup of Nations champions after a ruling by the court of arbitration for sport (Cas).
Senegal beat Morocco 1-0 in a chaotic Afcon final in January but the result was overturned two months later as a 3-0 default win for Morocco by an appeals panel appointed by the Confederation of African Football (Caf).
Senegal appealed and on Tuesday Cas published the verdict of its panel of three judges.
The three-person panel came to their decision unanimously, deciding that the field of play doctrine which decrees that any referee’s decision is final must ultimately hold sway.
“After having examined the arguments raised by the Parties, the Arbitral Panel considered that the Referee’s decision to resume the match or to stop it fell definitively within his sole authority,” a Cas statement said. “By blowing his whistle to restart play, the Referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met.
“In the Panel’s view, there is no doubt that the effects of the Referee’s decision were limited to the pitch. As such, the Panel considers that the Referee’s decision was covered by the ‘field of play’ doctrine.”
Claims by the Royal Moroccan Football Federation that Senegal had contravened articles of the Afcon Regulations, were rejected by the panel. “Since Articles 82 and 84 of the AFCON Regulations are intended solely to determine the outcome of a match when a team’s conduct leads the referee to call off the game permanently, they are therefore not applicable in this case.”
During the final, Senegal beat Morocco in Rabat after causing a 15-minute delay in play when they walked off in protest at Morocco being awarded a penalty in the last minute of normal time.
Senegal’s star forward Sadio Mané helped to persuade his team to return as tensions rose in the stadium and when the referee, Jean-Jacques Ndala, restarted the game, Morocco’s Brahim Díaz had his penalty saved. Senegal won with a Pape Gueye goal in extra time.
Football’s laws state that referee decisions are final but Caf appeal judges cited Afcon tournament regulations that if a team “refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee, it shall be considered loser and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition”.
The Cas judges heard evidence at a one-day hearing. Cas verdicts can be challenged at Switzerland’s supreme court, though only on limited procedural grounds.
More than $1m (£770,000) in fines were imposed by Caf disciplinary judges on the two federations, players and Senegal’s then coach, Pape Thiaw.

items.text:
Colombia: Car bomb attack injures at least 23
November 24, 2026
At least 23 people were injured in Colombia on Monday night when a car bomb tore through the central city of Villavicencio, local authorities confirmed on Tuesday.
The explosion occurred at approximately 9:30 p.m. (3:30 a.m. CET Tuesday) in front of the headquarters of the regional government of Meta province and caused severe structural damage to nearby buildings.
Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella confirmed the incident and said no deaths had been reported "so far."
Reporters for the AFP news agency said the blast knocked out power across parts of the city center, leaving damaged cars lining nearby streets and ripping open shopfronts.
"The doors were bent in, the windows shattered, some display cases inside broken," said local resident Johan Perez, who owns a hat shop. "We are alive by a miracle."
The Spanish EFE news agency reported that a well-known local restaurant was completely destroyed and suggested that the structural integrity of the government building itself may have been compromised, raising concerns that it could collapse.
Who is behind Villavicencio blast?
The attack has not been publicly claimed by any group but it came on the eve of the 10th anniversary of Colombia's landmark peace accord with FARC guerrillas.
The agreement persuaded the FARC, once Latin America's largest guerrilla army, to lay down its weapons after more than half a century of conflict.
Shortly before Monday's blast, President De la Espriella had denounced the peace accord as a "false peace."
According to the local Caracol radio station, investigators' initial theories point to a FARC commander known as "Antonio Medina" who leads the dissidents' 28th and 39th fronts, known as the "Amazonas Bloc."
De La Espriella blames 'narco-terrorists'
President De La Espriella, who took office in August and has launched a United States-backed military offensive against armed groups and drug traffickers, blamed "narco-terrorists" for the attack.
"I warn the narco-terrorists responsible: you will answer for every drop of blood you have spilled and every business and property you have destroyed," he wrote on social media.
"We will deploy the full power of the state to hunt you down, dismantle your organizations and take you out." De La Espriella added.
The incident marks the latest violent resurgence of a conflict that has shaken Colombia, the world's largest cocaine-producing nation, over the past two years.
Between January and November, authorities recorded 358 drone strikes, more than one a day, according to a Defense Ministry document obtained by AFP.
Last year, a presidential candidate was assassinated on the campaign trail.

items.text:
Senegal crowned AFCON 2025 champions by Court of Arbitration for Sport following appeal
An announcement confirmed CAS determined Senegal to be the winners of the tournament, which concluded in January; Senegal beat Morocco 1-0 in the final, but were stripped of the title in March, which led to their appeal
Tuesday 24 November 2026 14:30, UK
The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) have announced Senegal as the winners of AFCON 2025.
Senegal beat Morocco 1-0 in the final in January, but were stripped of the title by a Confederation of African Football (CAF) Appeal Board in March for breaking competition rules by walking off the pitch because of a late disallowed goal and a controversial penalty award.
Senegal's protest caused a delay of 15 minutes, and when their players returned to the pitch, Morocco's Brahim Diaz missed the penalty to force the match into extra time.
"The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has upheld the appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) against the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and the the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF, in French) concerning the final of the Africa Cup of Nations Morocco 2025 (AFCON 2025)," a CAS statement read.
"The decision rendered by the CAF Appeal Board is set aside and the decision by the CAF Disciplinary Board is reinstated. Consequently, the result obtained at the end of the AFCON 2025 final is confirmed (1-0 for Senegal)."
Morocco's appeal was initially rejected but a CAF panel did uphold it and found Senegal's walk-off meant they had forfeited the match, awarding a 3-0 win to Morocco.
Senegal then appealed to CAS, calling the decision "a travesty," and have now been reinstated as champions.
Morocco's initial appeal was rejected but a CAF panel did uphold it and found Senegal's walk-off meant they had forfeited the match, awarding a 3-0 win to Morocco.
CAF said Senegal infringed on article 82 of AFCON's regulations, which states if a team refuses to play or leaves the ground before the end of regulation time without the refereee's authorisation, it will be considered the loser and eliminated from the competition.
Article 84 states any team that violates article 82 will be permanently eliminated and lose the match 3-0.
Senegal then appealed to CAS, calling the decision "a travesty," and have now been reinstated as champions.
'Common sense prevails' but is this really over?
Sky Sports News' Chief Correspondent Kaveh Solhekol:
"Common sense has prevailed because the Court of Arbitration for Sport have effectively confirmed that Senegal did win the 2025 AFCON.
"Morocco were very unhappy because they felt that the rules of the tournament had been broken by Senegal when they left the pitch. They felt that at that stage Senegal should have forfeited the game.
"They went to the African Confederation Appeal Board and there was an appeal hearing in March. That appeal decided that yes, Morocco were right and they should be the winners and the result of the game was changed from a 1-0 win to Senegal to a 3-0 win to Morocco.
"Then we had the next chapter in this story because Senegal were also very unhappy with the decision of the appeal board, so they went to CAS in Switzerland. There was a hearing in October and now we have had the decision - a unanimous decision from the three judges.
"I don't want to tempt fate, because let's wait and see what the Moroccan Federation say, but what I would say to you is that they have fought this all the way, they believe that this is an injustice and they are one of the most powerful football associations in Africa.
"They are co-hosts of the next World Cup in 2030 and they have a very close relationships with the leadership at FIFA.
"I'm not suggesting that anything untoward is going on, but they still do have options. For instance, if they feel there has been something wrong in the procedures at the CAS hearing, they could go to the Swiss Federal Tribunal.
"I think the Moroccan Federation, according to what Reuters are reporting this afternoon, are unhappy with the way CAS handled this appeal and they have complained to CAS because they believe that one of the judges actually spoke on the phone to the president of the Senegal Federation on Sunday afternoon, so perhaps that is an avenue that they are going to explore."
'Unanimous decision' - CAS statement in full
The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has upheld the appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) against the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and the the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF, in French) concerning the final of the Africa Cup of Nations Morocco 2025 (AFCON 2025).
The decision rendered by the CAF Appeal Board is set aside and the decision by the CAF Disciplinary Board is reinstated. Consequently, the result obtained at the end of the AFCON 2025 final is confirmed (1-0 for Senegal).
The FSF appealed to CAS against a decision of the CAF Appeal Board declaring that the Senegal national team forfeited the AFCON 2025 final and recording the Moroccan national team as the winners.
In their appeal, the FSF argued that the decision of the Referee, Mr Jean-Jacques Ngambo Ndala, to resume the match at the 109th minute (90+19) during the AFCON 2025 final and to allow it to be concluded with a sporting result could not be reviewed, pursuant to the 'field of play' doctrine.
The FRMF argued, on the contrary, that the Referee's decision did not fall under the 'field of play' doctrine, as it cannot be applicable to the disciplinary consequences of the Senegalese team's behaviour. The FRMF alleged that, by leaving the pitch temporarily, the Senegalese team breached Articles 82 and 84 of the AFCON Regulations, which should have led the Referee to bring the match to an early conclusion. The FRMF also argued that the Referee erred in law and that his decision was arbitrary.

items.text:
Could Russia-Ukraine war threaten Libya’s fragile reunification process?
While the two European powers have long had a presence in Libya’s rivalry, the overt nature of Sunday’s attack introduces new complications.
The recent attack on a Russian warship in the port of Benghazi, Libya, has drawn condemnation from both sides of the country’s fractured political landscape.
On Monday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy took responsibility for the drone strikes on the Russian ship docked in the Libyan port a day earlier.
This led to outcry from Libyan officials from both sides of the political divide, who fear the attack threatens fragile efforts to unify the country after more than a decade of war and division.
Here’s what we know:
What is behind the Russian presence in Libya?
Since the fall of longtime leader Muammar Gaddafi in 2011, Libya’s fractious political landscape has settled into two rival administrations currently governing the country: the internationally recognised Government of National Unity (GNU) based in the western city of Tripoli and led by interim Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah, and authorities linked to renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar in the eastern city of Benghazi.
Haftar, who had moved to the United States when Gaddafi was still the leader, has long cultivated close ties with Russia. Moscow has allegedly provided his self-described Libyan National Army (LNA) with weapons, mercenaries and diplomatic backing, key to helping him consolidate control over much of the east.
In exchange, Russia has retained a military and logistical foothold in the country, including ports, airfields, storage, maintenance capacity, and overland routes critical to supporting its operations in the rest of Africa.
Russia is believed to have a military presence in Sudan, Mali, the Central African Republic, Niger, Burkina Faso, among others.
There are an estimated 1,000 to 1,800 Russian personnel in Libya, including from its Africa Corps, a unit within Moscow’s Ministry of Defence, which has tried to bring Russian private military companies in Africa under government control.
The importance of eastern Libya as a military hub for Russia only increased after Syrian President Bashar al-Assad, a key regional ally of Moscow, fell from power in December 2024, said Ruslan Trad, nonresident fellow of Global Security at the Atlantic Council.
“Russia’s bases in Libya are less about fighting in Libya itself than about sustaining Moscow’s wider military and political footprint across the Sahel and Central Africa. They function as a logistics bridge between the Mediterranean and Russia’s partners and deployments deeper in the continent,” Trad told Al Jazeera.
“Without this hub, Russia would have to sustain operations thousands of kilometres from Russia with far fewer reliable transit options.”
Why is there a Ukrainian presence in Libya?
The internationally recognised government in Tripoli has sought to counterbalance Russia’s involvement in Libya by forming its own international partnerships, most notably with Turkiye. The GNU has also adopted a firmly pro-Ukraine stance in recent years.
In 2022, the GNU issued an unqualified condemnation of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. It was the only Arab country to vote in favour of suspending Russia’s participation in the United Nations Human Rights Council later that year.
The relationship between the GNU and Ukraine deepened in 2023, with Prime Minister Dbeibah pushing for the establishment of an official embassy in Tripoli and opening talks on military cooperation. Shortly thereafter, Ukrainian forces began providing training and technical support to GNU forces.
Russia has long accused Ukraine of arming GNU forces and maintaining a presence in western Libya to target its interests in Africa, including a string of unclaimed attacks on Russian-linked vessels off Libya’s coast in recent months suspected to have been carried out by Ukrainian forces. Zelenskyy’s claim of responsibility for Sunday’s attack left no room for ambiguity.
“Ukraine’s presence in northwestern Libya is a limited, discreet military cooperation arrangement with the Government of National Unity,” Trad said. “Its main function is to support long-range drone operations against Russian shipping and military logistics in the Mediterranean.”
Suspected Ukrainian attacks in the Mediterranean include drone attacks in September on the Russian cargo ship, Lady Mariia, between Crete and Libya, and an attack that set Russian LNG carrier Arctic Metagaz ablaze in December, leaving it adrift between Malta and Libya.
But it is not clear whether Sunday’s attack was launched from Libyan soil.
Libya’s reconciliation process
Groups loyal to the GNU and Haftar’s LNA have fought a gruelling war since 2014, with thousands killed. Efforts to reconcile the eastern and western authorities have repeatedly failed.
Since 2025, regional and international efforts to bridge Libya’s divide have yielded cautious progress, resulting in a cooperation framework that seeks to unify the country’s political, military and economic institutions.
In April, Libya adopted a unified national budget for the first time in more than a decade. The move was welcomed in a joint statement by 10 countries involved in Libya’s conflict or the process to end it, including the United Arab Emirates, Egypt, France, Germany, Italy, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye, the United Kingdom and the US.
Russia also welcomed the move in an April 22 statement but warned against the involvement of “external actors” in shaping Libya’s future.
On August 30, the two sides agreed to presidential and legislative elections within 24 months under a single executive authority, in a UN-mediated deal, but questions still linger over their commitments to the process.

The Court of Arbitration for Sport on Tuesday ruled in favour of Senegal in the appeal to reclaim the Africa Cup of Nations title, 10 months after a chaotic final against Morocco. Senegal won the match in January but was s
items.text:
Senegal regain AFCON title after successful appeal at sport arbitration court
The Court of Arbitration for Sport on Tuesday ruled in favour of Senegal in the appeal to reclaim the Africa Cup of Nations title, 10 months after a chaotic final against Morocco. Senegal won the match in January but was stripped of the title in March, when it was awarded to Morocco.
Ten months after the Africa Cup of Nations final was chaotically played on the field between Morocco and Senegal, the title was awarded Tuesday by sports’ highest court to Senegal.
The Court of Arbitration for Sport set the target Monday to publish the verdict of its panel of three judges on Senegal’s appeal to regain the title the team won on the field in Morocco in January and then lost in a legal case in March.
A strict reading of The Laws of The Game, soccer’s ultimate rule book, saw Senegal win the case.
A broader interpretation of AFCON tournament rules would have given the victory to Morocco.
Senegal won the final 1-0 after extra time with chaos on the field and violent clashes in the stands. The result was overturned two months later as a 3-0 default win for Morocco by an appeals panel appointed by the Confederation of African Football (CAF).
Read moreAFCON 2025: CAS set to hand down ruling on controversial final
Senegal beat AFCON host nation Morocco after a 15-minute delay in play. Senegal’s team walked off the field to protest Morocco being awarded a penalty kick in the last minute of regulation time.
Match referee Jean-Jacques Ndala of Congo eventually allowed the game to restart, Morocco’s penalty by Brahim Diaz was saved and Senegal won with the only goal in extra time.
The laws of soccer state that referee decisions are final.
CAF appeal judges later cited AFCON tournament regulations that if a team “refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee, it shall be considered loser and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition”.
The CAS judges heard evidence at a one-day hearing last month and the court promised a verdict by the end of November with a full written ruling of its judges setting out reasons for their decision.
CAS verdicts can be challenged at Switzerland’s supreme court though only on limited procedural grounds.
The next AFCON tournament starts in June co-hosted by Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

items.text:
Millwall forced to partially close the Den after commission proves FA charges of discriminatory chanting
Millwall have been punished for discriminatory chanting relating to disability and sexual orientation by fans in a game against Charlton in January; a two-game partial stadium closure (one game of which is suspended) is first of its kind at this level; Millwall also fined £70,000
Tuesday 24 November 2026 14:04, UK
Millwall have become the first club in the top four divisions of English football to be punished with a partial stadium closure for discriminatory chanting after a regulatory commission proved two FA charges.
The unprecedented measure is for Millwall failing to ensure their supporters didn't engage in discriminatory chanting that includes reference to disability and sexual orientation during a home match with Charlton in January.
As well as a two-game partial stadium closure - one game of which is suspended until the end of the 2027/28 season - Millwall have been fined £70,000 plus hearing costs, warned about their future conduct, and have had their FA Action Plan extended until the end of next season.
Blocks 19, 20, 47 and 48 of the Dockers Stand will be closed when Millwall host Sheffield United on December 8 - a total of 1,274 seats.
In their written conclusions, the commission found "the club's degree of culpability in relation to the incidents was significant".
In response, speaking exclusively to Sky Sports, Millwall managing director Mark Fairbrother said: "As a club, we didn't do enough and on behalf of the club I apologise to everyone who has been affected by that chanting because it shouldn't happen."
Millwall pleaded guilty to the charges but Fairbrother said Millwall were "disappointed" with the outcome.
He also pointed to new processes the club have since put in place to try to avoid a recurrence - but called on other football clubs, the FA, and organisations such as Kick It Out to come together to find preventative solutions.
"We challenge everything we do and look at if there are ways that we can improve? It's highlighted where we need to be better," he said. "We had already put mitigations in place and need to continue to do so.
"But this is one football club. These instances are happening across football. This is a challenge for the sport in general.
"We see it this [past] week with the charges to Chelsea and also the FA for the England fans in Spain. So, we can put measures in place but we're one club. We can't solve all of society's issues.
"We need to work with all key football stakeholders to look at how can we all do this better? What does good look like? What does best practice look like? And making sure that we embrace that. But everyone else has a collective responsibility as well."
'Focus must be on fan education'
Fairbrother says "the stick approach" used against clubs whose supporters are found guilty of discriminatory chanting just "punishes the fans who actually are just here to enjoy themselves". Instead, he asks "what can we do in terms of the carrot approach to educate people to eradicate this?"
He also noted that supporters identified in the discriminatory chanting against Charlton were all under 18 years old.
"That shows a lack of understanding of the implication of these words," he said. "These words obviously hurt and they have a significant impact on those groups that it affects. But there's that lack of understanding of the issue and the impact."
Asked if he would be interested in working more with groups such as Kick It Out to address this aspect, Fairbrother said: "I'd embrace it. From a personal perspective, I think that would be really good and I implore them to please come work with us, come and look at what we do, challenge what we do.
"If you don't think something we're doing is good enough, come and tell us but look at solutions. If we all have a solutions-focused mindset, we can actually start to make real difference."
The regulatory commission also wrote in their conclusions that "the reputation of the club and English football would have been tarnished" by the chanting during a game shown live on Sky Sports. Fairbrother feels that.
"It hurts all of us in the club. But I know it hurts our fans as well because that is not who we are," he said.
Millwall play Charlton again at the Den on December 19 in a Championship fixture. On how the club are working to avoid a repeat of the discriminatory chanting heard in January, Fairbrother said: "We've put in place a number of procedures already.
"We've already had West Ham here earlier in the season, which was probably our highest-risk fixture for a number of years. That went without incident. But we had a different approach to different fan groups in terms of just reminding them of their responsibility.
"But also for us as a club, making sure that we're on the front foot in terms of everything we do. We will have that same approach to Charlton. You can't predict the future, but we have a more robust process in place now."
This latest issue was the first case of discriminatory chanting at the Den since an FA Cup tie with Everton in 2019 - but follows three other cases involving Millwall supporters away from home since April 2023.
Asked whether he is confident of making a difference, Fairbrother said that would require the support of Millwall fans to call out discriminatory language.
"For each of those instances - and all three of them were away games - there were specific small fan groups who obviously engaged with that chanting. This is now the first instance we've had here at the Den," he said.
"So for all fans, we need to check and challenge this. We need to make sure it doesn't build up. Don't engage with this type of chanting.
"It's not fair on [other Millwall supporters]. We need to all do better. As a club, we need to do better and we will do better for them. But also, it's a collective one. If it happens, if people see it, call it out. We all need to be more proactive on this.

items.text:
Israeli air strike kills senior Hamas security official in Gaza
Abu Nahl, 50, was killed in a crowded area leaving four others, including a Palestinian woman, wounded.
An Israeli strike on Gaza has killed a senior Hamas security official and wounded several others, according to local authorities.
The deceased senior Hamas official has been identified as Brigadier General Naim Abu Nahl, who was the director of Hamas’s internal security apparatus in Gaza, medics and police said on Tuesday. Gaza’s Ministry of Interior and National Security confirmed the death.
Abu Nahl was 50 years old and Director General of the Internal Security Office across the Gaza Strip. A statement from Gaza’s Interior Ministry said the security official was walking in the street when a drone strike killed him.
Four others, including a Palestinian woman, were wounded and taken to al-Shifa Medical Complex. The area where the missile struck is crowded with displaced people and shelters.
Gaza’s Interior Ministry said the assassination came after the Internal Security Service had made significant gains against what it described as “gangs collaborating with the occupation and operating in areas under Israeli military control.”
The Israeli army and the Shin Bet domestic security service said in a joint statement they had struck a senior Hamas figure, without identifying him, adding that further details would be provided later. Israel’s public broadcaster Kan later said the target was Abu Nahl. Citing Israeli sources, Kan said Abu Nahl had succeeded Moein al-Arbeid, who was detained by the Israeli army and Shin Bet during a special operation in September and remains in Israeli custody.
Several Palestinians were already reported killed earlier on Tuesday, including a child and police officers, while dozens were injured in Israeli air strikes on various parts of the Gaza Strip, according to local health officials.
There have been daily violations of the so-called “ceasefire” in Gaza, with Israeli air strikes continuing regularly in its genocidal war, with at least 1,680 people killed and 6,100 injured since the ceasefire was signed on October 11 last year.

items.text:
Records tumble as Indian teen Sooryavanshi smashes 53-ball 204 against UAE
The 15-year-old Sooryavanshi struck a staggering 28 sixes, the most ever in a senior men’s innings.
Teenage sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi hammered 204 off 53 balls for India A to break a host of records, including for both the fastest century and double-century in List A cricket.
The 15-year-old Sooryavanshi struck a staggering 28 sixes, the most ever in a senior men’s innings, as India passed their target of 250 against the United Arab Emirates on Tuesday in just 14.2 overs.
Sooryavanshi reached his hundred off 28 balls to take Australian Jake Fraser-McGurk’s record by one delivery.
He raised his 200 off 52 deliveries, smashing the 103-ball mark previously held by Chad Bowes.
Sooryavanshi also broke his own record for fastest 150, reaching that milestone from 40 balls.
“No words to say for him. I would only say it’s like absolute carnage,” India A captain Tilak Varma said after the Asia Cup Rising Stars match.
“The way he played, I think first five overs, the match was done. Five overs, we are 100, and the way he carried on after that, it was tremendous to watch. Honestly, everyone knows how he can hit the sixes.”
In July, Sooryavanshi became India’s youngest men’s international when he made his T20I debut against England in Manchester, eclipsing Sachin Tendulkar’s longstanding record.
He amassed 776 runs for Rajasthan Royals to finish as the tournament’s leading run-scorer in this year’s IPL, at a remarkable strike rate of 237.30.

items.title: We have not been bought, Ethekon tells critics
items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24- Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) chairman Erastus Ethekon has dismissed claims that the commission has been compromised or bought ahead of the 2027 General Election, insisting that it will discharge its constitutional mandate independently and transparen
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24- Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) chairman Erastus Ethekon has dismissed claims that the commission has been compromised or bought ahead of the 2027 General Election, insisting that it will discharge its constitutional mandate independently and transparently.
Ethekon said allegations of bribery, electoral manipulation and rigging were part of propaganda intended to undermine public confidence in the electoral process, warning that unverified claims could discourage Kenyans from participating in the elections.
Speaking during a consultative breakfast meeting with political reporters in Nairobi on Tuesday, the IEBC chairman urged journalists to scrutinise claims made by politicians and other political actors rather than amplify narratives that could erode confidence in the commission.
He said the commission was not hiding anything about its preparations or the management of election results, insisting that journalists, political party agents, observers and other stakeholders would be allowed to monitor the process from polling stations to the national tallying centre.
“There is nothing to hide, contrary to what some of the politicians are trying to make ordinary citizens believe. IEBC is not hiding anything because the results belong to the people and we will all be there,” Ethekon said.
He challenged journalists to confront politicians spreading claims about the finality of presidential election results at the national tallying centre, arguing that the matter had already been settled by the courts.
Ethekon maintained that results declared at polling stations are final and that subsequent processes at constituency and national tallying centres involve the collection, verification and announcement of results in accordance with the law.
“Results at the polling stations are final. The rest is secretarial work, something that all of us can do. But as IEBC, we have the constitutional mandate to make sure those results are collected, tallied and verified,” he said.
On November 20, 2026, Gachagua accused Ethekon of being President Ruto’s man, alleging that politicians had bought him a house in Karen to influence his handling of the 2027 General Election.
“Ethekon is Ruto’s man; they even bought him a house in Karen. He is planning to steal the elections, but we want to tell him that it is not possible,” Gachagua said.
The allegation was not new. In August 2026, Gachagua had claimed that politicians had purchased a house worth Sh200 million for Ethekon as part of an alleged scheme to compromise the commission.
He reportedly attributed the disclosure to National Assembly Majority Leader Kimani Ichung’wah, claiming that the house had been bought for the chairman, who had previously lived in a rented apartment.
Gachagua’s earlier allegation had put the property’s value at Sh80 million before the figure rose to Sh200 million.
He added that the commission would verify whether a presidential candidate had met the constitutional threshold of more than 50 per cent of votes cast and at least 25 per cent in more than half of the counties before declaring the winner.
The chairman said journalists would be present during the final stages of verification and announcement of results, alongside political party agents, international observers and other stakeholders.
Ethekon’s remarks come amid renewed political debate over the transmission and verification of presidential election results ahead of the August 2027 polls, with questions raised by political actors over the role of the national tallying centre.
He urged journalists to interrogate politicians making claims about the electoral process, instead of giving them platforms to repeat allegations without evidence.
“You should be able to confront them and ask them the right questions, not just putting their cameras on their faces and allowing them to spew anything under the sun, some things that even don’t make sense, and repeating lies,” he said.
The IEBC chairman also called for responsible election reporting, warning that sensational coverage and political propaganda could inflame tensions and undermine national cohesion.
He recalled the 2007-2008 post-election violence, in which more than 1,000 people were killed, saying irresponsible political communication and media coverage had contributed to the country’s descent into violence.
Ethekon, who said he was working with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) at the time, also recounted his personal experience during the 1992 election-related violence when he was a Form One student.
He said he was pulled out of a vehicle between Kitale and another destination and questioned about his ethnic identity by armed youths.
The experience, he said, reinforced the dangers of political incitement and the responsibility of institutions, politicians and the media to protect the country from another cycle of election-related violence.
“Sometimes in some cases elections have become a matter of life and death. So it’s a very, very sensitive issue that we all must understand,” he said.
The chairman warned that the growing spread of misinformation, disinformation, hate speech and propaganda on digital platforms posed a significant threat to the credibility of the 2027 elections.
He said some of the false narratives were being manufactured by individuals and groups within and outside the country with the intention of influencing political discourse and destabilising Kenya.
Ethekon urged media houses to invest in fact-checking and verification, particularly when reporting claims about election technology, voter registration and results transmission.
He cautioned against sensationalising sensitive electoral issues in pursuit of newspaper sales and online traffic, saying the consequences of irresponsible reporting could extend beyond media organisations to families and the country at large.
“While rumours may sell better, truth buys you credibility,” he said.

Less than two weeks after Jensen Huang, the leather-jacket-wearing face of the AI revolutio
items.text:
Jensen Huang’s Nvidia return: Who are the big winners and losers?
Jensen Huang returns to lead the most consequential company powering the AI revolution. We take a look at winners and losers from the scandal.
Less than two weeks after Jensen Huang, the leather-jacket-wearing face of the AI revolution, scandalously fell from the throne of the modern AI industry, he has reclaimed his leadership of the world’s most valuable semiconductor company, Nvidia.
It took a war room of Silicon Valley insiders lobbying the White House for US President Donald Trump to crack the whip on Monday and force chip giant Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang, 63, who fell from grace following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang, an executive and controlling shareholder of Megaspeed, an Nvidia client company that has since been blacklisted in the US.
What happens at Nvidia extends well beyond the California-based company.
Share values on the US stock market have become concentrated in a small group of increasingly valuable tech giants, which account for more than 60 percent of the Nasdaq-100. Tech and AI-linked companies together represent around half the S&P 500’s market value.
Huang’s return to Nvidia on Monday triggered a 30 percent rise in Nvidia shares, but has raised several questions about the reach of the Trump administration’s dictates as investigations into the company and its CEO continue. It has also heightened worries about the future of AI development amid Washington’s deepening rivalry with Beijing.
We take a look at major winners and losers from this whole scandal.
Winners
There are many.
Jensen Huang
The sacked CEO, who stunningly returned to applause from Nvidia employees on Monday, had left the board, which last week said it would not reinstate him.
From washing dishes at a Denny’s in the 1980s to building a $4 trillion technology giant, Huang led Nvidia for nearly 33 years and became one of Silicon Valley’s defining entrepreneurial stories.
He now joins a number of “cult-style” leaders in Silicon Valley, including Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and SpaceX’s Elon Musk, who appear too “big” to fire.
Allegations that Huang’s affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a businesswoman suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence, may have exposed restricted chip technology to Beijing were ultimately not enough to keep him out of the CEO’s office.
During the 11 days he was out of the office, media reports detailed at least two more extramarital affairs with employees at Nvidia, and revealed how he toxically berated his subordinates.
“If Jensen comes back, I’m not doing any HR trainings ever again,” an Nvidia employee wrote on an internal platform, reported Wired.
Lloyd Blankfein, the former CEO of investment bank Goldman Sachs, wrote on X: “Guess you can come back from the graveyard if you’re really, really, really indispensable.”
For his part, President Trump argued that he just returned from a trip to China – where he attended the APEC summit and met with Chinese President Xi Jinping, “So I guess I’m involved also.”
Speaking with CNBC, Trump added, “Every time you have a Chinese woman that’s good-looking or beautiful, they say she’s a spy.” However, he said, “I don’t believe that’s true,” in the case of Huang. He did not comment on US intel reports he received.
Nvidia shareholders
The chip giant holds the key to the modern AI computing industry; its customers include Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta, who rely on Nvidia hardware to build and operate their AI data centres.
Nvidia’s shares fell nearly 28 percent between November 11, when the board accepted Huang’s resignation, and November 20, amid mounting uncertainty over its future leadership.
By the end of Monday, November 23, Nvidia recovered approximately $956bn in market value, rising from its November 20 low of $3.04 trillion to $3.98 trillion, and remaining the world’s most valuable semiconductor company.
Among those shareholders is US President Trump. A review of Trump’s financial disclosures, first reported by The Washington Post, found that he held between $13m and $62m in Nvidia stock at the end of August, up from about $1.3m at the end of 2024.
Companies doing business with Nvidia
The AI industry at large felt the ripples from Huang’s exit from Nvidia, and his return is also boosting companies across the chip giant’s global supply chain, which are hoping for continuity in the product roadmap, manufacturing orders and investment plans.
Shares in Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which manufactures Nvidia’s advanced AI processors, surged 9.9 percent on Tuesday, hitting the company’s daily trading limit and adding $158bn to its market value in a single session.
Shares in Foxconn, which assembles AI servers powered by Nvidia chips, also rose nearly 10 percent.
Shares in South Korean memory-chip makers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics gained 6.7 percent and 6.6 percent, respectively.
Japanese chip-testing equipment maker Advantest shares jumped 12.5 percent.
On Tuesday, major Asian stock indexes in Seoul, Tokyo, and Taipei all rose.
Advocates for open access to tech
Huang has spent years lobbying in Washington against restrictions to tech exports, arguing that halting sales will surrender a strategically important market to domestic Chinese competitors.
That puts him at odds with US lawmakers who view access to Nvidia’s advanced chips as a national security risk, particularly given their potential military applications.
The US first introduced export controls on the chips in 2022 and has subsequently tightened China’s access to them.
In one exception, following a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping last year, Trump said he would allow H200 chip sales to approved Chinese customers. The US ‌eased its licensing policy for the powerful H200 in January, allowing export applications to be reviewed individually subject to security conditions.

items.text:
German FM Wadephul 'shocked' by Trump's Nvidia intervention
November 24, 2026
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul on Tuesday expressed shock over US President Donald Trump's admission that he persuaded chip-producing giant Nvidia to reinstall ousted CEO Jensen Huang.
Nvidia brought Huang back on Monday in a surprise decision, less than two weeks after the CEO stepped down amid a series of affairs.
What did Wadephul say about Trump's involvement in Nvidia?
"It shocked me, to be honest, because as far as I know, if I'm personally looking back, I have never seen or recognized such an intervention from the political side into a particular company," Wadephul told reporters at a foreign policy conference in Berlin.
"And I do have some doubts whether this is a very good model for the future," he added.
"But OK, that took place in the United States of America," the foreign minister said.
Wadephul went on to say there are enough reasons to defend the rules-based international order, and that includes political power not getting involved in the economic activities of companies.
Trump boasts about interference in Nvidia decision
Huang's shock reinstatement on Monday came on the back of a unanimous vote by Nvidia's board of directors.
The news was welcomed by Trump, who called it the "correct and proper decision" in a post on Truth Social. The president later said he had played a key role, having spoken "directly and indirectly" to the board of directors, urging them to reinstate the scandal-hit ex-CEO.
"I convinced them," Trump said. "I made the deal."
Huang came under massive fire after it was reported he had had an affair with the CEO of the Singapore-based company Megaspeed. She was also accused of being a spy working on behalf of Chinese intelligence.
Nvidia, Trump see stock surge after Huang's reinstallment
Nvidia's shares took a hit on Huang's stepping down, but rebounded by 30% on Monday after it was announced he was being reinstalled, adding over $900 billion (€820 billion) to the company's market value.
This share price surge also appears to have benefited Trump himself, with the Financial Times calculating that the president saw his Nvidia stock go up $15 million.
Huang's return has also brought some calm to the market that appeared to be teetering, with growing concerns about the viability of the AI sector, which now makes up a substantial part of the US stock market.
It also marks a turn around from the poor showing by Anthropic's IPO launch that saw its early gains quickly melt away amid fears that the AI sector has been overvalued.

items.text:
Land mine deaths hit a five-year high, report says
November 24, 2026
Land mines killed or injured more people in 2025 than in any year since 2020, according to the International Campaign to Ban Landmines' (ICBL) annual report.
The report stated that the number of recorded deaths was at least 6,929, which is a 10% increase compared with last year. According to the campaign, four out of five victims were civilians, and half of those were minors.
Experts say the true figure is likely higher as not all land mine related death and injuries are recorded as such.
Myanmar reported the highest annual casualty toll for the third year in a row, with 1,891 victims, amid a "massive" new mine use.
In Syria, the number of casualties climbed by 50% to 1,602 in 2025, after the large-scale return of displaced people following the ousting of president Bashar Assad.
Myanmar and Syria were followed by Afghanistan with 497 casualties.
'The Ottawa Treaty faces its greatest test,' report warns
The ICBL criticized Ukraine, over its continued use of land mines. Ukraine, which is currently being invaded by Russia, is one of the 162 state parties to the Mine Ban Treaty.
The treaty, known as the Ottawa Treaty, prohibits the use, production, storage and transfer of anti-personnel mines. The treaty was ratified by 166 countries, but not by China, India, Russia, Israel, North Korea, or the US, along with nearly 30 others.
Five European NATO countries, which share a border with Russia, have withdrawn from the treaty last year: Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Finland and Poland. Ukraine has also withdrawn, though this will not take legal effect until the war ends.
"The treaty’s norms face their greatest test since 1999," the report said, citing the withdrawals.
In 2025, Ukraine justified its move to withdraw from the treaty by citing the actions of Russia, which has never ratified the treaty and has been using mines on Ukrainian territory.
The campaign said Ukraine was still "fully bound by the treaty" but had breached its ban on producing anti-personnel mines. It said the country had manufactured both 3D-printed mines and mines designed to be dropped by drones.
Report also noted that Russia has used antipersonnel land mines extensively in Ukraine since its full-scale invasion began in 2022.
Nearly 50 thousand people killed by land mines since 1999
Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, Cambodia, Iraq, Morocco, North Korea, South Korea and Ukraine have "massive land mine contamination," meaning they have more than 100 square kilometers of land contaminated by land mines, the report assessed.
Since 1999, 49,859 people were killed and 118,525 injured by land mines, according to Landmine and Cluster Munition Monitor, the research and monitoring arm of the ICBL, and the Cluster Munition Coalition NGOs.

items.title: Government adds Sh5bn to Hustler Fund, raises borrowing limits
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24 – The Government is injecting an additional Sh5 billion into the Hustler Fund to make more affordable credit readily available to borrowers, President William Ruto has said.
The President explained that the move seeks to address the inadequacy of resources available to borrowe
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24 – The Government is injecting an additional Sh5 billion into the Hustler Fund to make more affordable credit readily available to borrowers, President William Ruto has said.
The President explained that the move seeks to address the inadequacy of resources available to borrowers on the platform.
Additionally, he announced that the Government is enhancing borrowing limits for 4.5 million regular borrowers, through the bridge loan facility, offering individual loans of up to Sh150,000.
To further expand access to affordable credit, he directed the Hustler Fund management to design a financing product that allows groups to access funds and determine how to lend to their members.
“I ask the Principal Secretary to design a KSh300 million product to be made available to groups so that they can have resources to lend to members,” he said.
The President made the remarks when he presided over the 17th anniversary celebrations of the Joyful Women Organisation at State House Nairobi on Tuesday in the company of First Lady Rachel Ruto, the patron of the organisation, and Deputy President Kithure Kindiki.
Also present were Cabinet Secretaries Hannah Cheptumo (Gender, Culture and Children Services), Rebecca Miano (Tourism and Wildlife), Opiyo Wandayi (Energy and Petroleum), Alice Wahome (Lands, Public Works, Housing and Urban Development), William Kabogo (ICT and tDigital Economy) and Soipan Tuya (Defence).
Others were Zimbabwe’s Minister for Tourism, Hospitality and Industry Barbara Rwodzi, Permanent Representative to the United Nations Office at Nairobi Ambassador Ida Odinga, Romania Ambassador to Kenya Gentiana Șerbu and Executive Secretary of the Organisation of African First Ladies for Development Nardos Berhanu.
The President commended the organisation for its remarkable journey of empowering women by expanding access to capital, equipping them with skills and supporting the growth of their enterprises.
At the same time, President Ruto said the Government is giving priority to issues that matter most to mothers, including putting food on the table, educating their children, accessing quality healthcare, securing decent housing and creating jobs for young people.
He said these concerns are driving the Government’s efforts to strengthen food security, increase investment in education, deliver universal health coverage, build affordable housing and expand youth employment opportunities.
On healthcare, the President said the Government is keen on making healthcare accessible, affordable and sustainable under the Social Health Authority (SHA).
To support mothers, President Ruto said SHA pays for all clinical visits to health facilities.
Unlike the defunct National Hospital Insurance Fund, the President explained that the Government’s contribution towards normal deliveries under SHA has increased from Sh2,500 to Sh15,000.
Further, he said, the Government has increased its contribution towards assisted deliveries from Sh11,000 to Sh30,000.
“Also, SHA has a maternal package that cares for mother and baby for six months unlike 42 days under NHIF,” he said.
The President urged mothers to make at least four visits to clinics before giving birth.
To address maternal and neonatal deaths, the Government is equipping hospitals in 26 counties.
He said the Government had equipped 638 hospitals at a cost of Sh1.5 billion to reduce and eventually prevent maternal and neonatal deaths during birth.
As a result, the President pointed out, the country has reduced maternal deaths from 355 per 100,000 live births to 283 per 100,000 and is working towards achieving the internationally acceptable standard of 70.
“Maternal and neonatal deaths are a challenge we must confront as a country,” he said. “Yesterday, for example, we lost nine mothers. We keep these statistics so that we can understand why they happened and deal with them.”
To enhance food security, President Ruto noted that the Government has reduced the cost of fertiliser and seeds to increase productivity, reducing the cost of food and consequently the cost of living.
At the same time, he stated, the Government has put in place robust measures to eliminate cartels in the agricultural sector and ensure farmers earn better incomes.
In regard to education, he said the Government has employed 100,000 teachers in the past three years to ease the shortage of staff in schools.
The Government, he explained, has also built 23,000 classrooms, streamlined the Competency-Based Education and Training system and addressed the funding model for higher education.
To provide decent housing for many Kenyans in informal settlements, create jobs for young people and begin to reduce the sub-division of agricultural land, he said the Government is building affordable housing through the Housing Levy.
The same fund, he said, is being invested in modern markets and hostels for university and college students.
Pointing out that the Government has a deliberate and intentional plan to create jobs and other opportunities for young people, President Ruto cited overseas employment, digital jobs, enhanced access to credit and the provision of NYOTA grants to support youth enterprises.
The President further said there are opportunities for young people and women to do business with the Government under the Access to Government Procurement Opportunities (AGPO) programme, with KSh250 billion set aside for them.
On her part, the First Lady disclosed that the Joyful Women Organisation has Sh4 billion revolving through table banking and supporting more than 300,000 businesses.
Additionally, she noted that the Hustler Fund has expanded access to affordable credit while the NYOTA Fund has empowered young people to start businesses.
She explained that capital alone is not enough and that the Joyful Women Organisation has continued to empower women with the knowledge and skills to build lasting opportunities through training and capacity-building programmes.

items.title: Israeli strikes on Gaza kill senior Hamas security official and six other people, medics say
items.summary:
Israeli strikes on Gaza kill senior Hamas security official and six other people, medics say
Israeli air strikes on the devastated Gaza Strip killed Brigadier General Naeem Abu Nahel, director-general of the Palestinian territory's Internal Security Service on Tuesday, the ministry said. Another six
items.text:
Israeli strikes on Gaza kill senior Hamas security official and six other people, medics say
Israeli air strikes on the devastated Gaza Strip killed Brigadier General Naeem Abu Nahel, director-general of the Palestinian territory's Internal Security Service on Tuesday, the ministry said. Another six people, including two police officers and a 17-year-old teenager, were killed in Israeli strikes across the enclave.
Israeli air strikes killed a senior Hamas security official and six other people, including two police officers, in the Gaza Strip on Tuesday, medics and police said.
Gaza's interior ministry, which operates under Hamas authority, said that an Israeli air strike in Gaza City had killed Brigadier General Naeem Abu Nahel, director-general of the Internal Security Service.
The Israeli military and the Shin Bet domestic security service said in a joint statement they ‌had struck a senior Hamas militant, without identifying him, adding that further details would be provided later.
A key mission of Abu Nahel's internal security service is to counter Palestinians suspected of collaboration with Israel's secret service and gather information about its plans.
Read moreGazans flee shelters as Israeli army launches ground operation beyond Yellow Line
Earlier on Tuesday, medics said three people were killed in an Israeli air strike at a police ‌post in Khan Younis in southern Gaza. The Hamas-run interior ministry said two of those people were police officers.
Five other people were wounded in the attack, medics added.
Gaza's police force condemned the strike as "part of an ongoing campaign targeting the police apparatus".
Another Israeli air strike near the so-called Netzarim corridor further north killed another ‌three people, taking Tuesday's death toll to at least seven. Bassal said that one of the three people was a 17-year-old teenager.
Commenting on the two strikes, the Israeli military told Reuters it had struck militants in both areas, without giving further details.
Israeli strikes continue through ceasefire
An October 2025 US-backed ceasefire halted major fighting in the shattered territory, but has not stopped Israeli attacks on Gaza or secured Hamas' disarmament.
Israel, which accuses Hamas of trying to regroup and rearm, has stepped up its attacks in Gaza in recent months. Hamas denies the Israeli allegations, saying it is committed to the ceasefire agreement and accusing Israel of trying to derail it.
At least 1,600 Palestinians and five Israeli soldiers have been killed since then, according to respective Palestinian and Israeli tallies.
Israeli troops now control around two-thirds of Gaza, up from more than half at the time of the ceasefire, with Hamas controlling a sliver of territory along Gaza's coast.
Israel's assault on Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians since 2023, caused a hunger crisis, internally displaced Gaza's entire population and led an independent United Nations commission as well as scholars to label Israel's actions a genocide.
Israel has maintained that its actions were carried out in self-defence after Hamas-led militants killed 1,200 people and took more than 250 hostages in an attack on Israel in October 2023.
Most of Gaza's population of 2.1 million now live displaced in tents or makeshift shelters in the devastated territory.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters and AFP)

items.title: ‘I’m loving it at Brugge’: Freddie Potts on going from West Ham’s bench to Champions League
items.summary: In April Freddie Potts was absorbing the disappointment of being substituted at half-time during West Ham’s FA Cup quarter-final defeat by Leeds. The midfielder was out of favour under Nuno Espírito Santo and could not have imagined that he would be preparing to face Liverpool in the Champions Leagu
items.text:
In April Freddie Potts was absorbing the disappointment of being substituted at half-time during West Ham’s FA Cup quarter-final defeat by Leeds. The midfielder was out of favour under Nuno Espírito Santo and could not have imagined that he would be preparing to face Liverpool in the Champions League seven months later.
It is the 23-year-old’s reward for taking the difficult decision to leave his boyhood club last summer. Potts noticed his minutes were drying up in pre-season, even though West Ham were not exactly stocked with talent after relegation, and was ready for a new challenge when Club Brugge offered about £10m to sign him.
“I thought this was the perfect place for me to take the next step,” Potts says of his move to the Belgian champions. “I’m not going to shy away – it was very hard. West Ham have been my club for my whole life. I still have a lot of love for West Ham. But I had to take into account what was best for my career and I’m loving it at Brugge.
“Every player wants to be in the team expected to win every week, and seeing how Club Brugge have performed in the Champions League before shows the project and how they want to develop the team and players. It was a very exciting place for me to come. They look to develop young players.”
Potts was six when he joined West Ham. His father, Steve, made 506 appearances for the club and is part of Scott Parker’s backroom staff there. His brother, Dan, came through the academy before moving to Luton in 2015. This is a West Ham family; it is not a surprise that moving to Belgium was emotional for Potts.
Yet it was the right move. Brugge are second in the Belgian Pro League, a point behind Union Saint-Gilloise, and have impressed in the Champions League. They have nine points from four games in the league phase and caused a stir when they beat Inter 4-3 at San Siro last month.
Potts calls it “one of the best nights of my career”. It was quite the turnaround for a player who mostly watched from the bench as West Ham tried to save themselves during the second half of last season. It helps that Potts knows how to stay calm. He was talked up as a future West Ham captain when he made his full debut and impressed in a 3-1 win over Newcastle last year. He had a run in the team but lost his place when Nuno switched to a 4-4-2 in January and settled on Mateus Fernandes and Tomas Soucek as his preferred partnership in central midfield.
That was when Potts remembered how he grew during loan spells at Portsmouth and Wycombe. “I know that you can have games where you feel like you are on top of the world, and then you can come straight back down,” he says. “The loans helped me out massively with West Ham because I managed to cope with the highs. The Newcastle game was a real high, but there were some lows after that and I feel like I was coping with it.”
Potts saw the reaction on social media when he left. Some West Ham fans were not happy with the club for allowing a homegrown player to depart. This season has been tough for West Ham, who are ninth in the Championship after a disappointing run and replaced Nuno with Parker this month. One problem has been the absence of a No 6. Potts, who can snap into a tackle and link play from deep, has been watching from afar.
“I still think they’re playing well,” he says. “They’ve got a great team, great players. I think Scott Parker is a really good manager and he’s got three teams promoted from the Championship. I don’t think it will be a problem again. West Ham will get promoted in the end.”
Potts has glitzier assignments and is adjusting to his surroundings. He cannot speak much Flemish but he has sipped a couple of Belgian beers and is enjoying life in Bruges. “I’m not going to lie, when I first joined I found it difficult. It’s completely different when you move country. But I was open to the challenge. At the start it was a challenge but now it’s really smooth.”
One of the biggest challenges has been adapting to a new style. Given the intensity of the Premier League it is a surprise to hear Potts say Brugge, managed by the 48-year-old Croatian Ivan Leko, have helped him become more physical.
“Straight away in training programmes it was a real surprise how hard everyone works,” Potts says. “It’s in the nature of the club to really work hard and give 100% every day. You see that straight away as you come in the door. No matter how hard it can be everyone gets on with it. No complaints. We’re a running team and everyone gives it their all. That’s the message from the top. It’s a real positive environment for someone of my age to be part of.”
Brugge have a couple of rising stars in attack: the rapid Portugal winger Carlos Forbs and the 22-year-old striker Nicolò Tresoldi, who scored a hat-trick in the win over Inter. There is a feeling Leko’s side could go on a run in Europe. They do not fear Liverpool. “It’ll be difficult for them coming to our place,” Potts says. “They’re a great team but we’re going to approach it like we have been doing with every game.
“Inter are one of the top teams in the competition. PSV are a great team and we got the win there. Liverpool will be tough but we’ve proved it against top teams before.”

Ollie Robinson signs for Nottinghamshire on three-year all-format contract as England bowler ends 11-year spell at Sussex
Former Sussex captain Ollie Robinson has signed a three-year all-format contract with Nottinghamshire; the England seamer has represented Sussex in the County Championship since 2015, taking on the role of red-ball captain in 2026; Robinson had a year left on his Sussex contract
Tuesday 24 November 2026 13:00, UK
Nottinghamshire have announced the signing of England bowler Ollie Robinson on a three-year all-format deal.
The signing signals the end of an 11-year spell for Robinson at Sussex - whom he captained during the 2026 County Championship Division One season - despite having a year left on his contract.
Robinson joins the 2025 Division One title winners with a stellar first-class record of 520 wickets at an average of 21.09, while boasting 104 wickets at an average of 19.25 for England's Test side.
- England thrash Australia by eight wickets in second T20I
- Cameron Bancroft article blows Sandpapergate open
- Listen to latest episode of the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast
"I'm absolutely delighted to be joining Nottinghamshire. I've always loved playing at Trent Bridge, and I'm really looking forward to calling it home," Robinson said.
"I have a real desire to win silverware, and with the quality of the squad at Notts, there's no doubt in my mind that we can do that.
"Everyone has told me the environment at Trent Bridge is as close to an international one as you can get, so I'm really excited to see that and make the most of it."
Robinson posted figures of 5-85 in his first and only Test appearance at Trent Bridge, taking 22 first-class wickets in four appearances at the ground, averaging 19.63.
"I'd like to give Sussex a lot of credit throughout this whole process," Nottinghamshire director of cricket Mick Newell added.
"They've been constructive and cordial to deal with, and we're grateful to them for that. We're all thrilled by the statement signing of Ollie, and we know our members and supporters will be too."
