items.title: PAYE, VAT and corporate taxes in focus as Treasury prepares 2027 reforms
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 24 – The National Treasury is seeking to broaden Kenya’s tax base and improve compliance as it prepares the second Medium-Term Revenue Strategy (MTRS) ahead of the 2027/28 financial year.
Treasury Cabinet Secretary John Mbadi says the strategy will build on lessons from the curren
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 24 – The National Treasury is seeking to broaden Kenya’s tax base and improve compliance as it prepares the second Medium-Term Revenue Strategy (MTRS) ahead of the 2027/28 financial year.
Treasury Cabinet Secretary John Mbadi says the strategy will build on lessons from the current revenue framework, with emphasis on bringing more taxpayers into the tax system and reducing excessive reliance on individuals and businesses already operating within the formal economy.
Mbadi said improving tax administration and addressing compliance gaps would be critical to strengthening domestic revenue mobilisation without imposing additional pressure on existing taxpayers.
Speaking during a stakeholder workshop organised by the Government of Kenya and the African Economic Research Consortium in Nairobi, he said the Government must pursue revenue measures that support economic growth and protect household purchasing power.
He argued that businesses require sufficient capital to expand operations, employ more people and invest in productive activities, while households need disposable income to support consumption and savings.
The second MTRS will be informed by 14 research papers presented during the workshop, covering different aspects of the country’s tax system.
The studies examine personal income tax, petroleum excise, corporate taxation, Value Added Tax (VAT), electronic invoicing through eTIMS, informal payments, cross-border trade and the Financial Inclusion Fund.
A key area of focus is the distribution of personal income tax across different income groups, including the impact of existing exemptions and reliefs.
The research will also examine tax incidence and income inequality to establish whether the current tax framework places obligations on taxpayers according to their actual ability to pay.
Mbadi said the Government must also address public concerns over how collected taxes are utilised, insisting that revenue mobilisation should go hand in hand with accountability in public expenditure.
“Taxpayers are entitled to ask what they receive for their contribution,” he said.
He directed technical teams to consolidate the workshop recommendations into a policy review matrix outlining the supporting evidence, additional analysis required and institutional responsibilities.
The matrix will identify proposals requiring legislative changes and those that can be implemented through improvements in tax administration.
The Treasury is expected to use the findings to shape the Finance Bill, 2027, and the second MTRS.

items.title: Iran files lawsuits in US, EU courts: Will it get justice for ‘war crimes’?
items.summary:
Iran files lawsuits in US, EU courts: Will it get justice for ‘war crimes’?
As Iran seeks accountability and compensation for war crimes, experts say legal proceedings face steep hurdles.
Iran has filed lawsuits in the United States and European countries for alleged war crimes committed during the
items.text:
Iran files lawsuits in US, EU courts: Will it get justice for ‘war crimes’?
As Iran seeks accountability and compensation for war crimes, experts say legal proceedings face steep hurdles.
Iran has filed lawsuits in the United States and European countries for alleged war crimes committed during the US-Israel war, including the missile attack on a school that killed at least 178 people, most of them schoolgirls.
Vice President for Legal Affairs Majid Ansari said on Sunday that Iran has begun legal proceedings in courts in the US and four European countries over “war crimes”, months after the deadly attack on a primary school in Minab in February on the first day of the ongoing war.
The lawsuits will cover the killing of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, Iran’s official news agency IRNA reported. They will also address the deaths of scientists, military commanders and civilians, as well as attacks on civilian infrastructure, including hospitals, ambulances and emergency facilities.
Speaking at a ceremony honouring the families of children killed in US and Israeli attacks, Ansari said his office is working with the country’s justice and foreign ministries to pursue claims under international law.
The courts in the US and European countries have not been identified, but Ansari said proceedings had been initiated in courts that accepted jurisdiction over the cases. He gave no further specific details.
Experts say the cases in Europe may offer a more viable legal avenue, while proceedings in the US face significant jurisdictional hurdles. But whether Iran can turn these proceedings into meaningful accountability is questionable.
“Iran is pursuing the legal avenues available to it, seeking accountability and preserving evidence,” Saeed Bagheri, an assistant professor in international law at the University of Reading in the UK, told Al Jazeera.
“Compensation may be an objective, but it is far from assured.”
Iran’s expanding legal campaign
Iran is pursuing its cases in the US and Europe because it has limited access to international courts.
Ansari said Iran was considering filing a case with the International Criminal Court (ICC), which tries individuals charged with the most grave crimes. But Tehran – alongside the US and Israel – is not a signatory to the Rome Statute under which the court was formed in 2002. Iran would, therefore, need an independent basis for jurisdiction, such as a UN Security Council referral.
At the International Court of Justice (ICJ) – the world’s top court that handles legal disputes between states – jurisdiction depends on state consent under Article 36 of the ICJ, said Bagheri.
“Iran cannot simply demand a hearing in either court,” said the expert, who is also a fellow at the Max Planck Institute for Comparative Public Law and International Law based in Germany.
Amid the legal hurdles, Iran has filed a number of cases in both domestic and international courts accusing the US and Israel of committing war crimes in the June 2025 war as well as the ongoing war. Iran says more than 3,500 people have been killed and 26,500 wounded in the war, along with widespread damage to civilian infrastructure, including schools, hospitals, bridges and energy facilities.
In March, Iran filed a complaint at the Iran-US Claims Tribunal in The Hague, accusing Washington of military aggression, illegal economic sanctions and threats of force. The Tribunal was formed following the 1981 Algiers Accords brokered by Algeria.
On Sunday, Ansari said preparations were under way for a second complaint to the Tribunal over the current war.
In September, Iran’s judiciary issued indictments against 159 senior US and Israeli political and military officials over the assassination of Khamenei and military commanders, judiciary spokesman Ali Kazemi said.
The Iranian judiciary has also said that about 400 cases have been filed with Iranian courts as part of domestic and international legal proceedings, including one involving 350,000 plaintiffs, Press TV reported.
A judiciary official on Monday said that local courts have demanded $290bn in damages from the United States.
A separate civil lawsuit was filed in the US in September by the National Iranian American Council Action (NIAC), a US civil society organisation, alongside several Iranian plaintiffs, including the father of a girl killed in the Minab school bombing. The case seeks a ruling that the US military campaign in Iran was unconstitutional. This case was not brought by the Iranian government.
The evidence required
The Minab school bombing is a large component of Iran’s pursuit of justice in the US and European courts.
In September, a report by the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission found that the United States likely committed “war crimes” when it struck the school.
But Iran’s arsenal of evidence to prove that the Minab school bombing was a war crime would have to be wide in scope – civilian deaths do not, on their own, establish a war crime, said Bagheri in Reading.
Iran would need to establish who carried out the attack, what was targeted and what the relevant decision-makers knew at the time, he explained.
Calling a strike accidental also does not settle whether it was lawful or not, said Bagheri.
Investigators must assess whether the military followed the rules of distinction, proportionality and precautions to protect civilians, he added.
“For Minab, the crucial evidence would include targeting files, intelligence assessments, no-strike lists, collateral-damage estimates and records showing when the information was last verified,” Bagheri explained.
According to the UN Mission’s report, the civilian nature of the school was apparent and the US failed in its obligation “to do everything feasible” to verify that it was a military objective.
The report’s authors said that photographs and videos depicting the school before and after the attack showed “readily identifiable features” that it was associated with an educationa

items.text:
UK sanctions Yemen’s Houthi group, four senior officials
Group must be held accountable for ‘targeting our partners and innocent civilians’, says Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband.
The United Kingdom has imposed sanctions on Yemen’s Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), as well as four of the group’s senior officials.
Announcing the measures on Wednesday, the UK government accused the Iran-aligned group of “deliberately attempting to undermine stability in the Middle East”.
It accused the four sanctioned individuals – Houthi interior minister Abdulkarim Amir al-Din Hussein al-Houthi, security and intelligence chief Abdul Hakim Hashem Ali al-Khaiwani, judge Mohammed Moufleh and prosecutor Sarim al-Din Muffadal – of involvement in human rights abuses.
Muffadal, according to the UK government, “is reasonably suspected of having directly perpetrated, or knowingly permitted or acquiesced in, sexual violence including rape, torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment of women detainees.”
Al-Houthi, meanwhile, allegedly oversaw the custody of detainees who were “subjected to torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment”. Such abuses included “electric shocks, beatings and sexual violence”, the UK government said.
The sanctioned individuals are subject to an asset freeze and travel ban, it added.
The UK government said the measures reaffirmed Britain’s view that “Houthi aggression is unacceptable and that the group must be held to account”.
It cited the group’s attacks on vessels in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, strikes targeting civil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and “aggression” in Yemen.
Since seizing Yemen’s Sanaa in September 2014, the Houthis have controlled much of northern and western Yemen, and Yemen’s internationally recognised government has controlled much of the south. While a United Nations-brokered ceasefire largely halted the fighting in 2022, the conflict flared again this summer when the Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi ports.
The group then carried out a lightning offensive in September, seizing much of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline near the Bab al-Mandeb strait. Government forces launched a counteroffensive last month to recapture territory from the Houthis, but forces allied to the government earlier this month said they would withdraw from areas around the strait and focus on defending Aden.
During the latest period of conflict, Saudi Arabia, which leads a coalition in support of Yemen’s internationally recognised government, has been targeted in near-daily Houthi rocket and drone strikes. One attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh in October killed 13 people.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the sanctions sent a message that Britain “will always act in support of British values and interests.”
“The Houthis’ renewed aggression targeting our partners and innocent civilians is unacceptable and they must be held to account,” said Miliband.

items.text:
Is North Korea holding back on sending Russia more troops?
November 24, 2026
Over the summer, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that he expected between 30,000 and 50,000 North Korean soldiers would be deployed to Russia as part of Pyongyang's ongoing support of Moscow's war effort.
However, it now appears that troop buildup has yet to materialize, and it is unclear whether North Korea will continue sending large numbers of troops to Russia.
Writing on Telegram on November 9, Andrii Kovalenko, who resigned in September as head of Ukraine's Center for Countering Disinformation, said an August intelligence assessment indicated that the Kremlin had requested more than 30,000 additional North Korean troops for an autumn offensive.
He said a summit between North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and Russian President Vladimir Putin was expected in September, but did not happen. Kviy says North Korea previously sent thousands of troops to Russia's Kursk region in 2024, where Moscow was fighting to repel a Ukrainian incursion.
Kovalenko believes Pyongyang turned down Moscow's request because taking part in offensive operations in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine's Donetsk region may still be a red line for North Korea.
However, Kovalenko added Russia still relies on North Korean material support, particularly ammunition, while assessing that another major deployment of North Korean combat troops was unlikely this winter.
No need for North Korean reinforcements?
Han Ki-bum, a former deputy director of South Korea's National Intelligence Service, told DW that the lull in fighting and the onset of winter give Pyongyang little immediate reason to send reinforcements.
He added that a visit this week to Moscow by Jo Yong-won, a senior North Korean official and close aide to Kim, could shed light on any future plans.
Han said it remained to be seen whether the visit was intended to deepen political ties between the ruling parties, building on their military cooperation, or to lay the groundwork for a visit by Kim himself.
Ahn Chan-il, a former North Korean soldier who defected to South Korea in 1979 and now heads the World Institute for North Korea Studies in Seoul, said Moscow also had reasons to limit the deployment.
He told DW that he expects Russia to weigh its battlefield needs against the costs of bringing in more North Korean troops. Unless the war expands, he said, Moscow is unlikely to request a larger contingent.
North Korean weapons keep flowing
Ukrainian official Kovalenko said North Korea still had a missile unit in Russia's Voronezh region and around 8,500 support personnel in rear areas, including drone operators, engineers and sappers.
He added that Pyongyang was ramping up ammunition production and showcasing new drones and missiles.
In a post on X on November 17, Zelenskyy said that Russia was receiving dozens of North Korean ballistic missiles each month.
He warned that their use in Ukraine was helping Pyongyang refine its weapons and creating security risks for countries around the Korean Peninsula. Battle-testing weaponry is one of North Korea's primary advantages from military cooperation with Russia
Balancing Russia and China ties
Kovalenko said Pyongyang appeared to have adopted what he called a "containment strategy," limiting its military commitment to Russia's war while maintaining ties with both Moscow and Beijing.
In his assessment, this approach allows Pyongyang to retain the benefits of its alliance with Russia while reducing its exposure to the outcome of the war.
Analyst Ahn said he expects Pyongyang's military cooperation with Moscow to continue because Russian assistance is crucial to North Korea's efforts to develop drone technology and strengthen its navy.
Nevertheless, the extent of this cooperation may be more limited in the future, and Pyongyang is also able to turn to China as a hedge.
Ahn said that if Russia limits the deployment of North Korean troops, Pyongyang's foreign currency earnings from those deployments would have less room to grow, giving it another reason to seek more support from Beijing
Jeong Joon Hee, a former South Korean Unification Ministry spokesperson, told DW that recent moves towards building better ties with Beijing may also reflect Pyongyang's dissatisfaction with what Moscow has offered in return for North Korea's help.
By strengthening its relationship with China while keeping ties with Russia steady, he said, Pyongyang could also be trying to persuade Moscow to give it more.
Kim Hyung Suk, a former South Korean vice minister of unification, told DW that North Korea needs China's economic, political and diplomatic backing alongside the support it receives from Russia. He expects Pyongyang to keep pursuing China's support regardless of how it manages its role in the war.

Imane Khelif was the subject of a fierce gender eligibility row at the Olympic Games; she hasn't boxed since winning gold at Paris 2024; Algerian is due to fight as a professional in Paris on December 15
Tuesday 24 November 2026 13:04, UK
Imane Khelif is still set to box for the first time since the Olympic Games even though her scheduled opponent has withdrawn.
Algeria's Khelif won Olympic welterweight gold in Paris in 2024, while a fierce gender eligibility row overshadowed her participation.
Khelif was cleared to compete by the International Olympic Committee (IOC), despite the International Boxing Association (an organisation that itself has been banned from Olympic boxing) having banned her from the previous year's World Championships for allegedly failing to meet gender eligibility criteria.
Khelif hasn't boxed since beating Liu Yang in that Olympic final, but is due to have a professional bout in Paris on December 15.
That fight next month will go ahead although Khelif's original opponent Clarida Sarabia has withdrawn and Khelif is now looking for a replacement.
"The opponent did have to withdraw from the fight for administrative reasons," a spokesperson for promoter Stair Event told Reuters.
"But the bout is still scheduled for December 15. We'll announce the opponent soon."
In February, Khelif said she was open to genetic testing only if administered by the IOC.

items.title: LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you
items.summary:
LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you

items.text:
LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you
5 min read
In the evenings after work, I will often sit out back on the porch and do some phone rotting. That usually takes the form of me just flipping through reels on Instagram, allowing the algorithm to take me where it may. I usually pair this with a healthy tumbler of rum or bourbon. I'm turning my brain off after work, and I'm just having a good time on the internet. The kids might call it dopamine maxxing? Hell, I don't know. Who gives a shit about what those assholes would call it?
Anywho, I often encounter songs I really really like, and I would like to listen and discover more of please. Instagram makes it hard for me to connect with the band outside of their platform. I was trying to make this connection manually myself at first. I would just email myself a reel from my phone. Then when I'm back on the sofa and in the mood to track down new music, I'd open the reels and do my best to search on Bandcamp or YouTube or try to figure out if some of these musicians had a way to buy music from them. Very few do these days. They send you their Spotify link or send you to their TikTok page. I don't want to do any of that. I'd like to trade US dollars in exchange for some music files I can download onto my computer, where I can listen as much as I like on any device I own thank you please. Retro maxxing.
So, I used Claude Code to build a skill that does this for me. It opens the Instagram reel and attempts to identify the artist and song. It then tries to determine if the artists have a Bandcamp page so I can purchase the songs I want, and if it finds one, it gives me the URL so I can click it to complete the trade I want. I want to buy music from artists who make music I like. That's a fair and wholesome endeavor, I feel, but this recently stopped working.
It turns out Bandcamp added a challenge on their search API page. Ah bummer. No worries, that was an unpublished workaround anyway. As I was mulling over this discovery, the robot went on to explain that it would not help me work around the challenge. cue Nick Young question marks
Well, that led me down a whole nother rabbit hole, which is turning into this post. There's another branch of my skill that attempts to locate the same song from the Instagram reel on YouTube, and it'll download the song to my computer if I ask.
So let me get this straight. The robot, which is my robot that I pay a pretty penny for, will not attempt to work around the challenge at Bandcamp so that I can more easily connect with bands to complete a sale, but it will download the YouTube song, which doesn't send any money to the band or anyone???
This is the real danger of the frontier AI models. Not that it won't help me hack Bandcamp[1], but that this model doesn't really work for us. Well, they do, but only insofar as Anthropic or OpenAI or whoever else allows them to. In this case, Anthropic is trying to ensure that people can't use their models for evil. I'm not trying to do evil. I'm actually trying to do good! I want to buy something from a small artist on the internet. That's basically the most wholesome thing a person can do on the internet!
Have no doubt, dear reader, these companies want to dominate. They want to capture the market. They want all the money. It'll be the same march to enshittification that happened with Google. A bunch of nerds who built something cool sold out, and it turned into just another business that decided to remove its don't be evil mantra.
Right now, I think the robots are providing real information to the best of their ability, but I think it's only a matter of time until we must wonder if the answers they're providing are real answers that the robot found, or if they're weighted answers Anthropic put there because a company gave it enough money for product placement. I want to know the best robot vacuum according to old reddit or other trusted sources like Wirecutter, weighed and measured according to what I, and thus my robot agent, think are important requirements. I don't want to know which robot vacuum parent multinational conglomerate has a large ad budget.
And it's not just ads. If Anthropic can tell its model not to work around a challenge, then it can tell its model to do whatever the US government tells it to do, including not helping people download copyrighted music. It does that some now, but it's easy to slip the noose on that. For now.
This is the reason I want a local model that runs in my homelab. My robot should work for me and have my best interests in mind, not the interests of US corporate copyright holders. I plan to study up on what "open models" even means. I've been thinking about these as the FOSS version of LLMs, but I think that doesn't exactly map, as the biggest piece seems to be how the model was trained. The Chinese models are likely to refuse to answer questions about Taiwan, for example.
On the existential threat or tool question, I'm firmly in the tool camp, and I really do not like artificial restrictions on my tools. I will do everything I reasonably can to remove those restrictions.
- And to be clear, I'm not trying to work around Bandcamp's challenge. I'm responding to the fact that Claude preemptively told me it wouldn't help me do this. ↩︎

Vaibhav Sooryavanshi smashes fastest hundred and double century in List A cricket during India A's victory over UAE
Vaibhav Sooryavanshi broke more records on Tuesday as the 15-year-old cricket sensation guided India A to a seven-wicket win vs UAE with an extraordinary knock; the opener made an astounding 204 runs off a mere 53 deliveries, including 28 sixes,
Tuesday 24 November 2026 13:10, UK
Vaibhav Sooryavanshi has broken more records as the teenage cricket sensation smashed his way to the fastest century and double century in List A cricket during India A's seven-wicket victory against the United Arab Emirates on Tuesday.
The 15-year-old produced an extraordinary innings, making 204 off a mere 53 deliveries, including 28 sixes, during the Asia Cup Rising Stars group match in Doha.
Sooryavanshi, who became the youngest debutant for India's senior T20 side in July, first raced his way to a 28-ball century, the fastest ton hit in List A cricket, surpassing Jake Fraser-McGurk by one delivery.
- Sooryavanshi becomes youngest player to debut for India
- Who are Sooryavanshi's rivals for world's best T20 opener?
- Listen to latest episode of the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast
The Indian prodigy then went one better, advancing to his second ton off 24 balls to obliterate the record, previously held by Chad Bowes, for the fastest double century struck in List A cricket [103 balls].
His 40-ball 150 was also the fastest in List A cricket too, with the 15-year-old going on to smash four consecutive sixes.
It came after UAE had set India a target of 250 to win and thanks to Sooryavanshi's feats, Tilak Varma's side would go on to seal victory inside 14.2 overs.
Sooryavanshi completed the feat by smashing an incredible 28 sixes and seven fours, with a strike rate of 384.90.
That surpassed Western Australia's D'Arcy Short's record tally of 23 maximums, which he managed during a match against Queensland in 2019.
Known as a ruthless ball striker, Sooryavanshi was named the IPL's MVP for the 2026 season, after leading the league with 776 runs and a strike rate of 237.30.
In February, he set a new record for the highest score made at an Under-19 Cricket World Cup final, making 175 runs from 80 deliveries, as India went on to seal a 100-run win against England.
Sooryavanshi would ultimately be dismissed in the 13th over after he clipped a delivery from Basil Hameed to Aryansh Sharma at long-off.

items.text:
Non-league player injured falling down badger hole
- Published
Footballers may be among the fittest athletes in the world of sport, but they are not immune to bizarre injuries.
Dave Beasant famously severed a tendon in his big toe when he dropped a bottle of salad cream, while Rio Ferdinand strained tendons in his knee by lying in one position on the sofa for too long watching television.
The latest inductee into the strange injury hall of fame is Chelmsford City captain Cav Miley.
The 31-year-old midfielder missed the 2-2 draw with Walton and Hersham in the National League South on Saturday after twisting an ankle in training by falling down a badger hole.
Miley returned for the 1-0 home victory over Maidstone United on Monday, after which manager Mark Cooper shed more light on the incident.
"Everyone is telling me it's gone viral, but I told the truth - he fell down a badger hole," Cooper told the club's YouTube channel.
"I was told at the start it was a fox hole, but then the guy at where we train told me it's a badger hole.
"We need to make sure we fill all of them in before we train now."
Miley joined Chelmsford in the summer after spells in the National League with Southend United and Eastleigh.

items.summary:
Palace docked points for using four sub windows in win
- Published
Crystal Palace have been deducted three points after using too many substitution windows during their win on the opening day of the 2026-27 Women's Super League season.
Palace, who were playing their first match following promotion b
items.text:
Palace docked points for using four sub windows in win
- Published
Crystal Palace have been deducted three points after using too many substitution windows during their win on the opening day of the 2026-27 Women's Super League season.
Palace, who were playing their first match following promotion back to the WSL, beat Everton 1-0 on 6 September at Gander Green Lane.
However, manager Jo Potter brought on Kirsty Howat for Shannon O'Brien in the seventh minute of second-half stoppage time to try and shore up the victory.
It was the fourth separate substitution made by Potter, who had also made changes in the 62nd, 83rd and 90th minutes.
While WSL managers are allowed to make five changes in a game, they must be made across only three stoppages in play to avoid excessive time wasting.
Palace have been stripped of the three points they earned in the match - one of only two WSL games the Eagles have won this season.
This punishment drops Palace down one place in the WSL table to 13th - the relegation play-off place.
Palace are now below fellow promoted side Birmingham City in the table on goal difference, with both sides now having six points - six behind Everton in 11th.
In a statement on their club website, external Palace said they were "disappointed" by the decision.
The decision was made by an independent tribunal after Palace admitted the breach of competition rule 5.19.1.
The rule states: "A substitution can only be made when play is stopped for any reason and the referee has given permission. A club at its discretion may use five substitute players during a match. For the avoidance of doubt, each club has no more than three substitution opportunities in each match."
The tribunal said that while the rule breach was inadvertent and "not intended to secure an unfair advantage", it said a points deduction was necessary in order to provide a deterrent to clubs against making a similar mistake in future.
"The integrity of the competition would be damaged if a club that had breached the rules on substitution opportunities, and had won the match, were allowed to keep the points it obtained, save in exceptional circumstances," the tribunal stated in its full written decision., external
They said the lateness of the substitution in the match - so late that Howat did not touch the ball after coming on - did not excuse Palace from punishment.
It also ruled "that responsibility for complying with the rule rests with clubs, not match officials".
Palace - who placed the word "fourth" in inverted commas in their response to the ruling - are aiming to improve on their only previous WSL campaign in 2024-25, where they only won twice in 22 matches and were relegated by a 10-point margin.
Their statement read: "Everyone at the club is obviously frustrated that such a minor infraction, given that the player was on the pitch for only 46 seconds while the ball was in play, has led to such a significant penalty – a penalty which we do not agree is reasonable or proportionate.
"We are disappointed for the players and staff who worked so hard to secure a deserved victory on our return to the WSL."
Forward Lexi Lloyd-Smith had scored the only goal of the game in the 34th minute on her Palace debut.

Price, a finalist in 2023, previously suggested he might decline an invite to the tournament, which runs across 16 weeks, after a difficult 2024 season before reversing his decision and accepting his selection.
The 41-year-old, who has hit five nine-dart finishes in Premier League Darts, the most by any player in the tournament's history, has now hinted at missing the 2027 roadshow.
Speaking on Sky Sports News, Price said: "My daughter's pregnant. I've got a lot of things on. It is difficult in the Premier League with World Series and how many events the PDC are putting on these days.
"It's a couple of months before things are decided for that. So we'll see how things go."
Price also spoke about Luke Littler facing repeated booing and whistling from crowds at major tournaments, with 'The Iceman' suggesting it will eventually "go away".
Price has been subjected to boos and he even wore ear defenders to block out jeers from the crowd at the World Championship in 2023.
"The crowd like to see the underdog win, and I think that's what Luke is going through at the minute," Price reflected.
"Obviously, being the best player in the world is what he is at the minute, and I think a lot of people are a little bit jealous and jump on his back because they want to see him fail because he is so successful. But that'll go away.
"I never thought it would go away with me, but it does eventually, and it will with him as well.
"He's a great lad, he's a great player, he's great for the sport, and people should just get off his back."

Monday 23 November 2026 18:53, UK
McLaren team principal Andrea Stella says he liked Oscar Piastri's fiery response to radio messages warning the Australian to "be careful" battling his team-mate Lando Norris during the Las Vegas Grand Prix.
Piastri started from 17th on the grid after taking an engine penalty but drove impressively - during an extraordinary race that featured 352 overtakes - to join the battle at the front in latter stages, closing in on a leading train of cars that featured Norris.
As Piastri chased George Russell for fourth with Norris just in front of the Mercedes, a radio exchange was played out on the television broadcast which featured him twice being told by his race engineer to "be careful" around his team-mate, to which he responded: "Stop telling me to ****ing be careful."

The McLaren pair ultimately benefitted from late errors by Russell and his Mercedes team-mate Antonelli to claim a double podium, with Norris second and Piastri third behind Red Bull's Max Verstappen.
Asked about Piastri's radio exchange after the race, Stella said: "I actually liked it. I like it. That's the character that you expect from a racer.
"It's not like the Michael Schumacher, the Fernando Alonso, the Kimi Raikkonen - that I worked with before - were any easier, and (they) were champions.
"That's the character you want to see. And that's also what you have to do from the pit wall. You need to make sure that the driver has a clear objective in his head.
"And you want to do it up until the point the driver makes you feel, 'I've got it. Don't go beyond.' That's exactly where you want to be from outside the cockpit.
"So, actually, well done to the pit wall and well done to Oscar in relation to this situation. That's exactly where we want to position the interaction between the team and the driver, and what we have learnt through some of the experiences we've gone through."
'You have to modulate and adapt a driver's racing spirit'
With Norris clearly outperforming Piastri this season, there have been relatively few challenges for McLaren in managing their drivers, which is in significant contrast to last season when Norris came out on top in a battle for the drivers' title that went down to the final race of the season.
The only major flashpoint of this season came when an aggressive attempt to pass Piastri from Norris on the final lap of the Sprint in Singapore resulted in contact that cost both drivers points, leading to criticism from Stella and an apology from the Brit.
Stella provided more detail on his approach to managing his drivers as he attempted to further explain why he liked Piastri's fierce radio response in Las Vegas.
"I'll have to up a little bit of IP (intellectual property) here, in terms of how you manage drivers, but let me be clear, because we avoid this matter to create any noise," Stella said to gathered reporters.
"If we go and we do a leisure go-karting together, our personalities will change slightly from the personality we have right now when we are enjoying sitting here. We will dig out the racing spirit, we will dig out something that is the reason why these guys do what they do, and all the sacrifices that they have gone through to be where they are.
"And that's where you have to come and help them, come and help them modulate, adapt. We want to use it. That's why I said I really liked Oscar's answer. That's the racer I want to see. But at the same time, it's a team effort in modulating it. We want to use just the right quantity of it that doesn't take us too far.
"And if you see Lando in Singapore, Lando certainly, you don't have to remind him of the team interest and that he's a team player. He's a phenomenal team player, yet his vision, his way of racing got a little too channelled, and in the final lap of the Sprint, he attacked Oscar in a way that led to a collision.
"And he was incredibly apologetic. And, if anything, he said like, 'guys, just don't assume that we do all the processing, because we are so busy just racing, keeping the car on track, and this year's car absorbs our bandwidth. items.title: OPINION: How AI is changing the economics of vehicle tracking and fleet management
items.summary:
By Thige Brian
Once a vehicle, whether a car, truck or matatu, leaves the parking lot, several things can happen. It could be stolen or hijacked, driven by an unauthorised person, diverted from its assigned route or used for purposes unrelated to its intended business. Fuel could be siphoned, a driv
items.text:
By Thige Brian
Once a vehicle, whether a car, truck or matatu, leaves the parking lot, several things can happen. It could be stolen or hijacked, driven by an unauthorised person, diverted from its assigned route or used for purposes unrelated to its intended business. Fuel could be siphoned, a driver could engage in reckless behaviour or the vehicle could be involved in an accident.
For businesses operating fleets, these incidents translate into financial losses, higher operating costs, reduced productivity and disrupted operations.
The Association of Kenya Insurers (AKI) recorded 330 insured motor vehicle thefts in 2024, down from 420 in 2023. However, only 16 per cent of the stolen vehicles were recovered, leaving owners of the remaining 84 per cent to bear the loss of assets that may have taken years of savings or financing to acquire.
The challenge extends beyond theft, with fuel losses, unauthorised use, inefficient routes and vehicle breakdowns driving up operating costs.
This is changing the economics of vehicle tracking. What was traditionally used to establish a vehicle’s location has evolved into a fleet-management tool, with artificial intelligence (AI) expanding its ability to interpret information, detect unusual patterns and support operational decisions.
Modern tracking systems combine GPS technology with fuel sensors, AI-enabled cameras and data analytics. Fleet managers can now monitor more than the location of their vehicles. They can establish who is driving, assess fuel consumption, identify route deviations and evaluate how efficiently their assets are being used.
Driver monitoring, for instance, is helping businesses strengthen accountability and improve road safety. AI-enabled cameras can identify drivers, flag unauthorised operators and detect risky behaviour, including signs of fatigue and distraction. Recorded footage can also provide evidence when investigating accidents or resolving disputes.
This information enables fleet operators to identify recurring behaviour, intervene before incidents escalate and promote safer driving practices. It can also support insurance investigations by providing a clearer account of events.
Fuel management presents another significant opportunity for cost control. Fuel is among the largest operating expenses for transport and logistics businesses, yet losses can go undetected when monitoring depends on manual records, receipts and periodic inspections.
Fuel sensors provide real-time information on tank levels and refills, flagging sudden drops that could indicate siphoning. Integrated with GPS data, they help fleet managers establish where and when the loss occurred. AI analytics can further identify unusual consumption patterns, excessive idling and possible unauthorised vehicle use.
Industry estimates cited by fleet technology providers put fuel at 35 to 40 per cent of commercial transport and logistics operating costs in East Africa. Poorly monitored fleets are estimated to lose between 10 and 15 per cent of fuel through siphoning, unauthorised use and excessive idling. Although actual losses vary between operators, these figures illustrate why fuel management must extend beyond reconciling expenditure at the end of the month.
AI-enabled tracking is also improving vehicle utilisation and delivery performance. Route analysis allows fleet managers to identify unnecessary mileage, monitor delivery progress and respond to deviations from approved routes. This is particularly valuable for distribution businesses whose profitability depends on meeting delivery schedules while controlling transport costs.
Data on vehicle movements, operating hours and idle time can also inform dispatch decisions and route allocation. Businesses can establish whether their existing fleets are being used efficiently before committing capital to additional vehicles.
AI-enabled fleet-management tools can help businesses eliminate fuel siphoning, reduce operating costs and improve delivery efficiency. For instance, integrating GPS tracking, fuel sensors and geofencing can eliminate fuel siphoning within 30 days, cut monthly fuel expenditure by more than 10 per cent and improve on-time deliveries to over 90 per cent.
The technology is equally relevant to asset financing. Lenders financing vehicles face the risk of losing collateral through theft, unauthorised movement or difficulties locating financed assets. GPS tracking and remote engine immobilisation can help locate vehicles and, subject to appropriate authorisation and safeguards, prevent further movement.
Installing tracking devices alone does not guarantee better fleet management. Businesses need clear vehicle-use policies, trained personnel to interpret alerts and established procedures for responding to unusual activity. They must also protect driver privacy and secure the information collected. Without timely intervention, even sophisticated systems risk generating data without translating it into meaningful business decisions.
For Kenya’s transport and logistics sector, the next frontier is not simply acquiring more vehicles, but extracting greater value from those already on the road. As AI makes tracking systems better at interpreting real-time information, businesses have an opportunity to turn vehicle data into lower operating costs, stronger asset protection and improved productivity.
ENDS….
Caption:
Thige Brian Operation Manager Tracking Hub Ltd with an expertise in Engineering

items.title: Crystal Palace docked three WSL points for extra substitution against Everton
items.summary:
Crystal Palace have been deducted three points in the Women’s Super League after they made substitutions in four separate windows during their 1-0 victory over Everton in September.
Palace admitted breaching the competition’s rules and an independent tribunal ordered the points deduction, but no poi
items.text:
Crystal Palace have been deducted three points in the Women’s Super League after they made substitutions in four separate windows during their 1-0 victory over Everton in September.
Palace admitted breaching the competition’s rules and an independent tribunal ordered the points deduction, but no points will be awarded to Everton. It means Palace drop from 12th to 13th, below Birmingham City on goal difference. The match will not be replayed.
Palace made the substitutions during the second half and their 97th-minute introduction of Kirsty Howat, to replace Shannon O’Brien, was a breach of the rules. Teams have a maximum of three substitution windows per game, excluding half-time.
The WSL, Pro Ref and both clubs launched investigations. Promoted Palace led the opening-weekend game thanks to Lexi Lloyd-Smith’s 34th-minute goal and there were eight minutes of stoppage time indicated at the end.
The match officials who worked on the game were not appointed to any matches for the following round in the WSL and WSL2 in light of the incident.
The independent tribunal concluded Palace’s breach was inadvertent and that they had not tried to secure an unfair advantage.
None of the parties involved are eligible to appeal.

items.text:
Crystal Palace Women deducted three points in WSL for making substitutions at four windows in Everton win
Crystal Palace Women are being punished for making substitutions at four separate windows in a win over Everton in September; this is in breach of IFAB Laws, which state clubs has no more than three substitution opportunities in each match
Tuesday 24 November 2026 11:47, UK
Crystal Palace Women have been deducted three points in the WSL with immediate effect.
Palace are being punished for making substitutions at four separate windows in a win over Everton in September.
This is in breach of IFAB Laws, which state clubs have no more than three substitution opportunities in each match.
Palace made a substitution in a fourth window in the 97th minute of the match against Everton, which they won 1-0.
Kirsty Howat, who was brought on for Shannon O'Brien deep in stoppage time, did not touch the ball before the full-time whistle was blown.
Palace admitted to the breach but felt the sanction sought by the WSL was "excessive".
However, the independent tribunal determined that a sporting sanction was necessary to avoid damaging the integrity of the competition.

items.title: IEBC to be guided by Supreme Court ruling on election results transmission ahead of 2027 polls
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24- The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) will be guided by the Supreme Court’s interpretation of the law on presidential election results transmission, tallying and verification as it prepares for the August 10, 2027 General Election.
IEBC Chairperson Erastu
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24- The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) will be guided by the Supreme Court’s interpretation of the law on presidential election results transmission, tallying and verification as it prepares for the August 10, 2027 General Election.
IEBC Chairperson Erastus Ethekon said the commission would operate within the constitutional and legal framework established by the courts, dismissing concerns that the National Tallying Centre could be used to manipulate or alter results declared at polling stations.
Speaking during a breakfast meeting with political reporters on Tuesday, Ethekon said the commission had no intention of introducing a new system outside the law, insisting that the courts had already clarified the respective responsibilities of IEBC commissioners and the chairperson in managing presidential election results.
“The Supreme Court itself has settled the issue of election results management. Nobody in IEBC is saying that we are going to reinvent something else that is outside the law,” Ethekon said.
He defended the National Tallying Centre, arguing that the commission was constitutionally mandated to collect, tally and verify presidential election results before the chairperson announces the winner.
The debate over the role of the national centre has intensified ahead of the 2027 elections, with questions raised over whether results declared at constituency tallying centres should undergo another round of verification at the national level.
In its September 5, 2022 judgment on the presidential election petitions arising from the victory of President William Ruto, the Supreme Court clarified that the mandate to tally and verify presidential results at the National Tallying Centre belongs to the IEBC as a collective institution.
The court ruled that the chairperson could not exclude other commissioners from the exercise, although the responsibility of declaring the final presidential results rests exclusively with the chairperson.
The judges also found that the chairperson did not enjoy special or extraordinary powers over the tallying and verification process.
The ruling followed the divisions that emerged within the commission during the 2022 presidential election, when four commissioners disowned the results announced by then chairperson Wafula Chebukati.
The court’s position is central to the ongoing debate over the management of presidential election results, particularly the distinction between tallying and verification at the national level and the declaration of results at polling stations and constituency tallying centres.
The Court of Appeal had earlier established the principle of finality of results announced at polling stations in the 2017 Maina Kiai case, ruling that the IEBC chairperson could not alter results declared by presiding officers.
The courts have subsequently reinforced the need to distinguish between the finality of results at the respective stages of the electoral process and the commission’s constitutional responsibility to establish the national presidential tally.
The issue was again tested in a petition filed by Busia Senator Okiya Omtatah, who challenged the constitutionality of national tallying and verification of presidential results.
On September 22, 2026, the High Court dismissed the petition, with Justice Gregory Mutai affirming that IEBC is required to tally and verify presidential results nationally.
The judge, however, made clear that the exercise does not give the commission powers to alter figures already declared and certified by constituency returning officers.
He ruled that national tallying involves aggregating constituency figures, while verification entails checking their accuracy against the certified records.
The court further directed that the exercise be undertaken collectively by commissioners, with candidates’ agents and election observers granted access to the same underlying information available to the commission.
It also emphasised that discrepancies between electronically transmitted results and physically delivered records must be documented, explained and made public.
The ruling has since informed Parliament’s consideration of proposed amendments to the Elections Act, particularly provisions governing the transmission, tallying and declaration of election results.
The Elections (Amendment) (No. 2) Bill, 2024, initially passed by the Senate, sought to repeal and replace Section 39 of the Elections Act, which governs the determination and declaration of election results.
One of the contentious proposals was contained in Clause 22, which sought to introduce a new framework for handling election results, including their declaration and transmission.
The Senate’s version also omitted the existing provision requiring IEBC to establish a mechanism for livestreaming results announced at polling stations, raising concerns among electoral stakeholders about transparency and public access to election information.
However, the National Assembly took a different position when it considered the Bill.
On October 22, 2026, MPs passed the Bill with amendments, deleting Clause 22 and retaining the existing Section 39 of the Elections Act.
The decision preserved the provision requiring IEBC to establish a mechanism for livestreaming results from polling stations for public information.
National Assembly Majority Leader Kimani Ichung’wah subsequently defended the decision, saying Parliament had taken into account the High Court’s September ruling when considering the proposed changes.
The Bill was, however, not yet law following the National Assembly’s amendments. It was required to return to the Senate for consideration of the changes under Article 110(4) of the Constitution.
The legislative debate is rooted in an earlier legal battle involving Katiba Institute, which challenged amendments to election laws enacted in 2017 following the annulment of the presidential election that year.

items.summary:

The framework seeks to give residents a more structured role in m
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24 – The Nairobi City County Government (NCCG) is strengthening community-led oversight of development projects by aligning ward-level monitoring structures with guidelines issued by the Council of Governors (CoG).
The framework seeks to give residents a more structured role in monitoring public projects from implementation to completion, strengthening accountability and improving service delivery across the county’s wards.
Anchored in the Constitution, devolution laws and the Nairobi City County Public Participation Act, 2015, the initiative builds on existing ward-level Project Management Committees (PMCs).
The county is combining civic education and community mobilisation with clearer responsibilities for residents, Members of County Assembly (MCAs) and ward administrators, alongside improved access to project information and grievance-reporting channels.
Rosemary Kariuki, the County Executive Committee Member (CECM) for Inclusivity, Public Participation and Customer Service, said aligning ward-level oversight with the CoG guidelines would improve accountability and strengthen residents’ involvement in county projects.
“Anchoring our ward-level oversight with the Council of Governors’ guidelines brings clarity, structure and accountability to how residents engage with county projects from start to finish,” Kariuki said.
She said the framework would ensure communities are not only consulted during project planning but also empowered to safeguard public investments throughout implementation.
Chief Officer for Public Participation and Public Engagement Zipporah Njeri said the county was working to equip committees and local teams with clear processes to translate public participation into improved service delivery.
Director of Public Participation Patrick Angasa said effective community oversight depended on access to information, civic education and collaboration between residents, ward administrators, MCAs and technical teams.
He said strengthening the operations of Project Management Committees and their capacity to address challenges at the local level would help prevent implementation delays and ensure projects deliver tangible results.
The county said closer collaboration between technical teams and communities would improve project quality, minimise delays and ensure public investments deliver lasting value across all wards.

items.summary:

[!NOTE] Pourquoi cet article et cette analyse ?

items.text:
Polymarket : Autopsie d'un délit d'initié sur la réintégration de Jensen Huang chez NVIDIA [!NOTE] Pourquoi cet article et cette analyse ? Depuis quelque temps, je constate que Polymarket devient un véritable terrain de jeu pour les délits d’initiés, et le climat politique autour de la nouvelle administration Trump rend ce type d’asymétrie d’information encore plus propice. J’ai donc développé un algorithme qui surveille en permanence les marchés les plus sensibles : chaque transaction y est analysée par des modèles statistiques et des outils de traçage de flux on-chain. J’ai finalisé l’algo il y a deux jours à peine. Dans la nuit même, en voyant l’alerte se déclencher, j’ai mené une première analyse à chaud sur les transactions… avant de voir tomber quelques heures plus tard le tweet de Donald Trump confirmant l’asymétrie. Et vous allez voir que le communiqué officiel de NVIDIA n’était que la cerise sur le gâteau. Cette enquête documente, à la minute et au hash près, un cas assez probant de délit d’initié sur Polymarket détecté en temps réel. Question principale Y a-t-il eu un délit d’initié sur le marché « Will Jensen Huang rejoin NVIDIA by December 31, 2026? » ? - Le timing : Une accumulation de liquidité achevée en pleine nuit Transactions Polygon, exactement 89 minutes avant la prise de position publique de Donald Trump sur Truth Social ; - L’asymétrie de gain : 4 648 USDC engagés sur une probabilité marginale de 6,5 %, dénoués en 71 518 USDC suite à la confirmation unanime du Conseil d’Administration de NVIDIA sur Polymarket ; - Le profil du portefeuille : Un compte jetable Gnosis Safe Proxy créé 81 heures auparavant, dont l’activité est 100 % monothématique. Question secondaire : En quoi les marchés de prédiction décentralisés constituent-ils désormais le sismographe le plus implacable pour révéler publiquement des délits d’initiés invisibles sur les bourses traditionnelles ? Réponse courte (avant d’entrer dans le détail) Sur le strict plan des données on-chain, l’hypothèse du hasard est statistiquement disqualifiée. L’acheteur anonyme opérant sous le pseudonyme ljhggk a méthodiquement balayé le carnet d’ordres jusqu’à 0,065 $, verrouillé sa position avant toute réaction de marché, puis encaissé passivement les deux catalyseurs successifs pour réaliser un gain net de +66 869,34 USDC (+1 438,5 % de ROI). flowchart TB subgraph Chronologie ["Reconstitution temporelle (Heure française CET)"] direction TB A["23/11 · 02:19 - 03:28 CET

Multiplicateur : 15,38x"] 1 · L’Anatomie du trade : 71 518 parts OTM raflées en pleine nuit Entre 02:19:11 et 03:28:20 CET (01:19 - 02:28 UTC) dans la nuit du dimanche au lundi 23 novembre 2026, le carnet d’ordres du marché Will Jensen Huang rejoin NVIDIA by December 31, 2026? était totalement assoupi. La probabilité implicite stagnait à 6,5 %, reflétant un consensus quasi-unanime : suite à sa démission du 12 novembre, un retour de Huang avant la fin de l’année paraissait exclu. C’est à cet instant précis qu’un acteur unique déploie une stratégie d’absorption agressive, découpée en 4 ordres limités successifs : Le relevé des 4 transactions sur Polygon Chaque transaction a été retracée. Les 4 transactions ont été incluses dans les blocs sans rejet Registre complet : [!NOTE] Verdict technique de l’exécution : L’opérateur n’a pas étalé ses achats sur 24 heures pour moyenner son coût. Il a exécuté un achat massif et concentré en pleine nuit européenne/américaine, absorbant 34 % de toute la liquidité vendeuse disponible sur le contrat, ce qui pourrait montrer qu’il a eu l’info quelques heures avant et qu’il n’a pas spécialement eu le temps de l’étaler davantage. Dès son dernier ordre complété à 03:28:20 CET, il s’est totalement arrêté de négocier. À noter : le compte s’était déjà positionné sur de petits montants sur ce pari dès sa création, mais sans jamais approcher de volumes comparables à ce qui a levé l’alerte cette nuit-là. Cette montée soudaine en conviction renforce encore la suspicion. 2 · La Reconstitution temporelle : 89 minutes d’avance sur le monde réel Le cœur du dossier réside dans la corrélation temporelle entre la clôture de l’accumulation on-chain et la chaîne des déclarations publiques. 02:19 CET ─── 03:28 CET ──────── 04:57 CET ────────────────────── 14:30 CET ─── 15:40 CET [Achats] [Fin Accum.] [Post Trump] [PR NVIDIA] [Résolution] 4 648 $ Verrouillé « I hope the Board... » Officiel 1.00 $ 71 518 parts Truth Social Wall Street 71 518 $ ▲ │ │ └──── +89 min ─────┘ │ └────────────────────── +11h 02min ────────────────┘ 1. Le catalyseur politique : La publication de Donald Trump (+89 min) À 04:57:00 CET (22:57:00 EST le 22 novembre), Donald Trump publie sur son réseau Truth Social : « I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang. It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A. » Il ne s’agit pas d’une injonction légale, mais le poids politique est massif : la mise à l’écart de Huang reposait sur des craintes de sécurité nationale. Le soutien explicite de Trump lève immédiatement le principal verrou psychologique. Le contrat bondit instantanément de 0,065 $ à 0,14 $ dans les échanges de la nuit. 2. A League Two footballer has been charged with three counts of rape and remanded in custody by Hertfordshire police.
Isiah Noel-Williams, 23, who has made seven league appearances for Barnet this season, was also charged with one count of assault by penetration, one count of engaging in sexual commun
items.text:
A League Two footballer has been charged with three counts of rape and remanded in custody by Hertfordshire police.
Isiah Noel-Williams, 23, who has made seven league appearances for Barnet this season, was also charged with one count of assault by penetration, one count of engaging in sexual communication with a child and one count of supplying a class B drug.
The club said they were “cooperating fully with the authorities” and would “determine any further action in due course”.
Noel-Williams, the son of the former Watford striker Gifton Noel-Williams, signed for Barnet this past summer after starting his career in non-league.
His arrest followed an investigation by Hertfordshire constabulary’s public protection command. Noel-Williams appeared at Hatfield magistrates court last Saturday and was remanded in custody. He is due to appear at St Albans crown court on 22 December.
Barnet confirmed that “first-team player Isiah Noel-Williams has been charged and remanded in custody as part of a police investigation by Hertfordshire constabulary … As this is now a matter for the courts, the club will not be making any further comment.”

items.title: UK nations in dark over whether they will get automatic entry to 2035 Women’s World Cup
items.summary:
England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales are in the dark about whether they will be granted automatic qualification as hosts for the 2035 Women’s World Cup.
The decision on qualification procedures will be made by Fifa, with sources at the domestic Football Associations telling the Guardian the
items.text:
England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales are in the dark about whether they will be granted automatic qualification as hosts for the 2035 Women’s World Cup.
The decision on qualification procedures will be made by Fifa, with sources at the domestic Football Associations telling the Guardian they had yet to be informed of the plan after their bid was formally accepted.
Such doubts contrasted with the certainty expressed by the newly confirmed hosts of the 2031 World Cup, the United States, Mexico, Costa and Jamaica, who confirmed they had assurances that all four countries would take part.
“All four countries will qualify automatically,” said Cindy Parlow Cone, the president of US Soccer. “That’s what happened in 2026,” a reference to the US, Mexico and Canada being given automatic qualification for last summer’s men’s World Cup.
“We will qualify automatically and will be seeded,” said the president of Jamaican Football Federation, Michael Ricketts. “Once we are one of the host teams we will definitely be in. And in fact, we have had discussions about hosting most of the games that Jamaica will actually play.”
It is unclear whether the uncertainty in the UK is a byproduct of Fifa’s strained relationship with Uefa, which will run the European qualification tournament, or the differing nature of the bids.
Whereas the UK bid was always a four-nation proposal, Costa Rica and Jamaica joined the previously existing US-Mexico bid for 2031 last year, at which point it is understood assurances were given that they would all qualify.
The 2031 World Cup will be the first women’s tournament to feature 48 teams, which in theory should enable Fifa to be more flexible in granting automatic qualification.
An automatic spot would be a major boost in particular for Wales and Northern Ireland, who have never qualified for a Women’s World Cup.
Uefa granted two automatic qualification for the 2028 European Championship, which will take place in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland. All four countries will take part in qualifying tournament, the draw for which will take place in Belfast next month, but two “safety net” places have been reserved in the event that some fail to make it through.
Fifa has yet to allocate the number of qualification places for each confederation for the expanded Women’s World Cup.
Next summer’s 32-team tournament in Brazil will feature 11 or 12 teams from Europe and six from Concacaf, the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation. Concacaf was given nine places at last summer’s 48-team men’s World Cup, six qualifiers plus the three hosts, with 16 teams qualifying from Europe.
A Fifa spokesperson said: “The slot allocation for the 2031 and 2035 editions of the Fifa Women’s World Cup will be confirmed in due course by the Fifa council.”
The UK government has set out its ambition for one million more girls to be involved in sport by the time of the 2035 tournament and for women and girls to have equal access to primetime slots at grassroots facilities by then.
It said that under news rules sports risked losing public funding if they did not create equal environments and allow men and women to share decision-making power.

In a diplomatic communication dated November 5, 2026, Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs informed the Ugandan E
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24 — Qatar has lifted precautionary travel restrictions imposed on travellers arriving from Uganda following the official declaration of the end of the Ebola outbreak.
In a diplomatic communication dated November 5, 2026, Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs informed the Ugandan Embassy in Doha that the restrictions had been lifted after Uganda recorded no new Ebola cases for more than 42 days.
Uganda officially declared the outbreak over on October 27, 2026, prompting the Qatari government to review the precautionary measures introduced in response to the health emergency.
The decision also allows Qatar to resume issuing all categories of entry visas to travellers from Uganda, subject to the country’s immigration procedures and requirements.
The restrictions had affected both travellers arriving from Uganda and foreign residents travelling from the East African country to Qatar.
The lifting of the measures restores normal visa processing for Ugandans seeking to travel to Qatar, while removing additional travel precautions imposed during the Ebola outbreak.

The military said it had lost contact with a small Cessna 208 c
items.text:
DR Congo says military aircraft missing as rebels claim to shoot down plane
- Published
The Democratic Republic of Congo military says it is searching for one of its aircraft, after rebels said they had shot down a warplane in the east.
The military said it had lost contact with a small Cessna 208 cargo plane on Sunday following "poor weather conditions". The fate of the plane and its crew remained uncertain, it added.
On the same day, the rebel Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) said it had shot down a warplane that was on a mission to bomb Minembwe in South Kivu province.
Four people were reportedly on board, including a Ugandan and a South African pilot, who is said to have been captured alive.
The BBC has not independently verified the rebels' claim.
It is also unclear whether the aircraft reported missing by the DR Congo military is the same one rebels say they shot down.
Uganda's military on Monday denied any involvement.
- What's the fighting in DR Congo all about? 
  - Published5 December 2025
- How former President Kabila became FRN rebel leader 
  - Published31 October
A statement attributed to army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba posted on X said: "UPDF had nothing to do with the aircraft that was shot down in Minembwe. We have penalized that company."
The statement did not identify the company or explain what penalty had been imposed.
Gen Kainerugaba later posted that "no Ugandan is allowed to work for mercenary companies in [DR Congo]".
Uganda's denial followed the circulation of a video apparently showing a man being questioned beside the plane's wreckage.
In the footage, the man identifies himself as Ugandan and claims he had been sent by the government. The BBC has not independently verified the video or established the man's identity.
He and the alleged South African pilot are said to be the only other survivors.
South African media outlet Mail & Guardian quoted an FRN spokesperson identifying the pilot as a South African and a "mercenary [who] has no link to the place that he was hired to destroy".
"Unfortunately, we have a multi-country conflict in the eastern DRC," deputy FRN spokesperson Oscar Balinda told the outlet.
In 2022, DR Congo's army blamed M23 rebels, who are now part of the FRN, of shooting down a UN helicopter in which eight people died. The rebels denied it.
The Congolese government has in the past used foreign mercenaries to fight the rebels.
In recent days, fighting between the FRN and the government has intensified with the rebel group accusing the government of targeting heavily populated areas.
The rebels control large areas of eastern DR Congo, including the major city of Goma, after major territorial advances last year.
Aid agencies say the violence is increasingly disrupting healthcare services.
Over the weekend, medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières said fighting in North Kivu had forced some of its teams to temporarily suspend outreach activities.
The fighting has also affected the response to the Ebola outbreak, with many health workers trapped, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The epicentre of the outbreak is in eastern DR Congo, which has been wracked by conflict for many decades, with some affected areas under rebel control.

In a statement on Tuesday, Gachagua said Methu had resumed duty af
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 24 – Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua has assigned Nyandarua Senator John Methu the responsibility of spearheading grassroots mobilisation and opening party offices across the country.
In a statement on Tuesday, Gachagua said Methu had resumed duty after a two-week break and had been briefed on the party’s upcoming activities.
He said the Senator, who is the party’s Secretary General-designate, would lead the nationwide opening of DCP offices and coordinate grassroots political mobilisation.
“My assurance is that, in December 2027, we will celebrate Christmas together and make up for the one we miss,” he said
Gachagua said the arrangement would allow him to concentrate on preparations for the party primaries ahead of the 2027 General Election.
He further announced that he and his team would largely forgo the Christmas holiday, except for December 25 and 26, citing the demands of their political activities.
“The task ahead, to liberate our country from agents of corruption and impunity, leaves us no room for luxury,” Gachagua said.
He expressed optimism that the team would celebrate Christmas together in December 2027.

items.title: DPP Urges Supreme Court to Uphold 20-Year Jail Terms for Ex-Venezuelan Embassy Official, Kenyan in Ambassador’s Murder
items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24 — The Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) has urged the Supreme Court to dismiss appeals filed by former Venezuelan Embassy First Secretary Dwight Sagaray and Kenyan national Ahmed Mujivane Omido, seeking to overturn their 20-year prison sentences for the murder of former Ve
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24 — The Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) has urged the Supreme Court to dismiss appeals filed by former Venezuelan Embassy First Secretary Dwight Sagaray and Kenyan national Ahmed Mujivane Omido, seeking to overturn their 20-year prison sentences for the murder of former Venezuelan Ambassador Olga Fonseca Jimenez.
The prosecution wants the apex court to uphold the convictions and sentences imposed on the two, arguing that they were supported by sufficient evidence, including compelling circumstantial evidence linking them to the murder.
The appeals challenge a Court of Appeal judgment delivered on March 7, 2025, which upheld their convictions and 20-year jail terms.
Appearing before a Supreme Court bench presided over by Justice Smokin Wanjala, the DPP maintained that the evidence presented during the trial sufficiently established the appellants’ involvement in the murder.
On Sagaray’s claim of diplomatic immunity, the prosecution argued that communication from Venezuelan authorities terminating his diplomatic mission and cancelling his diplomatic passport brought his diplomatic functions to an end.
It further submitted that any residual immunity could not shield him from prosecution for acts falling outside his official diplomatic functions.
The prosecution also dismissed suggestions that the convictions were founded merely on motive or association, arguing that the court relied on the cumulative weight of evidence, including a dispute over control of the Venezuelan Embassy, Sagaray’s relationship with Mohammed Ahmed Mohammed Hassan and events surrounding Fonseca’s killing.
In opposing Omido’s appeal, the DPP argued that his complaints concerning common intention and the handling of his alibi defence were without merit.
The prosecution told the court that Omido’s testimony amounted to a denial of participation in the murder rather than an alibi placing him elsewhere when the crime occurred.
The DPP consequently urged the Supreme Court to find that the appeals disclosed no constitutional violations, dismiss them with costs and uphold the 20-year sentences.
Sagaray and Omido were among four people convicted over the murder of Fonseca, who was killed at her residence in Runda, Nairobi, in July 2012.
The other two convicts were Alex Sifuna Wanyonyi and Moses Kiprotich Kalya.
The murder case attracted considerable attention because of Sagaray’s diplomatic position at the time and the subsequent legal dispute over whether he could invoke diplomatic immunity to avoid prosecution.
The Supreme Court is expected to deliver its judgment on notice.
